Call-stack walkthrough · Transformer.ipynb · a Transformer written from scratch in PyTorch

Inside a Transformer, one executed line at a time

This is the notebook's own model — 2 encoder layers, 2 decoder layers, 4 heads, 12,917 BPE tokens, 28,268,661 parameters — taken apart line by line. Each of the eighteen pages is a call stack: the frames are the lines Python actually runs, nested and ordered the way it runs them, and beside every frame sits the real tensor that line produced. Read a page top to bottom and you have read the execution.

Both of the notebook's training pairs travel through all eighteen together — a short sentence that has to be padded and a long one that sets the batch width — so at every line you can watch identical code treat the two differently, and see exactly where padding stops being harmless and who has to clean it up. Nothing here is illustrative. Shapes, masks, positional encodings, softmax rows, ReLU sparsity, LayerNorm statistics, dropout scaling and the cross-entropy loss are all computed from the notebook's own formulas and initialisers — and the numbers that can be checked against it do check: a vocabulary of 12,917 from 13,076 real BPE merges, and an untrained loss of 9.5737 against ln(12,917) = 9.4663 — the value a model that has learned nothing must produce, and the value this one produced when it was run.

d_model 512 num_heads 4 d_k 128 num_layers 2 d_ff 512 dropout 0.1 pad_idx 0 vocab 12,917 batch 2 × 7 optimiser Adam 1e-3
Sequence A · padded
"the dog sat on the floor" → "dog resting"
6 source tokens (1 <PAD> added) · 4 target tokens (3 <PAD> added)
Sequence B · sets the width
"the cat is sleeping on the sofa" → "the cat is sleeping peacefully"
7 source tokens · 7 target tokens · never padded
What’s new in v1.5 · 26 changes over 9 pages

v1.5 — real subwords, pre-norm layers, and half the parameters

Same two sentences, same 4 heads and 2 layers — and almost nothing else in common. The vocabulary falls from 12,917 to 26 because the word list leaves the BPE corpus, so words finally split into subwords: floor arrives as five symbols rather than one. The normalisation moves in front of every sub-layer, ReLU becomes GELU, the hidden layer quadruples, three vocabulary matrices collapse into one, and the parameter count halves to 14,728,218 — a figure computed here from the architecture and checked against the one the notebook prints.

8 of the 26 changes repair something the first eighteen pages already called a weakness. Step 1 said the tokenizer had no end-of-word marker so decode could not be exact; step 6 said weight tying was not used; step 7 said the <PAD> embedding was not zero; step 16 said this was post-norm, the older arrangement; step 17 said there was no warmup and no gradient clipping; step 18 said the batch kept generating after <EOS> and that the heatmap handed seaborn one label too many. Every one of those is fixed here. Each fix is drawn where it belongs: inside the step's own call stack, directly under the v1 line it replaces, so the line that ran and the line that replaced it are read one after the other.

vocabulary 26 merges 15 d_ff 2048 activation GELU norm pre-LN embeddings tied optimiser AdamW 5e-4 schedule warmup 20 smoothing 0.1 parameters 14,728,218
Sequence A · now the longer source
"the dog sat on the floor" → "dog resting"
11 source tokens (sets the width) · 8 target tokens (+8 <PAD>)
Sequence B · now the longer target
"the cat is sleeping on the sofa" → "the cat is sleeping peacefully"
10 source tokens (+1 <PAD>) · 16 target tokens (sets the width)
What’s new in v2 · the notebook walked cell by cell

v2 — a real 16k-token vocabulary, a KV cache, and beam search

The model itself barely moves: v2 keeps v1.5’s pre-norm layers, GELU, 2,048 hidden units and one tied embedding table. Almost everything around it is rebuilt. The tokenizer finally learns from the 50,000-word list — 16,000 merges in a few seconds, with a heap in place of the loop the notebook says took about 40 minutes — so the vocabulary grows from 26 to 16,111 and the parameter count to 22,979,823. Attention runs through PyTorch’s fused kernel; generation keeps a KV cache and feeds one token per step; and three ways of choosing words — greedy, sampling and beam search — are compared side by side. Training gains a DataLoader with padding per batch, warmup plus cosine decay, mixed precision, a validation pass, checkpoints and early stopping.

The notebook is organised as eleven code cells, and so is this walkthrough: one page per cell, top to bottom, numbered like the notebook’s own headings. Cells that only define things (the model, the tokenizer) are explained. Cells that run things carry the call stacks, and every frame names the cell its code lives in — cell 8’s training loop calls into cell 2’s model, so a stack visibly travels from cell to cell. Each v1.5 → v2 change is drawn where it happens, beside the line it replaced.

6 source tokens (+2 <PAD>) · 4 target tokens (+4 <PAD>)
Sequence B · sets both widths

v2.5 — rotary positions, RMSNorm, SwiGLU, top-p, EMA and BLEU, measured against v2

A Transformer reads a sentence and writes another one, a piece of a word at a time, by turning words into lists of numbers and doing arithmetic on them — arithmetic whose 22,979,823 settings are learned from examples. This walkthrough is written for readers who have never met one: every page opens with the idea in plain words, a comparison from everyday life, the new words it uses (tap one for its meaning), and a worked example with the page’s own numbers.

v2.5 is v2 with the improvements today’s large language models made standard: positions given by rotation (RoPE) instead of an added table, a leaner normaliser (RMSNorm), a gated feed-forward (SwiGLU), top-p sampling and a repetition penalty, weight decay only on weight matrices, an averaged copy of the weights (EMA), a BLEU score — and a beam search that no longer stops before its best answer has finished. Unlike the earlier versions, v2.5 was run here for real with PyTorch 2.8.0: it trained on its two sentence pairs in 15.6 seconds, and both answers came out right.

positions RoPE norm RMSNorm feed-forward SwiGLU 1,368 decoding greedy · top-k · top-p · beam 4 repetition penalty 1.2 weights kept EMA 0.999 scores exact match · BLEU parameters 22,979,823
The next level · the v3 notebook, written from v2.5, run for real and measured

v3 — eight techniques of today’s large models, on top of v2.5

v2.5 brought the model up to the standard the large language models of 2023 set: rotary positions, RMSNorm, a gated feed-forward, better ways to pick words. v3 takes the next step — what models of 2024 and 2025 do to run fast and cheap, and to change how they learn. Four of its eight changes are about speed and size: key/value heads shared between query heads (grouped-query attention), causal attention that lets PyTorch pick its built-in FlashAttention on a suitable GPU, speculative decoding and 8-bit weights. Four are about learning: QK-Norm with a soft cap on the scores, a mixture of experts, multi-token prediction and the Muon optimizer.

The v3 notebook is a new file, Transformer_V3.ipynb, written on the Desktop next to yours from v2.5’s code (your notebooks are only read). It was run here for real with PyTorch 2.8.0 in 59.9 seconds, both answers came out right, and every change was tested on its own code (check3.py, 15 checks).

Measured, honestly. On this small model and a CPU the speed and size changes work and keep the answers. The learning changes did not clearly beat v2.5 once v2.5 was given a larger learning rate: 96.5% exact on unseen reversals, the same as v3 — deep dive 26 has the whole experiment.

attention 4 query heads · 2 K/V heads QK-Norm + soft cap 30 feed-forward 4 experts · 2 per token extra head token after next decoding + speculative optimizers Muon + AdamW stored 8-bit option parameters 32,543,983 · 24,089,839 per token

From text to tensors

Words become integers, then the integers are forced into a rectangle. Both pages are call stacks over code that runs before the model is built.

STEP 01

Dataset → BPE tokenizer → token ids — one continuous trace

train() once, encode() four times5 changes in v1.5
What you’ll learn

How a sentence becomes a list of numbers the model can work with. You will see how a byte-pair-encoding (BPE) tokenizer learns its vocabulary by gluing together letters that often sit side by side, how it then cuts any sentence into those known pieces, how an end-of-word marker keeps track of where words stop, and why four special tokens — <PAD>, <SOS>, <EOS> and <UNK> — are given ids before anything else.

The big idea

A model can only do arithmetic, so text has to become numbers first. Think of inventing shorthand: you notice "t" and "h" appear next to each other all the time, so you give "th" its own symbol; then "th" and "e" keep appearing together, so "the" gets a symbol too. You keep going until no pair is common enough to be worth a new symbol. The symbols you end up with are the vocabulary, and a symbol's position in that list is its id. In this version the last letter of every word carries a marker, </w>, so a piece like "dog</w>" means "dog, and the word ends here". This version also learns only from the four sentences, so its vocabulary is tiny (26 entries) and many words stay split into several pieces.

A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers

Here is how the word "dog" becomes a single number, using the real merge list learned on this page:

  1. Start with its characters, the last one marked: d, o, g</w>.
  2. Merge #5 in the list glues "d" and "o" together, giving do, g</w>.
  3. Merge #6 glues "do" and "g</w>", giving dog</w>.
  4. Look the result up in the vocabulary: "dog</w>" is id 9.

To get there the tokenizer tried its merges in order, and two of its 15 merges changed "dog". Not every word is that lucky: sequence A, "the dog sat on the floor", comes out as 11 ids — 23, 9, 20, 6, 16, 23, 11, 14, 15, 15, 19 — because "sat" and "floor" never merged into single pieces.

What to look forThe green blocks show what this version changed: frame 2's corpus, frame 3's counting of each distinct word once, frame 5's </w> marker, and frame 20's cache. Frames 6 to 11 are the learning loop — it stops after only 15 merges. Frame 13 is the line that decides every id. Section B shows the final pieces and ids of all four sentences, and section D feeds in a word the tokenizer has never seen.

What you’ll learn

How a sentence becomes a list of numbers the model can work with. You will see how a byte-pair-encoding (BPE) tokenizer learns its vocabulary by gluing together letters that often sit side by side, how it then cuts any sentence into those known pieces, and why four special tokens — <PAD>, <SOS>, <EOS> and <UNK> — are given ids before anything else.

The big idea

A model can only do arithmetic, so text has to become numbers first. Think of inventing shorthand: you notice "t" and "h" appear next to each other all the time, so you give "th" its own symbol; then "th" and "e" keep appearing together, so "the" gets a symbol too. You keep going until no pair is common enough to be worth a new symbol. The symbols you end up with are the vocabulary, and a symbol's position in that list is its id. Writing a new sentence in shorthand is then easy: common words become one symbol, rare words become several.

A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers

Here is how the word "dog" becomes a single number, using the real merge list learned on this page:

  1. Start with its characters: d, o, g.
  2. Merge #73 in the list glues "o" and "g" together, giving d, og.
  3. Merge #1,693 glues "d" and "og", giving dog.
  4. Look the result up in the vocabulary: "dog" is id 3380.

To get there the tokenizer tried all 13,076 merges in order, and only two of them changed "dog". Every word of every sentence goes through the same list, so sequence A, "the dog sat on the floor", comes out as 6 ids: 11425, 3380, 10283, 8277, 11425, 4535.

What to look forFrames 6 to 11 are the learning loop: frame 7 lists the most common pairs on the first pass, and frame 10 is where the loop stops, after 13,076 merges. Frame 13 is the line that decides every id. Frame 20 rebuilds "dog" merge by merge. Section B shows the final tokens and ids of all four sentences, and section D feeds in a word the tokenizer has never seen.

STEP 02

Batching & padding

(2, 7) and (2, 7)unchanged in v1.5
What you’ll learn

How four sentences of different lengths become two neat rectangles of numbers — one for the inputs and one for the targets — and what the <PAD> tokens added along the way actually cost.

The big idea

Picture a bookshelf built for the tallest book: every shorter book leaves empty space above it. A tensor works the same way — every row has to be the same width — so each sentence shorter than the longest one gets filler tokens added to its end. The filler is <PAD>, id 0. It keeps the shapes tidy, but the model will still process those empty slots as if they were words unless something tells it not to, and that is exactly what the masks of the next three steps are for.In this version the sentences are counted in subword pieces, so the widths are larger than the word counts — and the padding lands on different sentences than in v1.

A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers

Here is the source side, using this page’s real sentences:

  1. Measure: sequence A’s source is 11 tokens long and sequence B’s is 10.
  2. Take the longest: max_src_len = 11.
  3. Pad the shorter one: sequence B gets <PAD> (id 0) added at the end until it is 11 long.
  4. Stack both rows into one tensor of shape (2, 11) — 2 sentences, 11 tokens each.

The targets are measured and padded separately. Their lengths are 8 and 16, so they become a (2, 16) tensor with 8 <PAD> tokens in it.

What to look forThe two tables at the top show where every <PAD> landed — the hatched cells are padding. Section A counts the cost: what share of each tensor is filler, and why attention, which compares every position with every other, wastes 21 of its 242 score cells.

The three mask builders

In the order the notebook defines them. Each page traces the function as one continuous call stack, with both sequences' real tensors at every frame.

STEP 03

make_padding_mask and src_mask — one continuous trace

built in one line, spent four frames deeper1 change in v1.5
What you’ll learn

What a padding mask is, how one short line of code builds it, and how it travels unused through the whole encoder until a single line uses it to stop every word from paying attention to <PAD> tokens.

The big idea

After step 2, some sentences end in filler. The model cannot tell filler from a real word by looking at the numbers, so it needs a separate note that says which positions are real. That note is the padding mask: one True or False per position — True for a real token, False for <PAD>. Think of it as a guest list at a door. It is written once, carried along, and only checked at the moment it matters: when every word decides which other words to listen to. In this version the padding lands on sequence B’s source, not sequence A’s.

A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers

Here are this page’s real source ids and the mask built from them:

  1. Sequence A’s ids: 23, 9, 20, 6, 16, 23, 11, 14, 15, 15, 19.
  2. Sequence B’s ids: 23, 8, 13, 21, 16, 23, 20, 15, 11, 5, 0.
  3. Compare every id with 0 (the <PAD> id). Sequence A becomes True True True True True True True True True True True; sequence B becomes True True True True True True True True True True False.
  4. Add two size-1 axes so the shape lines up with the attention scores: (2, 1, 1, 11).
  5. Later, every score in a False column is replaced with −3.4e38, so after softmax that position gets exactly 0 attention.

In total the mask is 22 True/False values, and they control 968 attention scores in every encoder layer.

What to look forFrames 2 and 3 build the mask. Frames 4 to 9 carry it along while the sentences become vectors and scores — frame 9 shows the <PAD> column still full of ordinary scores. Frame 10 is the single line that uses it: column 10 of sequence B is blocked in all 4 heads. The green block under frame 10 shows the safer mask value this version writes in. Sections B and C call the same function in two other places, and section E explains what each number of the shape (2, 1, 1, 11) means.

A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers

  1. Sequence A’s ids: 11425, 3380, 10283, 8277, 11425, 4535, 0.
  2. Sequence B’s ids: 11425, 1928, 6274, 10697, 8277, 11425, 10752.

STEP 04

make_causal_mask — hiding the future from the decoder

a number goes in, a triangle comes out1 change in v1.5
What you’ll learn

How the decoder is stopped from cheating during training. You will see a function that builds a triangle of True/False values from nothing but a length, why that triangle is the entire "no peeking at later words" rule, and how it is combined with the padding mask into the decoder’s final mask.

The big idea

Imagine a spelling test where the answer sheet is on the desk. To make the test fair, you cover every answer you have not reached yet. During training the decoder is shown the whole target sentence at once, so each position could simply read the word it is supposed to predict. The causal mask covers the future: position 0 may look only at itself, position 1 at positions 0 and 1, and so on. Drawn as a grid, the allowed cells form a triangle.%s

A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers

Here are the first four positions of sequence A’s decoder input, and what each one is allowed to look at:

  1. Position 0, "<SOS>", may look at: <SOS>.
  2. Position 1, "dog_", may look at: <SOS>, dog_.
  3. Position 2, "r", may look at: <SOS>, dog_, r.
  4. Position 3, "e", may look at: <SOS>, dog_, r, e.

Continue that pattern to all 15 positions and you get the full triangle: 120 of the 225 cells are allowed and 105 are blocked. Sequence A also ends in <PAD>, so combining the triangle with its padding mask blocks 28 more cells.

What to look forFrame 3 is the call — notice it receives only a number. Frames 4 to 7 build the triangle step by step: a square of ones, tril to cut off the upper half, then two extra axes. Frame 8 combines it with the padding mask, and frame 11 is where the blocked scores are finally overwritten. Frame 12 shows the result as a staircase: row 0 gives all of its attention to <SOS>.

What to look forFrame 3 is the call — notice it receives only a number. Frames 4 to 7 build the triangle step by step: a square of ones, tril to cut off the upper half, then two extra axes. Frame 8 combines it with the padding mask, and frame 11 is where the blocked scores are finally overwritten. Frame 12 shows the result as a staircase: row 0 gives all of its attention to <SOS>.

STEP 05

make_tgt_mask — padding and the future, in one tensor

two builders, one AND, then the decoder1 change in v1.5
What you’ll learn

How the decoder’s two rules — "ignore padding" and "do not look ahead" — are combined into a single mask with one AND, and how that one tensor is then used inside the decoder’s self-attention.

The big idea

Think of two stencils laid on top of each other. One stencil has holes only where real words are (the padding mask). The other has holes only for words that come earlier in the sentence (the causal triangle). Light gets through only where BOTH stencils have a hole. Combining two True/False grids with AND works exactly like that: a position stays visible only if both rules allow it. Doing it once, up front, means attention needs just one mask instead of two.%s

A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers

Take the last position of sequence A’s decoder input (the token "<PAD>"), and combine its two rules, one position at a time (T = allowed, F = blocked):

  1. Padding rule — is each position a real token? T T T T T T T T F F F F F F F
  2. Causal rule — is each position at or before this one? It is the last position, so every position is: T T T T T T T T T T T T T T T
  3. AND them: T T T T T T T T F F F F F F F. That row can look at 8 of the 15 positions.

Doing that for every position of both sentences gives the full mask: sequence A ends up with 92 open cells out of 225, and sequence B, which has no padding, with 120 — exactly the triangle.

What to look forFrame 1 shows the target being shifted for teacher forcing. Frames 3 and 4 build the two halves, and frame 5 is the AND. Frames 6 to 10 carry the combined mask into the decoder and produce the scores it will act on, and frame 11 is the one line that applies it. Frame 13 is where the decoder switches to the OTHER mask for cross-attention.

What you’ll learn

How the decoder’s two rules — "ignore padding" and "do not look ahead" — are combined into a single mask with one AND, and how that one tensor is then used inside the decoder’s self-attention.

The big idea

Think of two stencils laid on top of each other. One stencil has holes only where real words are (the padding mask). The other has holes only for words that come earlier in the sentence (the causal triangle). Light gets through only where BOTH stencils have a hole. Combining two True/False grids with AND works exactly like that: a position stays visible only if both rules allow it. Doing it once, up front, means attention needs just one mask instead of two.%s

A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers

Take the last position of sequence A’s decoder input (the token "<PAD>"), and combine its two rules, one position at a time (T = allowed, F = blocked):

  1. Padding rule — is each position a real token? T T T T F F
  2. Causal rule — is each position at or before this one? It is the last position, so every position is: T T T T T T
  3. AND them: T T T T F F. That row can look at 4 of the 6 positions.

Doing that for every position of both sentences gives the full mask: sequence A ends up with 18 open cells out of 36, and sequence B, which has no padding, with 21 — exactly the triangle.

What to look forFrame 1 shows the target being shifted for teacher forcing. Frames 3 and 4 build the two halves, and frame 5 is the AND. Frames 6 to 10 carry the combined mask into the decoder and produce the scores it will act on, and frame 11 is the one line that applies it. Frame 13 is where the decoder switches to the OTHER mask for cross-attention.

Building the encoder input

Random matrices, token vectors, and a sense of position.

STEP 06

init_weights — Xavier on every matrix

p.dim() > 15 changes in v1.5
What you’ll learn

How a brand-new model gets its starting numbers before it has seen any data: which weights are filled with Xavier random values, which are deliberately left alone, and where all 14.7 million parameters actually live.

The big idea

A model starts out knowing nothing, but its weights cannot all start at zero — every unit would compute the same thing and learn the same thing. So they start as small random numbers. The size of that randomness matters: think of passing a message down a long line of people, where each one either slightly shouts or slightly whispers it. Too loud and it becomes a roar; too quiet and it fades away. Xavier initialisation picks the spread for each weight matrix from its number of inputs and outputs, so the signal keeps roughly the same size as it passes through layer after layer. In this version the random values are drawn once per parameter, the encoder and decoder share one embedding table, and the <PAD> row is set to zero afterwards.

A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers

Here is the spread Xavier chooses for two of this model’s matrices:

  1. An attention matrix maps 512 numbers to 512, so fan_in + fan_out = 1024.
  2. Its values are drawn evenly between −a and +a, with a = sqrt(6 / 1024) = 0.0765.
  3. The embedding table has 26 rows and 512 columns, so fan_in + fan_out = 538 and a = sqrt(6 / 538) = 0.1056.
  4. Biases are not matrices, so they are skipped and keep PyTorch’s default range, ±0.0442.

Because this vocabulary is so small, the embedding’s spread is wider than the attention matrices’ — the opposite of v1, where 12,917 rows made it very narrow.

What to look forSection A lists every kind of parameter and what the initialiser does to it — the "dim" column is the test that decides. The small grid shows real random values from one attention matrix, all inside ±0.0765. Section B counts exactly where the parameters are, and why the vocabulary is almost none of it.

What you’ll learn

  3. The embedding table has 12,917 rows and 512 columns, so fan_in + fan_out = 13429 and a = sqrt(6 / 13429) = 0.0211.

A bigger vocabulary means a narrower spread, which is why step 7 has to multiply the embeddings by sqrt(512).

What to look forSection A lists every kind of parameter and what the initialiser does to it — the "dim" column is the test that decides. The small grid shows real random values from one attention matrix, all inside ±0.0765. Section B counts exactly where the parameters are, and why 70% of them are vocabulary tables.

STEP 07

Embedding lookup × √d_model

(2, 7, 512)2 changes in v1.5
What you’ll learn

How an integer id turns into a list of 512 numbers the model can reason with, why every list is then multiplied by sqrt(512), and what happens to the <PAD> token along the way.

The big idea

An id is just a row number. The embedding table is a big grid with one row for every token in the vocabulary, and each row is a list of 512 numbers. Looking up a token means copying its row — nothing more. The magic is that these numbers are learned: during training the model nudges them so that tokens used in similar ways get similar rows, like placing similar words near each other on a map with 512 directions instead of two. In this version the encoder and decoder share one small table of 26 rows, and the <PAD> row is all zeros.

A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers

Here is the second token of sequence A, using this page’s real numbers:

  1. The token "dog_" has id 9.
  2. Look up row 9 of the 26 × 512 table. Its first three numbers are -0.0011, -0.0773 and 0.0098 (512 in total).
  3. Multiply every number by sqrt(512) = 22.627: -0.0259, -1.7485, 0.2223, …
  4. Do this for every token and the (2, 11) batch of ids becomes a (2, 11, 512) batch of vectors.

The table started with random values of at most ±0.1056. Multiplying by sqrt(512) makes the word signal big enough not to be drowned out by the position signal added in step 8.

What to look forThe two tables at the top show the raw rows and the same rows after the multiplication, for both sentences — the <PAD> row is marked. Section A measures why sqrt(512) is needed: it compares the size of a word vector with the size of the position signal that step 8 adds on top.

Here is the second token of sequence A, using this page’s real numbers:

  1. The token "dog" has id 3380.

STEP 08

PositionalEncoding — built once, added on every pass

__init__ → encode → forward → dropoutunchanged in v1.5
What you’ll learn

How a Transformer learns the ORDER of words even though attention itself cannot see order: a fixed table of sine and cosine waves, one row per position, added to every word vector.

The big idea

Attention treats a sentence like a bag of words — shuffle them and it gets the same result. To fix that, each position gets its own "address" made of waves. Picture a row of clocks with hands turning at different speeds: the fast hand tells you exactly where you are among your neighbours, the slow hands tell you roughly where you are in a long text. Read all the hands together and every position has a unique pattern. That pattern is simply added onto each word’s vector, so the vector now carries both "which word" and "where it is".%s

A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers

Here is how the first four numbers of position 3’s address are calculated:

  1. Column 0 uses the fastest wave, frequency 1.0000: sin(3 × 1.0000) = 0.141.
  2. Column 1 uses the same frequency with cosine: cos(3 × 1.0000) = -0.990.
  3. Columns 2 and 3 use a slightly slower wave, frequency 0.9647: sin gives 0.245 and cos gives -0.970.
  4. The pattern continues for all 512 columns, with the waves getting slower and slower towards the right.

Position 3’s address is then added to whatever word sits at position 3. That is how "the_" at position 0 and "the_" at position 5 end up with different vectors, even though they are the same word.

What to look forFrames 1 to 6 build the table once, when the model is created; frames 7 to 12 use it on every batch. Frame 5 is the line that actually calculates every sine and cosine. Frame 9 adds the table to the word vectors. Section A shows the table itself — notice the left columns changing quickly and the right columns barely moving.

Inside multi-head attention

One tensor, three roles, four heads, one masked softmax.

STEP 09

MultiHeadAttention.forward — every line of the class

project → split → score → mask → softmax → V → W_o1 change in v1.5
What you’ll learn

The whole multi-head attention class from start to finish: what it owns, how it turns each word into a query, a key and a value, why it splits them into four heads, and how one class serves three different jobs in the model.

The big idea

Imagine four readers going through the same sentence, each looking for something different — one tracks who is doing what, another which words describe which, and so on. Each reader decides, for every word, which other words matter to it, and writes down a summary. At the end the four summaries are combined into one. That is multi-head attention: the four readers are the four heads, and "deciding which words matter" is the score-and-average step from step 11. The same class is reused to read the source, to read the output written so far, and to connect the two.%s

A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers

Here is the journey of one sentence through the class, with this page’s real shapes:

  1. Start with 11 word vectors of 512 numbers each: (11, 512).
  2. W_q, W_k and W_v turn them into queries, keys and values — still (11, 512) each.
  3. Cut each into 4 heads of 128 numbers: (4, 11, 128).
  4. In each head, score every word against every word: a 11 × 11 table, 121 scores.
  5. Turn scores into shares, take the weighted average of the values, glue the 4 heads back into 512 numbers, and mix them with W_o: (11, 512) again.

The shape that comes out is the shape that went in — which is what lets the layer add the result back onto its input. The class holds 1,050,624 parameters, and this model uses six copies of it.

What to look forFrames 1 and 2 show what the class owns. Frame 4 creates Q, K and V and splits them into heads; frame 5 is the table of scores; frame 6 is where every mask ends up. Frames 7 to 12 turn scores into the new word vectors. Frame 14 is the same class used for cross-attention in the decoder, and section B compares all three uses.

STEP 10

view + transpose — where the 4 heads come from

no parameters, no arithmetic, no copiesunchanged in v1.5
What you’ll learn

Where the four attention "heads" actually come from — two reshaping calls, view and transpose — and why creating them costs no extra parameters and copies no data.

The big idea

Picture a long row of 512 boxes. Draw lines after every 128 boxes and you now have 4 groups — without moving a single box. That is what view() does: it changes how the numbers are read, not the numbers. transpose() then swaps two axes so the groups line up the way matrix multiplication needs. Each group is a head, and each head runs attention on its own slice. Because the boxes never moved, four heads cost exactly the same as one wide attention.%s

A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers

Here is what happens to one token, "dog_", from sequence A:

  1. After W_q it is one row of 512 numbers.
  2. view(batch, −1, 4, 128) reads that row as 4 groups: numbers 0–127 are head 0, 128–255 are head 1, 256–383 are head 2, 384–511 are head 3.
  3. transpose(1, 2) swaps the token and head axes, so each head now holds a full table of 11 tokens × 128 numbers.
  4. At the end, transpose and view run in reverse (with contiguous() in between) to glue the 4 groups of 128 back into one row of 512.

Every number you see for "dog_" in frame 3 is exactly the same number you see in frame 4 — only the way they are grouped has changed.

What to look forFrame 3 lays one token’s 512 numbers out as 4 heads; frame 4 swaps the axes. Frame 7 shows why the swap was needed for matmul. Frame 11 is the only line that really copies data. Section B lists the stride at every stage — the proof that nothing else moved.

STEP 11

Scaled dot-product attention — one number at a time

matmul → ÷ √d_k → mask → softmax → dropout1 change in v1.5
What you’ll learn

How a word looks at the other words in its sentence. By the end of this step you will know what Q, K and V are, why every word is compared with every other word, what the "scaled" in scaled dot-product attention is for, and how padding is kept out of the result — including the safer mask value this version uses.

The big idea

Imagine a room where everyone asks one question and everyone wears a name badge. Each person compares their question with every badge, decides how much each person is worth listening to, and then takes a mix of what those people say — more from the relevant ones, less from the rest. That is attention. A word's question is its query (Q), its badge is its key (K), and what it says when someone listens is its value (V). The code makes all the comparisons at once with one matrix multiplication, turns them into shares that add up to 1 with softmax, and uses those shares to blend the values. One thing is different in this version: the "words" are subword pieces like the_ and s, where the _ marks the end of a word (step 1 shows where they come from).

A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers

Take the first piece of sequence A, "the_", and pretend the sentence were only "the_ dog_ s". These are the real numbers from head 0 of this page:

  1. Compare. The dot products of its query with the three keys are 10.59, -0.79 and -1.80. Bigger means "more relevant" — and a negative score means "points away".
  2. Scale. Divide each by √128 ≈ 11.31: 0.936, -0.069 and -0.159.
  3. Softmax, part one. Raise e to each score: 2.550, 0.933 and 0.853. Their total is 4.336. Note that e to a negative number is still positive, just smaller than 1.
  4. Softmax, part two. Divide each by that total: 0.588, 0.215 and 0.197. These are shares: allowing for rounding, they add up to 1.
  5. Blend. The new "the_" is made of 58.8% of the value of "the_", 21.5% of the value of "dog_" and 19.7% of the value of "s".

The real page does exactly this for all 11 pieces of both sentences at once, in four heads, using one matrix multiplication instead of a loop.

What to look forFrame 3 is the whole table of comparisons before scaling — one row per piece asking, one column per piece being asked. The green block under frame 5 is where padding is blocked: column 10 of sequence B becomes −3.4e38, written with torch.finfo so it stays safe in any precision; the v1 line above it shows what it replaced. Frame 6 is the moment scores become shares, and every row adds up to exactly 1.000. Section B works one comparison out by hand, Section C opens softmax up, and Section D shows that without the scaling one key would get about 10 trillion times the share of another.

The real page does exactly this for all 7 words of both sentences at once, in four heads, using one matrix multiplication instead of a loop.

What to look forFrame 3 is the whole table of comparisons before scaling — one row per word asking, one column per word being asked. STEP 12

context and W_o — how a word is rebuilt

matmul → merge → W_ounchanged in v1.5
What you’ll learn

How the shares from step 11 are actually used. By the end of this step you will know how each word is rebuilt as a weighted average of the other words’ values, how the four heads are put back together, why one more matrix, W_o, is needed so the heads can share what they found, and what the "residual connection" adds — including why, in this version, no LayerNorm follows it.

The big idea

Think of writing a summary from several sources. Step 11 decided how much to trust each source — say 50% this one, 30% that one, 20% the third. This step actually writes the summary: it takes 50% of the first source’s content, 30% of the second’s and 20% of the third’s, and adds them up. In the code the "content" is V, the value vectors, and one call to torch.matmul does this for every word at once. Each of the 4 heads writes its own summary with its own shares, so at the end the four summaries are laid side by side and passed through W_o, a learned matrix that blends them into one. Last, the summary is added back onto the original word, so the word is corrected rather than replaced. This version normalises BEFORE attention (pre-norm), so that addition is left exactly as it is.

A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers

One real number from this page: number 0 of the piece "cat_" in sequence B, head 0. Every piece it listens to contributes weight × value:

  1. "o" (position 7): 0.264 × +1.038 = +0.274. The biggest contribution.
  2. "f" (position 8): 0.131 × +1.203 = +0.158.
  3. "cat_" (position 1): 0.056 × -0.825 = -0.046. A negative value pulls the result down, even with a positive weight.
  4. The other 8 pieces add -0.065 between them. Three of those add exactly 0: <PAD>, which the mask blocked, and "on_" and "a_", whose links dropout cut at random.
  5. Add everything up: +0.321, allowing for rounding. That is the new number 0 of "cat_" — you can find it in frame 3, and Section B shows every multiplication.

The same 11 weights are reused for all 128 numbers of the piece, and the whole calculation runs for every piece, every head and both sentences in a single torch.matmul.

What to look forFrame 3 is the rebuilding — compare its rows with the value rows in frame 2. Frame 4 only rearranges numbers: the 4 heads side by side, with columns 0–127 still belonging to head 0 alone. Frame 5 is where the heads mix. Frame 6 only adds the result back onto x — the LayerNorm already ran before attention. Section B does one weighted average by hand; Section C shows all 4 heads contributing to one number that W_o produced, with head 2 contributing the most.

What to look forFrame 3 is the rebuilding — compare its rows with the value rows in frame 2. Frame 6 adds the result back onto x and applies LayerNorm. Section B does one weighted average by hand; Section C shows all 4 heads contributing to one number that W_o produced, with head 0 contributing the most.

Closing the encoder block

Per-token thinking, then residual and normalisation, twice, stacked twice.

STEP 13

PositionwiseFeedForward — the half that never looks sideways

fc1 → ReLU → dropout → fc22 changes in v1.5
What you’ll learn

What the feed-forward block does, and why a Transformer needs it next to attention. By the end of this step you will know what "position-wise" means, what hidden units are, why a non-linear function is essential, and why this version uses GELU and a hidden layer four times wider than v1.

The big idea

Attention is a meeting: words share information. The feed-forward block is the desk work afterwards: each word goes back to its own desk and processes what it collected, alone. It does that with two matrices. The first spreads the word’s 512 numbers across 2,048 "hidden units" — little detectors, each asking "does this word look like my pattern?". GELU then turns the detectors that said yes up and the ones that said no down — not to exactly zero like ReLU, but to small negative values, so nothing is thrown away completely. The second matrix combines the detectors back into 512 numbers. Every word goes through the very same desk, but because different detectors fire for different words, each word is effectively processed differently.

A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers

Take the piece "dog_" in sequence A and look at its first 6 hidden units:

  1. fc1 gives: -0.86, -0.88, +0.03, -0.16, -0.54, -0.16.
  2. GELU keeps positive values (shrinking small ones a little) and turns each negative one into a small negative number: -0.17, -0.17, +0.02, -0.07, -0.16, -0.07. Nothing becomes exactly 0.
  3. Across all 2,048 hidden units of "dog_", 995 came out of fc1 negative. Under ReLU all 995 would be 0; after GELU only 44 are within 0.01 of zero.
  4. The next piece, "g", has 1014 negative units, and only 555 of them are the same ones as for "dog_". Each piece leans on a different part of the block.
  5. Dropout then zeroes about 1 in 10 at random (training only), and fc2 folds the 2,048 hidden units back into 512 numbers.

That is the whole block: 2,099,712 parameters, run on every piece of both sentences at once — and no piece ever sees another.

What to look forFrame 1 is paired with the change to d_ff: 512 hidden units became 2,048. Frame 2 shows the input already normalised by norm2 — this version normalises first (pre-norm). Frame 4 is paired with the switch from ReLU to GELU: the v1 half shows ReLU’s flat zeros, the v1.5 half compares the two functions and then shows this model’s real hidden layer after GELU. Section B counts how few units GELU leaves near zero: between 38 and 60 of 2,048.

What you’ll learn

What the feed-forward block does, and why a Transformer needs it next to attention. By the end of this step you will know what "position-wise" means, what hidden units are, why a non-linear function like ReLU is essential, and how each word ends up using a different part of the same block.

The big idea

Attention is a meeting: words share information. The feed-forward block is the desk work afterwards: each word goes back to its own desk and processes what it collected, alone. It does that with two matrices. The first turns the word’s 512 numbers into 512 "hidden units" — little detectors, each asking "does this word look like my pattern?". ReLU then keeps only the detectors that said yes (positive) and silences the rest. The second matrix combines the surviving detectors back into 512 numbers. Every word goes through the very same desk, but because different detectors fire for different words, each word is effectively processed differently.

A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers

Take the word "dog" in sequence A and look at its first 6 hidden units:

  1. fc1 gives: -0.69, +0.36, -1.35, +0.12, +2.21, -2.10.
  2. ReLU keeps the positive values and turns every negative one into 0: 0, +0.36, 0, +0.12, +2.21, 0.
  3. Across all 512 hidden units of "dog", 270 came out of fc1 negative, and ReLU turned all 270 into exactly 0 — about half.
  4. The next word, "g", switches off 276 units, but only 224 of them are the same ones as for "dog". Each word uses a different part of the block.
  5. Dropout then zeroes about 1 in 10 of the rest at random (training only), and fc2 folds the 512 hidden units back into 512 numbers.

That is the whole block: 525,312 parameters, run on every word of both sentences at once — and no word ever sees another.

What to look forFrame 3 is the hidden layer straight out of fc1 — notice how many values are negative. Frame 4 is ReLU: every one of them becomes a flat 0.000. Frame 5 strikes through the units dropout removed. Frame 7 adds the result back to x and normalises it, which finishes one encoder layer. Section B counts the switched-off units for every word: between 252 and 276 of 512.

STEP 14

EncoderLayer — the wrapper that makes the stack possible

residual + LayerNorm, twice2 changes in v1.5
What you’ll learn

How one encoder layer is put together, and why this version moves the LayerNorm. By the end of this step you will know what the residual connection is, what LayerNorm does to a word’s numbers, what "pre-norm" means, and why the encoder now ends with one extra LayerNorm called enc_norm.

The big idea

Think of editing a document. A bad way is to ask each editor to retype the whole document from scratch — any mistake loses the original. A good way is to let each editor suggest changes that get applied on top of the text. That is the residual connection: attention and the feed-forward block only propose a change, and the change is ADDED to the word. LayerNorm rescales a word’s 512 numbers to average 0 and spread 1. In this version (pre-norm) the editors read a tidied-up COPY of the word — norm(x) — while the change is added to the original x: x + change(norm(x)). The original text is never rescaled on the way, which makes very deep stacks much easier to train. Because nothing rescales x inside the layers, one LayerNorm is added at the very end.

A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers

Follow the piece "dog_" of sequence A through the encoder, measuring the length of its 512-number vector at each point:

  1. It enters layer 0 with length 36.7.
  2. norm1 makes a copy for attention to read. The copy has length √512 ≈ 22.6, but x itself is left alone.
  3. Attention’s proposed change, after dropout, has length 13.3. Added to x, the new x has length 37.9 — mostly the original word, nudged.
  4. The feed-forward half adds its own change: 40.9 after layer 0, and 44.7 after layer 1. x keeps growing, because nothing rescales it.
  5. enc_norm, the new final LayerNorm, brings it back to length 22.6. That is enc_out.

Across the batch, the input is 1.51× to 3.17× longer than attention’s proposed change, so every layer only nudges each word.

What to look forFrame 2 is the new first line, h = norm1(x): a normalised copy for attention to read. Frame 5 is paired with the v1 line it replaces — v1 normalised x itself after the addition; v1.5 only adds. The last frame is paired with the new enc_norm that closes the encoder. Section B does one LayerNorm by hand on the copy norm1 makes; Section C compares the lengths of the two vectors being added.

What you’ll learn

How one encoder layer is put together. By the end of this step you will know what the residual connection is and why every sub-layer adds its answer to its input, what LayerNorm does to a word’s numbers, and why these two small pieces are what make it possible to stack layers at all.

The big idea

Think of editing a document. A bad way is to ask each editor to retype the whole document from scratch — any mistake loses the original. A good way is to let each editor suggest changes that get applied on top of the text. That is the residual connection: attention and the feed-forward block only propose a change, and the change is ADDED to the word they were given (x + change). After each addition, LayerNorm rescales the word’s 512 numbers so they have average 0 and spread 1 — like setting the volume back to a standard level — so the next part always receives input of the same size. In this version the LayerNorm comes after the addition: norm(x + change). That arrangement is called post-norm.

A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers

Follow the word "dog" of sequence A through the attention half of encoder layer 0, measuring the length of its 512-number vector at each point:

  1. It enters the layer with length 18.3.
  2. Attention proposes a change; after dropout that change has length 17.6 — about as big as the word itself, because the model is untrained.
  3. The change is added: x + change has length 25.3.
  4. norm1 rescales it: mean 0.5481 and standard deviation 0.9760 become 0 and 1, so the length becomes √512 = 22.6.
  5. The feed-forward half does the same thing again, and after both layers the word still has length 22.6 — LayerNorm keeps it there.

Across the batch, the input is only 1.02× to 1.20× longer than attention’s proposed change, so each sum is a real mix of the two.

What to look forFrame 3 thins attention’s proposal with dropout. Frame 4 is the residual addition — the "short path". Frame 5 is norm1, where every row gets mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Frames 6 and 7 wrap the feed-forward block the same way, and frame 8 runs the whole layer 2 times to produce enc_out. Section B does one LayerNorm by hand; Section C compares the lengths of the two vectors being added.

Decoder, output and generation

Shifted targets, a rectangular attention matrix, and finally words.

STEP 15

Teacher forcing — training all 6 positions in one pass

tgt[:, :-1] and tgt[:, 1:]1 change in v1.5
What you’ll learn

How the decoder is trained on a whole sentence in one go, even though it writes one token at a time when it is used. By the end of this step you will know what "shifting the target by one" means, why the causal mask is essential for it, and what teacher forcing gives up.

The big idea

Imagine teaching someone to continue a sentence. You could let them write the whole thing and only correct them at the end — slow, and one early slip ruins the rest. Or you could cover the sentence with a card, slide it one word to the right at a time, and at each step ask "what comes next?" — always showing them the CORRECT words so far. Teacher forcing is the second way, done for every position at once. The target is shifted by one so that each position’s answer is the next token, and the causal mask plays the part of the card: no position can see its own answer, or anything after it.

A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers

The target for sequence A, and the two slices made from it. In this version the word "resting" is split into pieces, so there are more positions:

  1. The whole target: <SOS> dog_ r e s t ing_ <EOS> + <PAD> × 8.
  2. decoder_input = tgt[:, :-1] drops the last token: <SOS> dog_ r e s t ing_ <EOS> + <PAD> × 7.
  3. expected = tgt[:, 1:] drops the first token: dog_ r e s t ing_ <EOS> + <PAD> × 8.
  4. Line them up by position. Position 0 reads "<SOS>" and must produce "dog_". Position 1 reads "dog_" (and everything before it) and must produce "r". Position 2 must produce "e".
  5. The mask hides everything to the right of each position — 105 of the 225 cells, plus padding. 8 of the 15 positions only have <PAD> to predict, and the loss ignores them.

All 15 predictions come out of a single forward pass. That is teacher forcing.

What to look forFrame 1 is the slice — read each column downwards. Frame 2 is the 15 × 15 mask: 1 = allowed, plain 0 = future, hatched 0 = padding. Frames 5 to 7 follow head 0 of the decoder’s self-attention: raw scores, then blocked cells, then shares that add up to 1 over each row’s own past. Frame 8 is paired with the pre-norm change for the decoder: all three sub-layers now read a normalised copy of x. Section B turns sequence A into 15 prediction problems; Section C compares training with generation.

The big idea

Imagine teaching someone to continue a sentence. You could let them write the whole thing and only correct them at the end — slow, and one early slip ruins the rest. Or you could cover the sentence with a card, slide it one word to the right at a time, and at each step ask "what comes next?" — always showing them the CORRECT words so far. Teacher forcing is the second way, done for every position at once. The target is shifted by one so that each position’s answer is the next token, and the causal mask plays the part of the card: no position can see its own answer, or anything after it.

A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers

The target for sequence A, and the two slices made from it:

  1. The whole target: <SOS> dog resting <EOS> + <PAD> × 3.
  2. decoder_input = tgt[:, :-1] drops the last token: <SOS> dog resting <EOS> + <PAD> × 2.
  3. expected = tgt[:, 1:] drops the first token: dog resting <EOS> + <PAD> × 3.
  4. Line them up by position. Position 0 reads "<SOS>" and must produce "dog". Position 1 reads "dog" (and everything before it) and must produce "resting". Position 2 must produce "<EOS>".
  5. The mask hides everything to the right of each position — 15 of the 36 cells, plus padding. 3 of the 6 positions only have <PAD> to predict, and the loss ignores them.

All 6 predictions come out of a single forward pass. That is teacher forcing.

What to look forFrame 1 is the slice — read each column downwards. Frame 2 is the 6 × 6 mask: 1 = allowed, plain 0 = future, hatched 0 = padding. Frames 5 to 7 follow head 0 of the decoder’s self-attention: raw scores, then blocked cells, then shares that add up to 1 over each row’s own past. Section B turns sequence A into 6 prediction problems; Section C compares training with generation.

STEP 16

Cross-attention — where the summary reads the article

q from target, k and v from source1 change in v1.5
What you’ll learn

How the decoder reads the source sentence. By the end of this step you will know what cross-attention is, why its queries and keys come from different sentences, why its score table is a rectangle rather than a square, and why it sits in the middle of every decoder layer.

The big idea

Think of a translator. First they read the whole source sentence carefully — that is the encoder, and its notes are enc_out. Then they start writing. Before writing each word they glance back at the source and ask "which part of the original matters for the word I am about to write?" That glance is cross-attention. It is the same attention you met in steps 9 to 12, with one change: the questions (queries) come from what the decoder has written so far, while the labels (keys) and contents (values) come from the source sentence. Because the two sentences have different lengths, the table of scores is a rectangle, and because the source already exists in full, no causal mask is needed — every position may look at every source word.

A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers

The shapes, for sequence A, and one real row of shares:

  1. The source sentence has 11 pieces: the_ dog_ s at_ on_ the_ f l o o r_.
  2. The decoder is writing 15 positions, so there are 15 queries — each made from norm2(x), a normalised copy of what has been written so far.
  3. Every query is compared with every source key, giving a 15 × 11 table of scores — 15 rows, 11 columns.
  4. Softmax turns each row into shares. Position 0 (reading <SOS>) splits its attention over the source like this: 0.04, 0.09, 0.15, 0.03, 0.24, 0.02, 0.18, 0.13, 0.02, 0.01, 0.08. Together they add up to 1.
  5. In the last decoder layer, averaged over the 4 heads, position 1 — reading "dog_", about to produce "r" — looks most at "the_" (0.141).

A perfectly even row would give every source piece 0.091. This model is untrained, so its rows are still fairly flat; training turns them into sharp peaks.

What to look forFrames 2 and 3 are the key moment: 15 query rows from the target, but 11 key rows from the source. Frame 4 is the rectangular 15 × 11 score table. Frame 5 applies the same src_mask as the encoder — and no causal mask. Frame 6 is the table the step-18 heatmap draws. Frame 9 is paired with the pre-norm change for the decoder. Section B reads the table row by row, Section C compares the three attention blocks, and Section D shows a whole decoder layer.

A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers

The shapes, for sequence A, and one real row of shares:

  1. The source sentence has 7 positions: the dog sat on the floor (plus padding).
  2. The decoder is writing 6 positions, so there are 6 queries.
  3. Every query is compared with every source key, giving a 6 × 7 table of scores — 6 rows, 7 columns.
  4. Softmax turns each row into shares. Position 0 (reading <SOS>) splits its attention over the source like this: 0.08, 0.05, 0.14, 0.10, 0.37, 0.26. Together they add up to 1.
  5. In the last decoder layer, averaged over the 4 heads, position 1 — reading "dog", about to produce "resting" — looks most at "the" (0.249).

STEP 17

The output head and the loss — 512 numbers to one scalar

linear → reshape → cross-entropy → backward7 changes in v1.5
What you’ll learn

How the model is graded and how it learns from the grade. By the end of this step you will know what logits are, what cross-entropy loss measures, why padded positions are ignored, and what this version adds: a tied output head, label smoothing, gradient clipping, AdamW and a learning-rate schedule.

The big idea

Think of a multiple-choice exam with one question per position and one answer option for every token in the vocabulary. The output head fills in a score for every option. Softmax turns those scores into probabilities that add up to 1. Cross-entropy then grades each answer by looking only at the probability given to the CORRECT option: confident and right costs almost nothing, confident and wrong costs a lot (the cost is −log of that probability). Positions whose correct answer is padding are not graded at all. The grades are averaged into one number, the loss, and backward() works out how every parameter should move to make that number smaller.

A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers

Sequence A, position 0: the decoder reads "<SOS>" and must produce "dog_". On this untrained model:

  1. The output head gives 26 scores, one per token. Here it is tied to the embedding table, so each score measures how closely the position’s vector matches that token’s embedding.
  2. Before training, each position’s vector still looks mostly like the token it is READING, so the top score goes to "<SOS>" itself. "dog_" gets odds of about 21 million to one against.
  3. The loss for this position is −log p = 16.8755 — far more than an even guess, which would cost ln(26) = 3.2581.
  4. The same is done for all 30 positions; 8 have <PAD> as the answer and are dropped, leaving 22. At all 22 of them the favourite is the token being read.
  5. Their average is 17.9115; with label smoothing mixed in, 17.9342. The notebook’s real run started at 18.6929, so this is what an untrained tied model really does.

Training fixes the copying quickly. After 200 epochs the loss settles at 0.6709, just above 0.6261 — the lowest value label smoothing allows.

What to look forFrame 1 is paired with the tied output head and the new dec_norm. Frames 4 to 7 open CrossEntropyLoss up into its steps; frame 7 is paired with label smoothing and shows the loss this model really scores. Frame 8 (backward) is paired with gradient clipping and the new progress printout, and frame 9 with AdamW and the learning-rate schedule. Sections B to D score one position by hand, list all 30 rows, and review the training loop.

What you’ll learn

How the model is graded and how it learns from the grade. By the end of this step you will know what logits are, what cross-entropy loss measures, why padded positions are ignored, what loss.backward() and optimizer.step() do, and what the training loop leaves out.

The big idea

Think of a multiple-choice exam with one question per position and one answer option for every token in the vocabulary. The output head fills in a score for every option. Softmax turns those scores into probabilities that add up to 1. Cross-entropy then grades each answer by looking only at the probability given to the CORRECT option: confident and right costs almost nothing, confident and wrong costs a lot (the cost is −log of that probability). Positions whose correct answer is padding are not graded at all. The grades are averaged into one number, the loss, and backward() works out how every parameter should move to make that number smaller.

A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers

Sequence A, position 0: the decoder reads "<SOS>" and must produce "dog". On this untrained model:

  1. The output head gives 12,917 scores, one per word in the vocabulary.
  2. Softmax gives "dog" a probability of 0.000063 — odds of about 15,810 to one against. A completely even guess would give each word 0.0001.
  3. The loss for this position is −log(0.000063) = 9.6684.
  4. The same is done for all 12 positions; 3 of them have <PAD> as the answer and are dropped, leaving 9.
  5. Their average, 9.5737, is the loss. An even guess would score ln(12,917) = 9.4663, and the notebook’s real run started at 9.465688 — so an untrained model lands right where it should.

Training repeats this 100 times. The run ended at a loss of 0.000031: with 28,268,661 parameters and only 900 graded predictions, the model simply memorises its two sentences.

What to look forFrame 1 is the output head, the largest matrix in the model. Frames 2 and 3 flatten the batch. Frames 4 to 7 open CrossEntropyLoss up into its four steps: log-softmax, pick the correct token, drop the padding, average. Section B scores position 0 by hand, Section C lists all 12 rows, and Section D looks at what the training loop does and does not include.

STEP 18

generate() — the loop that writes the summary

one token per pass5 changes in v1.5
What you’ll learn

How the trained model actually writes an output. By the end of this step you will know why generation runs one token at a time, what torch.no_grad() and model.eval() switch off, how the loop grows the output for a whole batch, how this version handles a sentence that finishes early, and what the attention heatmap shows.

The big idea

Think of writing a sentence with a friend who can only add one word at a time. They read the source sentence once and keep their notes (the encoder output). Then they write the first word, read everything written so far, write the next word, read again, and so on — until they write "the end" (<EOS>). That is generation. It uses exactly the same weights as training, but instead of being handed the correct previous word, the model has to use its OWN previous word. At each step the decoder produces a score for every token, and the loop simply takes the highest one (greedy decoding) and appends it.

A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers

Generating both sentences in one batch, with max_len = 15:

  1. The encoder runs once for both sources. Its output, enc_out, is reused at every step.
  2. Both rows start with <SOS>. At each step every row gets its highest-scoring token appended.
  3. Sequence A writes <SOS> dog_ r e s t ing_ <EOS> — 7 steps — and is marked finished when it writes <EOS>. From then on it only receives <PAD>.
  4. Sequence B keeps writing: <SOS> the_ cat_ is_ sleeping_ p e a c e f u l l y_ <EOS>. That is 14 tokens plus <EOS>, but max_len = 15 allows only 14 new tokens, so the loop ends by running out of steps.
  5. Decoding joins the pieces and turns each _ back into a space: "dog resting" and "the cat is sleeping peacefully" — both targets exactly.

Because the decoder re-reads the whole prefix every time, those 14 steps cost 105 position-decodes per sentence instead of 14.

What to look forFrames 1 and 2 are the two switches that separate using the model from training it. Frames 3 and 4 run once, outside the loop. Frames 6 to 9 are one pass of the loop, and frame 8 is paired with the new "finished" flags that pad a sentence once it is done. Frame 12 is paired with the fixes to decoding and to the heatmap. Section B is the heatmap, with each row labelled by the token it predicted, and Section C counts the repeated work.

What you’ll learn

How the trained model actually writes an output. By the end of this step you will know why generation runs one token at a time, what torch.no_grad() and model.eval() switch off, how the loop grows the output and when it stops, what the attention heatmap shows, and why this simple loop wastes work.

The big idea

Think of writing a sentence with a friend who can only add one word at a time. They read the source sentence once and keep their notes (the encoder output). Then they write the first word, read everything written so far, write the next word, read again, and so on — until they write "the end" (<EOS>). That is generation. It uses exactly the same weights as training, but instead of being handed the correct previous word, the model has to use its OWN previous word. At each step the decoder produces a score for every token, and the loop simply takes the highest one (greedy decoding) and appends it.

A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers

Generating the output for sequence A, "the dog sat on the floor":

  1. The encoder runs once. Its output, enc_out, is reused at every step.
  2. Start with just <SOS>. The decoder reads it, and the highest score goes to "dog".
  3. Append "dog". Now the decoder reads "<SOS> dog" — both positions, from scratch — and picks "resting".
  4. Append "resting". Reading all three, it picks <EOS>, so the loop stops after 3 steps.
  5. Drop the special tokens and join the rest: "dog resting" — exactly the target.

Because the decoder re-reads the whole prefix every time, those 3 steps cost 6 position-decodes instead of 3.

What to look forFrames 1 and 2 are the two switches that separate using the model from training it. Frames 3 and 4 run once, outside the loop. Frames 6 to 9 are one pass of the loop: rebuild the mask, decode the whole prefix, take the last row’s best token, append it. Frame 11 is the exit. Section B is the heatmap the notebook draws, and Section C counts the repeated work.

Deep dives

Two of v1.5’s biggest changes, taken apart and measured: where the LayerNorm sits, and how the parameters are counted and first drawn.

STEP 19

Post-LN against Pre-LN — a deep dive

norm(x + F(x)) vs x + F(norm(x))the same page in both versions
What you’ll learn

What actually changes when the LayerNorm moves from after the addition (Post-LN, in v1) to before the sub-layer (Pre-LN, in v1.5). By the end of this page you will know what each arrangement does to the numbers, why Pre-LN trains deep models more easily, what it costs, and which of the common claims about the two are true.

The big idea

Every layer does two things to x: a sub-layer proposes a change, and a LayerNorm keeps the numbers at a sensible size. The question is the ORDER. Post-LN (v1) adds the change and then normalises the result: x = norm(x + F(x)). Think of a photo that is re-exposed after every edit — it always has the same brightness, but the original is adjusted at every step. Pre-LN (v1.5) normalises a copy for the sub-layer to read and adds the change to the untouched original: x = x + F(norm(x)). The original is never re-exposed, only added to — so a gradient can flow straight down the stack, but x keeps getting bigger and needs one final LayerNorm at the end.

A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers

Same weights, same input, only the LayerNorm moved — follow the token "dog_" through this model’s 2-layer encoder:

  1. It enters with length 35.1.
  2. Post-LN: after the first attention step it is rescaled to 22.6, and it stays at exactly that length after every step.
  3. Pre-LN: after the first attention step it is 36.2, and it keeps growing, to 43.6 after both layers; the final LayerNorm brings it back to 22.6.
  4. Each Post-LN step turns x more (direction kept 0.84 on average) than each Pre-LN step (0.95).
  5. In a 48-block stack, what survives the skip connections alone is 0.008 for Post-LN and exactly 1 for Pre-LN — but Pre-LN’s last block only changes x by 0.15 of its length, against 0.50 for its first.

That is the whole trade: Pre-LN keeps the path clean and trains more easily; Post-LN keeps every layer’s full influence.

What to look forSection A draws both wirings — follow the thick line. Section B shows the actual numbers at every stage, side by side, and a bar chart of the length of x. Section C measures how far each sub-layer turns x. Section D is the 48-block experiment in four charts. Section E lists the pros and cons, and Section F checks the common claims one by one.

What you’ll learn

What actually changes when the LayerNorm moves from after the addition (Post-LN, in v1) to before the sub-layer (Pre-LN, in v1.5). By the end of this page you will know what each arrangement does to the numbers, why Pre-LN trains deep models more easily, what it costs, and which of the common claims about the two are true.

The big idea

Every layer does two things to x: a sub-layer proposes a change, and a LayerNorm keeps the numbers at a sensible size. The question is the ORDER. Post-LN (v1) adds the change and then normalises the result: x = norm(x + F(x)). Think of a photo that is re-exposed after every edit — it always has the same brightness, but the original is adjusted at every step. Pre-LN (v1.5) normalises a copy for the sub-layer to read and adds the change to the untouched original: x = x + F(norm(x)). The original is never re-exposed, only added to — so a gradient can flow straight down the stack, but x keeps getting bigger and needs one final LayerNorm at the end.

A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers

Same weights, same input, only the LayerNorm moved — follow the token "dog_" through this model’s 2-layer encoder:

  1. It enters with length 35.1.
  2. Post-LN: after the first attention step it is rescaled to 22.6, and it stays at exactly that length after every step.
  3. Pre-LN: after the first attention step it is 36.2, and it keeps growing, to 43.6 after both layers; the final LayerNorm brings it back to 22.6.
  4. Each Post-LN step turns x more (direction kept 0.84 on average) than each Pre-LN step (0.95).
  5. In a 48-block stack, what survives the skip connections alone is 0.008 for Post-LN and exactly 1 for Pre-LN — but Pre-LN’s last block only changes x by 0.15 of its length, against 0.50 for its first.

That is the whole trade: Pre-LN keeps the path clean and trains more easily; Post-LN keeps every layer’s full influence.

Section C measures how far each sub-layer turns x. Section D is the 48-block experiment in four charts. Section E lists the pros and cons, and Section F checks the common claims one by one.

STEP 20

Half the parameters, and how every weight starts

28,268,661 → 14,728,218 · drawn once, zeroed, seededthe same page in both versions
What you’ll learn

What really changed in the parameters between v1 and v1.5, and in how their starting values are chosen. By the end of this page you will know where 13.5 million parameters went (and why weight tying is not the main reason), how v1 accidentally drew most matrices five times, what the Xavier formula does to tables of different sizes, and why the untrained v1.5 model starts out confidently wrong.

The big idea

A parameter is one number the model can learn, and before training every one of them needs a random starting value. Xavier initialisation picks the range of those random values from the shape of each matrix, so that signals keep a sensible size as they pass through. For ordinary layers that works well. But an embedding table has one row per token, so its shape — and therefore its range — depends on how big the vocabulary is. v1 had 12,917 tokens and three separate vocabulary tables; v1.5 has 26 tokens and one shared table. That single difference changes the parameter count, the range of the starting values, and what the model does before it has learned anything.

A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers

The same two sentences, measured in both models before training:

  1. v1 has 28,268,661 parameters, 70.2% of them in vocabulary tables; v1.5 has 14,728,218.
  2. Tying the three tables at v1’s vocabulary saves 13,227,008; shrinking the vocabulary to 26 saves 6,613,083; the wider feed-forward layers add 6,297,600 back.
  3. v1 draws 81,624,064 random numbers to fill 28,229,120 matrix entries (2.9×); v1.5 draws each once.
  4. The embedding range is ±0.0211 in v1 and ±0.1056 in v1.5, so the token part of the input is 6.2 long in v1 and 30.8 in v1.5, against a position part of 16.0.
  5. The untrained v1 scores every token within ±1.23 and starts at a loss of 9.57 ≈ ln V. The untrained v1.5 gives the token it is reading a score of 15.51 and starts at 17.91, far above ln 26 = 3.26.

Half the parameters, a bigger processing core, cleaner starting weights — and one surprising side effect that training removes in the first twenty epochs.

START

Start here — a Transformer in six pictures

no code · for readers new to AIunchanged in v1.5

In one sentenceA Transformer turns words into numbers, lets them compare notes, and learns from examples which next word is likely.

In plain words

This page is for you if you have never met AI. It shows, in six pictures, what the notebook builds: a program that reads one sentence and writes another. No code yet — each picture names the cells where it happens, and every number in it comes from running the notebook on this machine.

Picture it

Imagine a translation office with no rule book at all. On the first day a clerk is hired who knows nothing. They are handed an example — “the dog sat on the floor” should become “dog resting” — and asked to guess the answer, one word at a time. Every guess is checked against the real answer, and after each check the clerk adjusts, very slightly, thousands of tiny habits. After enough rounds the guesses come out right.

Inside the office the work always runs in the same order. A cutter chops the sentence into familiar pieces. A filing room swaps each piece for a card of 512 numbers. The cards sit round a table and compare notes, then each one thinks on its own — and that meeting is repeated a few times. Finally a writer reads the cards and gives every one of the 16,111 pieces it knows a chance of being the next word, and writes the likeliest.

The clerk’s “habits” are the model’s 22,979,823 numbers. Nobody types them in: training finds them, one small correction at a time.

Another way to see itOr think of the autocomplete on your phone, grown up: it also guesses the next word from what came before. This model does the same, but first it reads a whole sentence it has to answer.

Where the picture stops workingA clerk would understand a rule. The model never does: it only finds numbers that make the right answers likely on the examples it was shown.
