What v2.5 changes here — and why it helps

Nothing on this page changed in v2.5. What you see is exactly what v2.5 runs.

A worked example, with this page’s real numbers

Follow the sentence “the cat is sleeping on the sofa” through the trained model:

  1. It is cut into 8 tokens, each with its own id.
  2. Each token becomes 512 numbers. After training, “cat” and “dog” point a little the same way: 0.20 on a scale where 1 means identical and 0 unrelated.
  3. To write its first word the model gives every one of its 16,111 tokens a probability; “the” gets 92.8%.
  4. Training brought the loss from 9.60 — a blind guess — down to 1.30 in 72 epochs.

Six pictures, one machine. The rest of the walkthrough opens each of them up.

Where to lookRead the pictures in order, 1 to 6. The map at the bottom shows which notebook cell does what, and the green cells are where v2.5 changed the code.

The mathsThe whole model in one lineread the sentence once, then score every possible next token4 formulas · 8 worked examples
H=Encoder(dE[x])

The encoder turns the source tokens x into one row of numbers per token, read in both directions.

In plain English

The encoder reads the whole sentence first. Each word of the sentence first becomes a list of 512 numbers — its row of the table E — multiplied by √512 ≈ 22.6 so that it is not drowned out by what the layers add later. Then the encoder’s layers let every word look at every other word, to its left and to its right, and update its numbers. What comes out, H, is still one row per word, but each row now describes the word in this sentence: “bank” next to “river” ends up with different numbers than “bank” next to “money”.

Picture it

A careful reader who goes through the whole sentence before saying anything, and writes a note beside every word about what it means here. H is that set of notes; the writer keeps checking them.

Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · The same word, two different rows: “the” in sequence B
  1. The tiny model reads “the cat is sleeping on the sof a”. “the” stands at positions 0 and 5.
  2. Before the encoder both get the same row: √8 × E[the] starts (−0.03, 0.69, −1.88).
  3. After the encoder, H[0] starts (−0.69, 1.36, −0.18) and H[5] starts (−0.74, 1.35, −0.27).

So: The encoder rewrites each word in the light of the sentence: the first “the” is followed by “cat”, the second by “sof”.

Example 2 · How many numbers the real encoder hands on
  1. A 7-word sentence: E[x] is 7 rows of 512 numbers, each multiplied by √512 = 22.63.
  2. H keeps the shape: 7 × 512 = 3,584 numbers, one row per word.

So: The encoder changes the numbers, never the shape.

ht=Decoder(dE[y<t],H)

The decoder reads the answer so far, y before position t, and looks at H in every layer.

In plain English

The decoder is the writer. At position t it only has the words written so far — the masks stop it from peeking at later ones. In every layer it looks twice: at its own earlier words, to keep the sentence going, and at H, to stay true to the sentence being read. h_t is its summary of “what should come next”, as 512 numbers.

Picture it

A translator writing one word at a time with the source page open beside them: before each word they reread what they have written so far, and glance at the source notes (H) for what still needs saying.

Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · The same first step, two different source sentences
  1. Both answers start with <SOS>, so the decoder gets the same input row.
  2. Reading “the cat is sleeping on the sof a”: h₀ starts (−1.24, −0.96, −9.90) → first word “the”.
  3. Reading “a dog is running on the sof a”: h₀ starts (−15.96, −0.73, −7.21) → first word “a”.

So: h_t depends on the sentence being read, through H in every layer.

Example 2 · What h_t is allowed to use
  1. At t = 3 the answer so far is “<SOS> the cat is”.
  2. h₃ is built from those 4 tokens and all 8 rows of H — never from “sleeping”, which comes later.

So: The decoder writes left to right, like a person.

p(·|y<t,x)=softmax(E·RMSNorm(ht)+b)

One score per vocabulary token, turned into probabilities — the same table E that read the tokens in scores them on the way out.

In plain English

To turn that summary into a word, the model compares h_t with the row of every token in the same table E: multiply the two lists number by number and add up. The more two rows point the same way, the bigger the score. With a bias added, that gives 16,111 scores (logits), one per token. Softmax turns them into probabilities: e^score makes every score positive and makes big ones much bigger, and dividing by the total makes them add up to 1. Example: scores 2, 1 and 0 become 0.67, 0.24 and 0.09.

Picture it

A talent show with 16,111 contestants: each one’s score is how well its row matches what the writer has in mind (h_t), and softmax turns the scores into shares of the vote.

Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · The tiny model after “<SOS> the cat is”
  1. Highest logits: sleeping 4.57, a −0.05, peac −0.08.
  2. Softmax over all 15 tokens: “sleeping” gets 90.5%, “a” 0.9%.

So: One row of scores becomes one probability per token, and the right word wins.

Example 2 · Three candidate words by hand
  1. Scores: sleeping 3.0, running 1.5, sofa 0.2. e^score: 20.09, 4.48, 1.22; total 25.79.
  2. Probabilities: sleeping 77.9%, running 17.4%, sofa 4.7%.

So: A score gap of 1.5 already means 4.5 times the probability.

L=−1T∑t=1Tlogp(yt|y<t,x)

Training makes the right next token likely at every position at once (cell 8 adds label smoothing).

In plain English

The loss measures how surprised the model is by the right answer. If it gave the right next token a probability of 0.9, the cost is −log 0.9 = 0.105; if only 0.01, the cost is −log 0.01 = 4.6. The log punishes confident mistakes hard. Training lowers the average cost over all T positions, which pushes up the probability of every right next token. All positions are trained at once, because the whole answer is fed in (teacher forcing, cell 8).

Picture it

A quiz where you bet on your answer: put 90% on the right one and you lose little; put 1% on it and you lose a lot. Training is learning to bet confidently — and correctly.

Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · A weather forecaster’s bets
  1. Monday: rain at 80%, it rains → −log 0.8 = 0.223.
  2. Tuesday: rain at only 10%, it rains → −log 0.1 = 2.303.
  3. L over the two days: (0.223 + 2.303) ÷ 2 = 1.263.

So: One confident miss costs about 10 times a fairly sure hit.

Example 2 · The tiny model’s loss on sequence B
  1. The right next token gets, position by position: 0.906, 0.909, 0.908, 0.905, 0.908, 0.905, 0.906.
  2. L = −(1/7) × Σ log p = 0.098.

So: Every position is right with about 0.91 — a small loss, but not 0.

what v3 adds to v2.5 · for readers new to AIunchanged in v1.5

In one sentencev3 keeps v2.5’s model and adds eight techniques of today’s large models: four to run faster and smaller, four that change how it learns.

In plain words

v2.5 already has what the original Transformer lacked. v3 adds eight techniques that today’s large models use, in two groups: four make the model faster and smaller to run, four change how it learns — made for very large models; the last deep dive measures what they do here. This page shows all eight in pictures, each with real numbers; the pages after it take each one apart.

Picture it

Imagine a restaurant that has become busy every night. The cooking itself is already good; what has to change is how fast plates go out, how much room the kitchen needs, and how quickly new cooks get good.

So the cooks stop keeping a private shelf each and share one per pair. The chef asks for a kitchen tool that can taste a pot spoon by spoon with a running tally — used when the kitchen has it. An apprentice plates the next dish while the chef finishes this one; if the chef nods, two plates go out together. The recipe binders are rewritten in shorthand, a quarter of the pages.

And the training changes: the ovens get thermostats so nothing runs away, orders go to the two most suitable of four specialist cooks, trainees learn to think two dishes ahead, and a coach makes every muscle work, not only the strongest.

Another way to see itAnother way to see it: v2.5 decided what the model computes; v3 changes how cheaply it computes it and how efficiently it learns — the answers it is trained toward are the same.

Where the picture stops workingA restaurant’s gains are certain; these are not. Several of these techniques pay off at scale — thousands of tokens of context, billions of numbers, a GPU — and some cost time on a small model on a CPU. The pages say which, with measurements.

What v3 changes here — and why it helps

A worked example, with this page’s real numbers

From the v3 notebook, run here for real:

  1. It has 32,543,983 learned numbers (v2.5: 22,979,823), but a token passes through only 24,089,839 of them: the experts it is not sent to sit idle.
  2. Its cache keeps 1,024 numbers per written token instead of v2.5’s 2,048.
  3. Writing “the cat is sleeping peacefully” took 4 passes of the model for 7 tokens — the answer identical to plain greedy decoding.
  4. Stored in 8 bits its weights take 32.9 MB instead of 130.2 MB, with the same answers.

OVERVIEW

What changed in v2, and why

27 changes · grouped by purposeunchanged in v1.5
What you’ll learn

What v2 changes compared with v1.5, and — for every change — what it is for and what it measurably gets you, before the walkthrough starts.

The big idea

v1.5 fixed the model. v2 keeps that model and fixes everything around it. A useful way to read any change is to ask what it is FOR: faster, less memory, better output, better training, a silent bug fixed, something that can now be reused, or a better way to measure. Every green v1.5 → v2 block in the cell pages carries one of those purposes as a chip, and this page lists all of them in one table.

A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers

The six headline numbers, all measured here:

  1. Training the tokenizer on the word list: about 35 minutes the v1.5 way, 2.6 s with v2’s heap.
  2. The vocabulary: 26 tokens in v1.5, 16,111 in v2.
  3. Writing a 63-token answer: 2,016 decoder position passes without a cache, 63 with it.
  4. Beam search found a sentence 0.030 more likely than greedy’s on this model.

The model is the same; what it can do with it is not.

What to look forThe six cards are the headline. The table groups all 27 changes by purpose, with the measured effect and the cell page that explains each one.

OVERVIEW

What changed in v2.5, and why

9 changes · two real training runsunchanged in v1.5

In one sentencev2.5 keeps v2’s size and swaps in the parts modern models use: how positions, thinking, choosing and training work.

In plain words

v2.5 is v2 with nine improvements that today’s large language models made standard — and one fix. This page lists them all, what each is for, and what it measurably did here.

Picture it

Think of a car that gets a full service, not a new engine. The engine size stays the same — v2.5 has exactly v2’s 22,979,823 numbers — but several parts are swapped for the kind every modern car now has. Some parts change how the car drives (the model), some how the driver picks a route (choosing the words), some how the car is looked after (training), and one is on the dashboard (grading the answers).

The car gets a real sense of distance: RoPE lets a word feel how far away another word is, instead of reading a seat number printed on its card. The volume leveller is simplified (RMSNorm), and the thinking stage gets a throttle on every cylinder (SwiGLU’s gate). The route planner now considers more roads when it is unsure and fewer when it is sure (top-p), is nudged away from driving in circles (the repetition penalty), and no longer gives up one turn before the best destination (the fixed beam stop).

In the workshop, rust protection now goes only on the metal, not on the dials (weight decay only on weight matrices), and the mileage is read from a logbook average instead of one jittery reading (the EMA). On the dashboard, a new gauge shows “almost right” instead of only “right” or “wrong” (BLEU).

Another way to see itOr the same cook with the same ingredients, given sharper knives, a better thermometer and a habit of tasting before serving: the dish is the same idea, made more reliably.

Where the picture stops workingA service does not make every road faster. On this machine’s CPU a v2.5 training step is slower, and on the two-sentence task both versions learn both answers — deep dive 17 is where the differences are measured.

What v2.5 changes here — and why it helps
  • three model changes — RoPE, RMSNorm, SwiGLU — the building block modern models use
  • three decoding changes — top-p, a repetition penalty, a correct beam stop — better and more trustworthy answers
  • two training changes — decay only on weight matrices, an EMA of the weights — training that does not work against itself
  • one evaluation change — BLEU — partial credit for partial answers
A worked example, with this page’s real numbers

Both notebooks were trained here, for real, on their two sentence pairs:

  1. Both learn both answers. v2.5 reaches 100% on the training words by epoch 20; v2 by epoch 60 (one run each — a hint, not proof).
  2. Beam search on “the cat is sleeping on the sofa”: v2 answers “the is sleeping peacefully”, v2.5 “the cat is sleeping peacefully”.
  3. Put v2.5’s stop on v2’s own trained weights and v2’s answer becomes “the cat is sleeping peacefully”: the rule, not luck, dropped the word.

Deep dive 17 measures the model changes properly, on thousands of sentences.

In plain English
Positions
v2 added a fixed pattern of waves to each word’s numbers at the start, so the position was mixed into the meaning. v2.5 leaves the words alone and turns the queries and keys inside attention by an angle that grows with the position, so attention sees how far apart two words are.
Normalisation
Both bring every row to a steady size. LayerNorm also takes away the row’s average and adds a learned bias; RMSNorm skips both, doing less work for about the same result.
Feed-forward
v2 bent each hidden unit on its own; v2.5 lets one projection open and shut the units of another — a gate.
Weight decay
v2 pulled every number towards 0, norm gains and biases included; v2.5 only the weight matrices.
Weights evaluated
v2 validated and saved the latest weights; v2.5 a slowly moving average of them, which is smoother.
Sampling
v2.5 adds top-p, a shortlist that follows the model’s confidence, and a penalty for tokens already written.
Beam search stops
v2 could stop just before a longer, better answer finished; v2.5 stops only when no live beam can win.
Score
BLEU gives partial credit where exact match is all or nothing.
Picture it

The same car after a service: same body and engine size, but newer parts in four places — how position is read, the normaliser, the feed-forward, and how answers are chosen and scored.

Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Levelling the row (2, 4, 6) both ways
  1. v2 LayerNorm: mean 4, spread 1.633 → (−1.22, 0.00, 1.22).
  2. v2.5 RMSNorm: size 4.320 → (0.46, 0.93, 1.39).

So: LayerNorm centres, RMSNorm only levels.

Example 2 · A norm gain under 10,000 steps of weight decay
  1. v2: 1.0 × (1 − 5 × 10⁻⁶)^10,000 = 0.951 if nothing pushes back. v2.5: stays 1.000.

So: v2.5 leaves the gains alone.

Every row has its own deep dive (6 to 16) and its own card there, with each symbol explained.

OVERVIEW

What changed in v3, and why

8 changes · faster and smaller · how it learnsunchanged in v1.5

In one sentenceEight changes, grouped by purpose, each with its cost and what it measurably did here.

In plain words

v3 is v2.5 with eight changes that today’s large models use. This page lists them, what each is for, what it costs, and what it measurably did here.

Picture it

A family car is good at what it does. Turned into a delivery van that runs all day, what matters changes: fuel, stops and upkeep cost money on every trip.

So the van gets a smaller tank that goes as far, a co-driver who calls the next turn so the driver rarely stops to look, a manual printed small, limits on the engine, two specialist mechanics per job instead of one generalist, and a new way of training its drivers. Same road, same destination — cheaper trips, and a different way of learning the route.

Another way to see itOr a restaurant moving from dinner service to all-day delivery: the same dishes, cooked and packed for volume.

Where the picture stops workingA van’s savings show on the road; most of these show on GPUs serving many readers, not on this CPU. The notebook run here: v3 reached 100.0% exact match, at 0.64 s an epoch against v2.5’s 0.15 s. What the training changes did is measured in deep dive 26.

What v3 changes here — and why it helps
  • grouped-query attention — the KV cache holds half as many numbers
  • causal attention without a mask — lets PyTorch pick its built-in FlashAttention kernel when the GPU, the precision and the mask allow (deep dive 20); its online softmax is written out and checked
  • speculative decoding — the same answers in fewer passes of the model
  • 8-bit weights — a quarter of the bytes, the same answers
  • QK-Norm and a soft cap — attention scores and output scores cannot run away
  • a mixture of experts — twice the feed-forward numbers for the same work per token
  • multi-token prediction — a second training signal per position, and the guesses that speculative decoding checks
  • Muon for the weight matrices — updates that move every direction by the same amount
A worked example, with this page’s real numbers

v3 and v2.5, each trained here on the notebook’s two sentence pairs:

  1. Both learn both answers: exact match 100.0% and BLEU 100.0 for v3.
  2. v3’s best validation loss came at epoch 69 (1.3030); v2.5’s at epoch 72 (1.3002).
  3. One epoch took v3 0.64 s and v2.5 0.15 s on this CPU: the experts and the second loss cost time here.

Two sentences only show that everything runs. Whether v3 learns better is measured on thousands of sentences in the last deep dive.

Vocabulary

one string, read by rankunchanged since v2unchanged since v2unchanged in v1.5
What you’ll learn

What the 50,000-word list is for in v2, and why the ORDER of its lines has become information. By the end you will know how a rank turns into a count, and why that matters to the tokenizer.

The big idea

A tokenizer learns which letter combinations deserve a token of their own by counting how often they appear. Counting needs frequencies — and a plain list has none: every word appears once. But this list is sorted from the most common English word to the rarest, and Zipf’s law says the word at rank r shows up roughly 1 / r as often as the top one. So the position of a word can stand in for its count, the way a chart position stands in for sales.

A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers

The cell itself only stores one long string; the counting happens four cells later:

  1. The string has 423,272 characters: 50,000 words, one per line, all different.
  2. "the" is on line 1, so it is counted 1,000,000 times; "of", on line 2, 500,000 times.
  3. "dog" is on line 2,138: counted 468 times. "sofa", line 11,172: 90.
  4. The last word, "empyema", still gets 20 — the formula never reaches its floor of 1.

v1.5 had this same cell and never read it. v2 reads it once, and every token id on every later page comes out of that read.

What to look forFrame 1 is the only line that runs here. Frames 2 and 3 jump ahead to the one line that reads it (cell 5) and the method that turns ranks into counts (cell 3); the chart is the rank-to-count rule with the sentences’ words on it. Section B compares what each version trained its tokenizer on.

In one sentenceA list of 50,000 common words, most common first, from which the tokenizer learns its pieces.

In plain words

Cell 0 is a list of 50,000 English words, the most common first. The tokenizer learns its pieces from it. Nothing in this cell changed in v2.5: its code is v2’s line for line (only v2’s own [NEW] comments are renamed [v2]), so the picture below is v2’s page, and still exact.

Picture it

Before anyone can write in shorthand, someone has to decide what the shorthand symbols are. Cell 0 hands the tokenizer a list of the 50,000 most common English words, in order of how often they are used — a word-frequency dictionary.

The order matters. A word near the top (“the”, “of”, “and”) is treated as if it appears very often, so the pairs of letters it is made of are counted many times, glued together early, and the word ends up as a single token. A rare word near the bottom will usually be spelled from several smaller pieces.

Another way to see itLike a keyboard designer who puts the most-used keys where your fingers already rest: the list tells the tokenizer which words it will have to type most.

Where the picture stops workingThe list is only used to build the tokenizer. The model itself never reads it.

What v3 changes here — and why it helps

Nothing on this page changed in v3. What you see is exactly what v3 runs.

A worked example, with this page’s real numbers

The list is one long text:

  1. “the” is first and “dog” is word 2,138; “sofa” is word 11,172.
  2. Cell 5 gives each word a count from its rank, so common words weigh more.

The list never changes; it only decides which pieces the tokenizer learns first.

Where to lookThe page shows where the list is read and how a word’s rank becomes its count.

The mathsZipf’s law: from a rank to a countthe list is ordered from most to least common2 formulas · 4 worked examples
f(wr)≈Cr

How often a word is used falls roughly as one over its rank (Zipf’s law).

In plain English

Count the words of any large text and a pattern appears: the most common word is used about twice as often as the second, three times as often as the third, and so on — the count is roughly C ÷ rank. “the” is everywhere; the word at rank 1,000 is a thousand times rarer; “empyema”, at rank 50,000, almost never appears.

Picture it

City sizes in a country: the biggest city is about twice the second and three times the third. Word counts follow the same staircase.

Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Cities of a country
  1. Largest city 8,000,000 people (C). Zipf: the 2nd ≈ C ÷ 2 = 4,000,000, the 4th ≈ C ÷ 4 = 2,000,000, the 10th ≈ 800,000.

So: Rank × size stays about the same number C.

Example 2 · The top of the notebook’s list
  1. C = 1,000,000: “the” (r = 1) 1,000,000, “of” (r = 2) 500,000, “and” (r = 3) 333,333.
  2. Check: rank × count ≈ 1,000,000 for each.

So: The list’s order alone sets every count.

f(wr)=max(1,round(106r))

What the code computes (zipf_word_freqs, cell 3, used in cell 5): an estimated count for every word of the list.

In plain English

The vocabulary file lists words in order of frequency but gives no counts, so the code invents believable ones from the order: 1,000,000 ÷ rank, rounded. “the” gets 1,000,000, “of” 500,000, “and” 333,333, the word at rank 1,000 gets 1,000. max(1, …) makes sure every word counts at least once (the last one still gets 20). The tokenizer then spends its merges on the letter pairs of common words first, as it would on real text.

Picture it

Guessing how often songs are played from a chart that lists only their places: number 1 must be everywhere, number 1,000 far rarer. The code does the same with words, so the tokenizer learns the common ones first.

Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Three words of the list
  1. “with” r = 13 → round(10⁶ ÷ 13) = 76,923, “cat” r = 3,234 → round(10⁶ ÷ 3,234) = 309, “empyema” r = 50,000 → round(10⁶ ÷ 50,000) = 20.
  2. “the” is counted 3,236 times as often as “cat”.

So: The tokenizer then spends its first merges on the letters of common words.

Example 2 · Why max(1, …)
  1. A word at rank 3,000,000 would get round(10⁶ ÷ 3,000,000) = round(0.33) = 0.
  2. max(1, 0) = 1: every listed word counts at least once (the list ends at 50,000, where the count is still 20).

So: No word is ever invisible to the tokenizer.

symbolwhat it isin the notebook
rthe word’s rank: its line in this list1 (“the”) to 50,000 (“empyema”)
wrthe word at rank r“the”, “of”, “and”, …
Ca scale: the count given to rank 110⁶
f(wr)its estimated count1,000,000 for “the”, 1,000 at rank 1,000, 20 at the end

Why it matters: BPE (cells 3 and 5) merges the most frequent pairs first. Without these counts every word would weigh the same, and “the” would count no more than “empyema”.

fifteen settingsunchanged in v1.5
What you’ll learn

What the notebook imports and every setting it fixes before anything runs, which later cell uses each one, and what v1.5 did instead.

The big idea

A recipe lists its ingredients and oven temperature before the first step. Cell 1 is that list: the tools the other cells will need, and fifteen numbers that decide the size of the model, how long a sentence may be, how many sentences go into a batch, and when training stops. Keeping them in one place means one edit changes a run — and the checkpoint can save the exact settings it was trained with.

A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers

Three settings and what they turn into later:

  1. MAX_SEQ_LEN = 64: sentences are cut at 64 tokens (cell 6), the position table gets 66 rows (cell 7), and generation may write up to 63 tokens (cell 9).
  2. BATCH_SIZE = 32, but there are only two pairs, so a batch holds min(32, 2) = 2.
  3. PATIENCE = 20: training stops after 20 epochs without a better validation loss (cell 8).

Nothing is computed here — but every later page reads a name defined on this one.

What to look forFrame 1 lists the new imports with the cell that uses each. Frame 2 is the random seeds (one of which nothing uses). Frame 4 is every setting beside v1.5’s. Section B covers the two settings with the widest consequences.

Imports and config

four new knobsunchanged in v1.5

In one sentenceEvery setting in one place: the tools, the model’s size, the training plan, and v2.5’s four new knobs.

In plain words

Cell 1 imports the tools and sets every knob in one place. v2.5 adds four knobs and one import; nothing else moves.

Picture it

Every app has a settings screen: you do not change how the app is built, you choose how it behaves. Cell 1 is that screen for the whole notebook. It brings in the tools (PyTorch for the arithmetic, matplotlib and seaborn for the pictures), fixes the random seed so every run gives the same numbers, and writes every knob in one place.

Some knobs set the size of the machine — 512 numbers per token, 4 attention heads, 2 layers on each side, 2,048 units in the feed-forward. Some set the practice — at most 200 epochs, stop after 20 without progress, a learning rate of 0.0005. v2.5 adds four new knobs: how slowly the slowest RoPE hand turns, how slowly the averaged weights follow, how much probability top-p keeps, and how hard to brake on repeated words.

Another way to see itOr the header of a recipe card — oven temperature, baking time, tin size — written above the method so you can change them without touching the steps.

Where the picture stops workingKnobs are chosen by a person and never learned. Good values come partly from experience and partly from trying.

What v2.5 changes here — and why it helps
  • ROPE_BASE = 10000.0 — how slowly the slowest pair of numbers turns (RoPE)
  • EMA_DECAY = 0.999 — how slowly the averaged copy of the weights follows training
  • TOP_P = 0.9, REPETITION_PENALTY = 1.2 — how answers are sampled and how repeats are discouraged

A worked example, with this page’s real numbers

A knob is chosen by you, not learned:

  1. The model’s shape knobs are v2’s: 512 numbers per token, 4 heads, 2 layers each side.
  2. So the parameter count is v2’s too: 22,979,823.

Table A says, for each new knob, what turning it up or down does.

Where to lookSection A is the plain-words table; section B shows each new line beside v2’s.

The mathsThe sizes the config setsderived from D_MODEL, NUM_HEADS, NUM_LAYERS and D_FF4 formulas · 8 worked examples
dk=dmodelh=5124=128

Each head works on its own slice of every token’s numbers.

In plain English

Each token carries 512 numbers. With 4 heads they are cut into 4 slices of 128, and each head works only on its slice. Each head can learn to look for something different — one the subject of a verb, another the word just before — at no extra cost: 4 × 128 is still 512.

Picture it

Four readers sharing one page of notes, each reading only their own quarter: together they still cover all 512 numbers, but each can specialise.

Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · The notebook
  1. d_model = 512, h = 4 → d_k = 512 ÷ 4 = 128.

So: Each head works on a quarter of every token’s numbers.

Example 2 · Two well-known models
  1. BERT-base: d_model = 768, 12 heads → d_k = 768 ÷ 12 = 64.
  2. LLaMA-7B: d_model = 4,096, 32 heads → d_k = 4,096 ÷ 32 = 128.

So: Larger models mostly add heads, keeping d_k at 64–128.

hidden=8·⌊⌊2dff/3⌋+78⌋=1368

The SwiGLU width: two thirds of d_ff, rounded up to a multiple of 8 (cell 2).

In plain English

SwiGLU needs three matrices where v2 had two, so each is made narrower to keep the size the same. Step by step: 2 × 2,048 = 4,096; ÷ 3, rounded down = 1,365; + 7 = 1,372; ÷ 8, rounded down = 171; × 8 = 1,368. The “+ 7, ÷ 8, × 8” rounds up to a multiple of 8, a width the hardware handles efficiently.

Picture it

Repacking two big suitcases into three smaller ones of the same total volume: three matrices at two-thirds width hold what two full-width ones did.

Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · d_ff = 2,048 (the notebook)
  1. 2 × 2,048 = 4,096; ⌊4,096 ÷ 3⌋ = 1,365; + 7 = 1,372; ⌊1,372 ÷ 8⌋ = 171; × 8 = 1,368.

So: Two thirds of 2,048, rounded up to a multiple of 8.

Example 2 · d_ff = 1,000 and d_ff = 3,072
  1. d_ff = 1,000: ⌊2,000 ÷ 3⌋ = 666; + 7 = 673; ⌊673 ÷ 8⌋ = 84; × 8 = 672.
  2. d_ff = 3,072: ⌊6,144 ÷ 3⌋ = 2,048; + 7 = 2,055; ⌊2,055 ÷ 8⌋ = 256; × 8 = 2,048 (already a multiple of 8).

So: The “+ 7” only matters when two thirds is not a multiple of 8.

max_len = MAX_SEQ_LEN + 2 = 66

Positions RoPE has angles for: the longest sentence plus <SOS> and <EOS>.

In plain English

RoPE works out its angles once, for a fixed number of positions. A sentence holds at most 64 tokens (MAX_SEQ_LEN); the + 2 leaves room for <SOS> and <EOS>, so the tables cover every position the model can meet.

Picture it

Numbering enough seats for the largest group that can come, plus two for the hosts (<SOS> and <EOS>).

Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · A 10-token answer
  1. <SOS> and 9 more tokens use positions 0 to 9: RoPE reads rows 0–9 of its 66-row tables.

So: Short sentences use only the top of the tables.

Example 2 · The longest possible answer
  1. Answers are cut to 64 tokens, <SOS> and <EOS> included: positions 0 to 63.
  2. The tables have 66 rows (MAX_SEQ_LEN + 2): 2 spare.

So: max_len only has to cover the longest sentence.

P=V(d+1)+N(4(d2+d)+3d·hidden+2d)+N(8(d2+d)+3d·hidden+3d)+2d

Every learned number: the shared table and the output bias, then N encoder and N decoder layers (attention, feed-forward, norms), then the two last norms. With these sizes P = 22,979,823.

In plain English

Counting every learned number. The table E has 16,111 rows of 512, and the output layer adds one bias per token: 16,111 × 513 = 8,264,943. One attention has four 512 × 512 matrices and four biases: 1,050,624. One feed-forward: 3 × 512 × 1,368 = 2,101,248. An encoder layer (one attention, one feed-forward, two norms of 512) holds 3,152,896; a decoder layer (two attentions, one feed-forward, three norms) 4,204,032. Two of each, plus enc_norm and dec_norm: 8,264,943 + 2 × 3,152,896 + 2 × 4,204,032 + 1,024 = 22,979,823 — the number the notebook prints.

Picture it

An inventory of a house, room by room: the shared dictionary, then each encoder and decoder layer, then the two last norms — the total is the number the notebook prints.

Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · The real model
  1. V(d + 1) = 16,111 × 513 = 8,264,943 (table and output bias).
  2. Encoder: 2 × (4 × (512² + 512) + 3 × 512 × 1,368 + 2 × 512) = 6,305,792.
  3. Decoder: 2 × (8 × (512² + 512) + 3 × 512 × 1,368 + 3 × 512) = 8,408,064. Last norms: 1,024.
  4. Total: 22,979,823 — the number cell 7 prints.

So: The table and the feed-forwards hold most of it.

Example 2 · The tiny model (V = 15, d = 8, hidden 16)
  1. 15 × 9 = 135; encoder 2 × (4 × 72 + 384 + 16) = 1,376; decoder 2 × (8 × 72 + 384 + 24) = 1,968; last norms 16.
  2. Total: 3,495, as PyTorch counts for it.

So: The same formula, any size.

CELL 2

The model

definitions · 9 changesunchanged in v1.5
What you’ll learn

What cell 2 defines, which later cell runs each piece, and every way v2’s model code differs from v1.5’s — with numbers from the v2 model.

The big idea

This cell is a set of blueprints. Running it builds nothing; it only teaches Python what a Transformer is. The layers are the same ones v1.5 used, so the model computes the same kind of function. What changed is how it is RUN when writing an answer: v1.5 re-read the whole answer so far before adding each new word, like re-reading a letter from the top before every word. v2 keeps notes — the KV cache — so each step only processes the newest word.

A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers

A few of the changes, measured on the untrained v2 model and sequence A:

  1. Generating 8 tokens the v1.5 way pushes 36 positions through the decoder; with the cache, 8. The scores come out identical.
  2. At the first step, <SOS> scores 0.7895 — rank 17 of 16,111. _block_special now makes it impossible to generate.
  3. The top token scores only 0.9931: an untrained model is nearly indifferent, which is why every generated word repeats.

The call stacks that use these definitions are on the pages for cells 7 to 10; every frame there that runs code from this cell says "cell 2".

What to look forSection A is the map: each definition, who calls it, and whether it changed. Section B is the green blocks, each with v1.5’s line above v2’s, the chip saying what it is for, why the old line was weak and the new one better — the KV-cache block draws the cache step by step beside v1.5’s recompute. Section C follows the cache call by call inside MultiHeadAttention.forward: store, compute once, append, reuse.

CELL 2

The model

3 parts · RMSNorm and SwiGLU · RoPE · choosing wordsunchanged in v1.5

In one sentenceThe model is a meeting held in rounds: listen to the others, think alone, and keep what you knew.

In plain words

Cell 2 is the model itself — the blueprint of every part. v2.5 changes three of them: how a word’s position enters (RoPE), how vectors are rescaled (RMSNorm) and how each word is “thought about” (SwiGLU). It also changes how answers are chosen. Three pages, one per idea, each split into small numbered steps.

Picture it

Picture a meeting that is held in rounds. Every word of the sentence is a person at the table, holding a card of 512 numbers that says what they know. In each round two things happen. First everyone listens: each person asks a question (their query), everyone else holds up a label (their key), and the person collects a mix of the others’ notes (their values), weighted by how well each label matched the question. That is attention. Then everyone thinks on their own for a moment and updates their card. That is the feed-forward.

Before each of the two moves a moderator makes sure nobody is shouting or whispering: every card is brought to the same loudness (RMSNorm in v2.5). And nobody throws their card away — each move’s result is added on top of it (the residual shortcut), so what was known before is never lost.

The meeting also needs to know who sits where, or “dog bites man” and “man bites dog” would be the same meeting. In v2 a seat-number pattern was printed onto every card. In v2.5 each person wears a watch whose hands are turned by their seat number, and when a question meets a label the two watches show how many seats apart the two people are (RoPE). At the end a writer reads the final cards and scores every word that could come next (part 3).

Another way to see itOr a book club: in each round everyone reads everyone’s notes (attention), then writes their own summary (feed-forward). Two rounds for the readers of the input (the encoder), two for the writers of the answer (the decoder).

Where the picture stops workingPeople understand what they say. The model’s “notes” are only numbers, shaped by training until the right answers come out likely.

Who is who — the picture, then the code

thinking alonethe feed-forward: SwiGLUFeedForward in v2.5
the moderatorRMSNorm: norm1, norm2 (and norm3 in the decoder)

What v2.5 changes here — and why it helps
  • RMSNorm instead of LayerNorm (page 1) — the same job in 3 steps instead of 5
  • SwiGLU instead of the GELU feed-forward (page 1) — a learned gate on every unit, same size
  • RoPE instead of an added position table (page 2) — a score depends only on how far apart two words are
  • a repetition penalty, top-p, the fixed beam stop (page 3) — better choices when writing
A worked example, with this page’s real numbers

Traced on the real numbers of this model:

  1. RMSNorm on the word “cat”: the average of its squared numbers is 0.05771, so its size (RMS) is 0.24024; dividing by it brings the RMS to exactly 1.
  2. RoPE: “sleeping” looking at “cat” two words back scores 0.5091 wherever the two sit. In v2, with the same starting weights, the score swings between -0.72 and 0.21.
  3. Top-p keeps 13,438 tokens when the model is unsure (untrained) and 1 when it is sure (trained).
  4. On v2’s own trained weights, the new beam stop turns “the is sleeping peacefully” into “the cat is sleeping peacefully”.

Every step on these pages is a line of the notebook, drawn with the numbers it produced.

Where to lookPage 1 follows one word through a layer. Page 2 starts with the four-step picture of RoPE — read it first. Page 3 has three short stacks: the penalty, top-p, the beam stop.

The mathsIn and out: the embedding, and the tied output layerTransformer.encode / decode3 formulas · 6 worked examples
xi=√d·E[ti]

Token id t_i picks row t_i of the table, which is scaled by √d.

In plain English

A token id is just a row number. The table E holds one learned row per token, and looking a token up means copying its row. Multiplying by √d makes the rows big enough not to be drowned out by what attention and the feed-forward add later. Example, in the tiny model: “cat” has id 4, so it gets row 4 of the 15 × 8 table, times √8 ≈ 2.83.

Picture it

Looking a word up in a dictionary: the id is the page number, and the row of numbers is the definition you copy out.

Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · “cat” in the tiny model
  1. id 4 → row 4 of the 15 × 8 table: (−0.2800, 0.4608, 0.2958), …
  2. × √8 = 2.828 → (−0.79, 1.30, 0.84), …

So: A look-up is copying a row, then one multiplication.

Example 2 · The real model’s scale
  1. √512 = 22.63: a table entry of 0.05 enters the encoder as 1.13.

So: The scaling keeps the word loud enough next to what the layers add.

z=E·RMSNorm(h)+b

At the end, the same table scores the decoder’s row against every token: one logit per token.

In plain English

Weight tying: the same table E is used again, the other way round. The decoder’s last row h, levelled by RMSNorm, is compared with every row of E — multiply number by number and add up — and a row that points the same way as h scores high. So a token’s row means the same thing coming in and going out, and the model saves a second table of 16,111 × 512 (8.2 million numbers).

Picture it

The same dictionary read backwards: you have a description in mind (h) and ask which entry matches it best — every entry gets a score.

Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Which entry matches the description h = (1, 2)?
  1. Rows: cat (2, 1), dog (1, 2), sofa (−1, 0.5). Dot products: 1·2 + 2·1 = 4, 1·1 + 2·2 = 5, 1·(−1) + 2·0.5 = 0.
  2. dog points the same way as h and scores highest.

So: The table, read backwards.

Example 2 · The tiny model scoring “sleeping” after “<SOS> the cat is”
  1. RMSNorm(h₃) · E[sleeping], term by term: 1.06 − 0.08 + 0.01 + 1.14 + 0.56 + 0.08 + 1.88 + 1.19 = 5.823.
  2. + bias −1.254 = 4.569 — the logit of “sleeping”.

So: 8 products and a bias make one score; 15 such scores make the row.

pv=softmax(z)v=ezv∑uezu

The logits become probabilities: positive, and adding up to 1.

In plain English

Softmax turns any scores into probabilities. Example: logits 3, 1 and −1 give e³ = 20.1, e¹ = 2.72 and e⁻¹ = 0.37; their total is 23.2, so the probabilities are 0.867, 0.117 and 0.016. Adding the same number to every logit changes nothing — only the differences between logits matter.

Picture it

Sharing a pie by votes, where e^score turns a slightly stronger vote into a much bigger slice: every slice is positive, and the slices make one whole pie.

Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Logits 3, 1 and −1
  1. e³ = 20.09, e¹ = 2.72, e⁻¹ = 0.37; total 23.17.
  2. p = 86.7%, 11.7%, 1.6%.

So: e^score turns gaps into ratios: a gap of 2 is ×7.4.

Example 2 · Add 10 to every logit
  1. Logits 13, 11 and 9 give p = 86.7%, 11.7%, 1.6% — exactly the same.

So: Only the differences between logits matter.

The mathsRMSNormdivide a row by its size, then scale each column2 formulas · 4 worked examples
RMS(x)=1d∑j=1dxj2+ε
The size of a row: the root of the mean of its squares (ε keeps it from being 0).
In plain English
RMS is the typical size of the numbers in a row, whatever their signs: square each one (so −3 and 3 count the same), take the average, and undo the squaring with a square root. Example: the row (3, −4) has squares 9 and 16, mean 12.5, root 3.54. ε = 0.000001 is added under the root so a row of zeros never leads to dividing by zero.
Picture it
A volume meter: it shows how loud the whole row is, not which notes are playing.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · The row (3, −4)
  1. Squares 9 and 16; mean (9 + 16) ÷ 2 = 12.5; + ε = 12.500001.
  2. √12.500001 = 3.536.
So: RMS is the typical size, whatever the signs.
Example 2 · A real row: “sleeping” entering norm3 in the tiny model
  1. x = (−0.91, 1.52, 1.70, −2.39, 2.09, −0.81, 2.30, −3.38).
  2. Mean of the 8 squares 4.184 → RMS = √4.184 = 2.046.
So: One number sums up the whole row’s size.
RMSNorm(x)=xRMS(x)⊙g
Every row comes out with size about 1; then column j is multiplied by its learned gain g_j.
In plain English
Dividing by the RMS brings every row to size 1 — loud rows turned down, quiet ones up — while each row keeps its pattern: which numbers are big, which are negative. Continuing the example: (3, −4) ÷ 3.54 = (0.85, −1.13). Then the learned gains g let the model turn some columns up and others down again; they start at 1, so at first nothing changes.
Picture it
A sound engineer’s fader: every track is brought to the same loudness, the melody (the pattern) is untouched, and the learned gains are the mix of each instrument.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · A quiet and a loud recording of the same tune
  1. Quiet (0.3, −0.4) ÷ 0.354 = (0.85, −1.13).
  2. Loud (3, −4) ÷ 3.536 = (0.85, −1.13) — the same.
So: The tune is kept, the volume forgotten.
Example 2 · Then the learned gains (1.2, 0.5)
  1. (0.85, −1.13) ⊙ (1.2, 0.5) = (0.85 × 1.2, −1.13 × 0.5) = (1.02, −0.57).
So: The gains turn columns up or down after levelling.

The mathsThe SwiGLU feed-forwardtwo widened copies, one gating the other2 formulas · 4 worked examples
FFN(x)=Wdown(SiLU(Wgatex)⊙Wupx)
Widen the token twice, let one copy open or shut each unit of the other, shrink back.
In plain English
After attention has let the tokens share information, the feed-forward works on each token alone — its thinking step. The token’s numbers are widened twice, by two different matrices. One copy goes through SiLU and becomes a row of gates: near 0 means closed, larger means open. Multiplying the two copies unit by unit switches each hidden unit on or off depending on the token itself. W_down then mixes the results back into a row of the original width, which is added to the token.
Picture it
A panel of specialists for each word (16 here, 1,368 in the real model): each one’s gate decides whether they speak at all, their value is what they would say, and W_down is the editor who folds it all into one short report.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Two hidden units, by hand
  1. x = (1, 2). W_gate x = (1·1 − 1·2, 0.5·1 + 0.5·2) = (−1.0, 1.5) → SiLU → (−0.269, 1.226).
  2. W_up x = (2·1, 1·2) = (2.0, 2.0). Gate ⊙ value = (−0.538, 2.453).
  3. W_down = (1, 1): output −0.538 + 2.453 = 1.915.
So: Unit 1’s gate is negative, so it barely contributes; unit 2 carries the result.
Example 2 · “sleeping” in the tiny model
  1. Of its 16 hidden units, 7 have a gate above 0.5 (open).
  2. The loudest is unit 13: gate 1.333 × value −1.407 = −1.876.
  3. W_down folds the 16 products into 8 numbers: (0.11, 1.37, 1.53), …
So: Each token opens its own few units.
SiLU(a)=a·σ(a)=a1+e−a
The gate’s bend: near 0 for clearly negative a, nearly a itself for clearly positive a.
In plain English
σ(a) = 1 ÷ (1 + e^(−a)) is a soft switch between 0 and 1: σ(−4) ≈ 0.018 (almost off), σ(0) = 0.5, σ(4) ≈ 0.982 (almost on). SiLU multiplies a by its own switch: SiLU(−4) ≈ −0.07, SiLU(0) = 0, SiLU(4) ≈ 3.93. Unlike a hard on/off switch it bends smoothly, so training can always nudge it a little.
Picture it
A dimmer rather than an on/off switch: strongly negative inputs stay almost dark, strongly positive ones get almost full brightness, and in between it turns smoothly.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · A shut gate: a = −3
  1. σ(−3) = 1 ÷ (1 + e³) = 0.0474.
  2. SiLU(−3) = −3 × 0.0474 = −0.142.
So: Strongly negative stays almost 0.
Example 2 · An open gate: a = 2
  1. σ(2) = 1 ÷ (1 + e⁻²) = 0.8808.
  2. SiLU(2) = 2 × 0.8808 = 1.762.
So: Strongly positive passes almost whole.

The mathsThe maskswhich token may look at which — True = may look4 formulas · 8 worked examples
padj=[sj≠PAD]
make_padding_mask: a token may be looked at only if it is not filler.
In plain English
A mask is a table of yes/no answers to “may I look at that token?”. Sentences in a batch differ in length, so short ones are filled up with <PAD>. Filler carries no meaning, so the padding mask says no for every <PAD>. Example: “the dog sat <PAD> <PAD>” gives True, True, True, False, False.
Picture it
Empty seats at a dinner table: they are on the seating plan, but nobody talks to an empty chair.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · A cinema row with two empty seats
  1. “the dog sat <PAD> <PAD>” → [s ≠ PAD] = True, True, True, False, False.
  2. 3 of the 5 places may be looked at.
So: Padding only makes the batch a rectangle.
Example 2 · The tiny model’s batch
  1. “the cat is running” is padded to 8 to sit beside “the cat is sleeping on the sof a”.
  2. Mask: T, T, T, T, F, F, F, F — 4 real, 4 filler.
So: Every query of that sentence ignores the same filler columns.
causalij=[j≤i]
make_causal_mask: position i may look at itself and the positions before it.
In plain English
In training the decoder gets the whole answer at once, but when it writes for real the next word does not exist yet. So position i must not look at any position after i, or it would learn to copy the answer instead of predicting it. [j ≤ i] gives a staircase: row 0 sees only itself, row 1 sees 0 and 1, row 2 sees 0, 1 and 2 — a lower triangle of True.
Picture it
An exam where you may look back at your earlier answers but never ahead at the answer sheet: position i sees only what comes before it.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · 4 positions
  1. Row 0: T F F F · row 1: T T F F · row 2: T T T F · row 3: T T T T.
  2. True cells: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 of 16.
So: Each position sees itself and the past.
Example 2 · Sequence B’s 7 decoder positions
  1. Row 3 (“is”) may see <SOS>, the, cat, is: 4 of 7.
  2. In all: 1 + 2 + … + 7 = 28 of 49 cells.
So: Never the word it has to predict.
tgtij=[j≤i]∧[yj≠PAD]
make_tgt_mask: both at once, for the decoder’s self-attention.
In plain English
The decoder’s self-attention needs both rules at once: do not look ahead, and do not look at filler. ∧ means “and”: a cell is True only when both are True.
Picture it
Two rules on one door — invited and on time: ∧ means you get in only if both hold.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · “<SOS> the cat is running fast”, padded to 7
  1. Row 2: T T T F F F F (causal only).
  2. Row 6, the <PAD> position: T T T T T T F — the filler column is hidden.
So: Both rules at once: not later, and not filler.
Example 2 · Counting the True cells
  1. Causal alone: 28 of 49. With the padding rule: 27 — the <PAD> column loses its one True cell.
So: Padding at the end only touches the last column.
s′ij={sijif the mask is Trueminif it is False (≈ −3.4 × 10³⁸)
Inside attention: a hidden score becomes the smallest number a float holds, so softmax gives it exactly 0.
In plain English
Scores go through softmax, which uses e^score. Replacing a forbidden score by the most negative number a float can hold makes its e^score exactly 0, so that token gets 0% of the attention and the other shares still add up to 100%. The code uses that number rather than −∞ itself because a row made entirely of −∞ would give 0 ÷ 0.
Picture it
Muting a microphone completely: the speaker is still in the room but adds nothing, and everyone else’s share of the conversation grows to fill the gap.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Muting one score
  1. Scores 2, 1, 3, the third hidden. Unmasked, it would take 66.5%.
  2. Masked: e² ÷ (e² + e¹) = 73.1%, 26.9%, and exactly 0.
So: The hidden token gets exactly 0.
Example 2 · A row where everything is hidden
  1. All 4 scores become min (−3.4 × 10³⁸): softmax gives 0.25 each — a harmless, equal mix.
  2. With −∞ instead, e^(−∞ − (−∞)) is 0 ÷ 0: NaN, which would spread through the model.
So: That is why the code uses the smallest float, not −∞.

The mathsMulti-head attentionevery token gathers from the others, h times in parallel3 formulas · 6 worked examples
Q=XWq⊤+bq,K=XWk⊤+bk,V=XWv⊤+bv
Three learned views of the tokens, then split into h heads of d_k numbers.
In plain English
Every token’s row is multiplied by three learned matrices, giving three new rows: a query (“what am I looking for?”), a key (“what do I contain?”) and a value (“what do I hand over if I am chosen?”). The numbers of each are then cut into heads.
Picture it
A library search: the query is your question, the keys are the labels on the shelves, the values are the books you take home. Every token is both a reader with a question and a shelf with a label.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · A 2-number token, by hand
  1. x = (1, 2). W_q = [[0.5, 0], [0, 1]] → q = (0.5, 2). W_k = [[1, 0], [1, 1]] → k = (1, 3).
  2. W_v = [[0, 1], [1, 0]] → v = (2, 1).
So: One token, three different views of it.
Example 2 · “sleeping” in the tiny model
  1. Q row (8 numbers): (−1.88, −1.53, 1.12, −0.40, −2.05, 1.20, −1.63, 1.05).
  2. Split into 2 heads of 4: head 0 (−1.88, −1.53, 1.12, −0.40), head 1 (−2.05, 1.20, −1.63, 1.05).
So: Each head asks with its own half.
headk=softmax(QkKk⊤dk+M)Vk
Each query is compared with every key; the scores become shares; the values are mixed by those shares.
In plain English
In one head, a query is compared with every key by a dot product — large when they point the same way. Dividing by √d_k (√128 ≈ 11.3 in the real model) stops the scores from growing just because the rows are long, which would make softmax too sharp. M adds −∞ where the mask forbids looking. Softmax turns the scores into shares that add up to 1, and the output is the values mixed by those shares. Example: shares 0.7, 0.2 and 0.1 give 0.7·v₁ + 0.2·v₂ + 0.1·v₃.
Picture it
Shining a torch over the other words: the higher a word’s score, the more of its value you take home. Dividing by √d_k is turning down a microphone that would otherwise get louder the longer the rows are.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Asking three colleagues
  1. q = (1, 0); keys (2, 0), (0, 2), (1, 1); d_k = 2 → scores 1.41, 0.00, 0.71.
  2. Softmax → shares 0.576, 0.140, 0.284.
  3. Values 10, 20, 30 → 0.576 × 10 + 0.140 × 20 + 0.284 × 30 = 17.08.
So: You lean on the colleague whose key matches.
Example 2 · “sleeping”, head 0, in the tiny model
  1. It may look at <SOS>, the, cat, is, sleeping (the mask hides the rest).
  2. Shares: <SOS> 77.9%, the 0.7%, cat 11.4%, is 2.7%, sleeping 7.2%.
  3. The largest, 77.9%, goes to “<SOS>”.
So: Heads often park their attention on <SOS> when they need little from the other words — a well-known habit (an “attention sink”); the next largest share goes to “cat”.
MultiHead(X)=Concat(head1,…,headh)Wo⊤+bo
The heads are put back side by side and mixed by one more matrix.
In plain English
Each head returns its own slice of numbers per token; the heads are glued back side by side (Concat) into a full row. One last matrix W_o mixes them, so what one head found can be combined with what another found.
Picture it
Four reporters covering the same scene from different angles: their notes are stapled together, and an editor (W_o) writes one combined story.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Two heads, by hand
  1. Head 1 returns (1, 2), head 2 returns (3, 4) → Concat = (1, 2, 3, 4).
  2. W_o rows (0.5, 0, 0.5, 0) and (0, 1, 0, −1): output (2.0, −2.0).
So: W_o mixes what the heads found.
Example 2 · The real model
  1. 4 heads × 128 = 512 numbers → W_o is 512 × 512 = 262,144 weights + 512 biases.
So: The merge costs as much as one of Q, K or V.

The mathsRoPE: positions as rotationsapply_rope, on every query and key of self-attention3 formulas · 6 worked examples
θi=base−2i/dk,i=0,…,dk2−1
One speed per pair of numbers: fast for the first pair, very slow for the last.
In plain English
A head’s numbers are read as pairs, and each pair is like a clock hand that will be turned. θ_i is how fast pair i turns per position: pair 0 at 1 radian (57°) per word, the next ones slower and slower, the last of the real model’s 64 at about 0.00012. Fast pairs tell neighbouring words apart; slow pairs can still tell far-apart positions apart without going round the clock.
Picture it
A clock with many hands, each turning at its own speed: the fast hand tells moments close together apart, the slow hand tells far-apart times apart.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · The real model (d_k = 128)
  1. θ₀ = 10000⁰ = 1 · θ₁ = 10000^(−2/128) = 0.866 · θ₁₀ = 0.237.
  2. θ₆₃ = 10000^(−126/128) = 1.2 × 10⁻⁴.
So: 64 speeds from fast to almost still.
Example 2 · The tiny model (d_k = 4)
  1. θ₀ = 1, θ₁ = 10000^(−2/4) = 0.01.
So: Just a fast hand and a slow hand.
[q′2iq′2i+1]=[cospθi−sinpθisinpθicospθi][q2iq2i+1]
Pair i of the token at position p is turned by the angle p·θ_i (the same for keys).
In plain English
This is the usual way to turn a point (x, y) around the centre by an angle: new x = x·cos − y·sin, new y = x·sin + y·cos. The angle is position × speed, so a word at position 5 is turned five times as far as one at position 1. The pair keeps its length and changes only its direction: the word keeps its meaning and gains its position as a turn.
Picture it
Turning a compass needle: it keeps its length — the word’s meaning — and only its direction changes, by an amount set by the word’s position.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · A clock hand at position 3 (θ = 1)
  1. Angle 3 × 1 = 3 rad = 171.9°.
  2. (1, 0) → (cos 3, sin 3) = (−0.990, 0.141); length 1.
So: Turned, never stretched.
Example 2 · The pair (3, 4) at position 1 (θ = 1)
  1. (3 cos 1 − 4 sin 1, 3 sin 1 + 4 cos 1) = (−1.745, 4.686).
  2. Length before 5, after 5.000.
So: The word’s numbers keep their size.
q′m·k′n=qm⊤Rn−mkn
After both turns, the score depends on how far apart the two tokens are, not on where they stand.
In plain English
Attention compares a query and a key by a dot product, which depends on the angle between them. Turn the query by m steps and the key by n steps, and the angle between them changes by n − m steps. So “the word two places before me” looks the same at the start of a sentence as in the middle: the model learns relative positions, not absolute ones.
Picture it
Two dancers who each turn by their own position: the angle between them depends only on how many places apart they stand, wherever they are on the floor.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Two words 2 apart, anywhere
  1. q = k = (1, 0), θ = 1. Query at 2, key at 0: cos(2 − 0) = −0.416.
  2. Query at 7, key at 5: cos(7 − 5) = −0.416.
So: Only the distance reaches the score.
Example 2 · Near and far
  1. Query at 5, key at 4 (distance 1): cos 1 = 0.540.
  2. Key at 0 (distance 5): cos 5 = 0.284.
So: Different distances give different scores.

The mathsOne layer: three additionsDecoderLayer.forward (the encoder layer has the first and the last)3 formulas · 6 worked examples
x←x+SelfAttn(RMSNorm1(x))
The answer looks at itself — earlier tokens only.
In plain English
x is the stream: one row per token, which each block adds to. First a levelled copy goes into masked self-attention, where each word of the answer gathers from the words before it. The result is added to x, not put in its place, so nothing that was there is lost — a residual connection. It also lets the training signal flow straight back through many layers.
Picture it
Writing notes in the margin instead of rewriting the page: what was there stays readable, and each block adds its own note.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Margin notes, by hand
  1. x = (1.0, 2.0); self-attention returns (0.3, −0.5) → x = (1.3, 1.5).
So: Added, not replaced.
Example 2 · “sleeping” in the tiny model
  1. x starts (−1.28, 0.63, −0.04); self-attention adds (−0.42, 0.71, 0.14) → (−1.70, 1.34, 0.10).
So: What it gathered from the earlier words joins its own numbers.
x←x+CrossAttn(RMSNorm2(x),H)
It looks at the sentence being read.
In plain English
Second, cross-attention: queries from the answer, keys and values from H, the encoder’s reading of the source sentence. This is where the decoder reads: while writing a word it can look mostly at the source words that word depends on.
Picture it
A translator glancing back at the source between words: the answer so far asks, the source sentence answers.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · By hand
  1. x = (1.3, 1.5); cross-attention returns (0.1, 0.4) → (1.4, 1.9).
So: The source sentence adds its part.
Example 2 · “sleeping” in the tiny model
  1. x (−1.70, 1.34, 0.10) + cross-attention (0.79, 0.19, 1.61) = (−0.91, 1.52, 1.70).
So: This is where the sentence being read enters.
x←x+FFN(RMSNorm3(x))
Each token is worked on by itself.
In plain English
Third, the feed-forward works on each token alone. The pattern is always the same — level a copy, compute, add — so layers can be stacked: each receives a stream of the same shape and hands one on.
Picture it
After the group discussion, each person thinks alone for a moment — then adds their conclusions to their own notes.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · By hand, and a block with nothing to say
  1. x = (1.4, 1.9); feed-forward returns (−0.2, 0.6) → (1.2, 2.5).
  2. A block that returns (0.01, −0.02) leaves x almost as it was — replacing x would have erased it.
So: Adding lets a block safely do almost nothing.
Example 2 · “sleeping” in the tiny model
  1. x (−0.91, 1.52, 1.70) + feed-forward (0.11, 1.37, 1.53) = (−0.80, 2.90, 3.23) — what layer 0 hands to layer 1.
So: Three additions make one layer.

The mathsChoosing the next token_block_special, then argmax2 formulas · 4 worked examples
z′v={−∞v∈{PAD,SOS}zvotherwise
Two tokens can never be written.
In plain English
Two tokens are never a valid output: <PAD> is only filler and <SOS> only marks the start. Setting their scores to −∞ makes their e^score 0, so they can never be chosen, whatever the model says.
Picture it
Two names crossed off the ballot before the vote: whatever happens, they cannot win.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Crossing two names off the ballot
  1. Scores: <PAD> 2.5, <SOS> 1.0, cat 2.0, dog 1.2 — unblocked, <PAD> would take 47.6%.
  2. Blocked: <PAD> and <SOS> → −∞; cat 69.0%, dog 31.0%.
So: They can never be written.
Example 2 · The tiny model after “<SOS> the cat is”
  1. Logits of <PAD> −0.49 and <SOS> −0.49, against “sleeping” 4.57.
  2. After blocking, their probability is 0 instead of 0.57% and 0.57%.
So: Training already made them unlikely; blocking makes it certain.
yt=argmaxvz′v=argmaxvpv
Greedy decoding takes the highest score. Softmax keeps the order, so the highest logit is also the most probable token.
In plain English
argmax means “the position of the largest value”. Softmax never changes the order of the scores — a bigger score always gets a bigger probability — so the token with the highest logit is also the most probable one. When only the top token is needed, the softmax can be skipped.
Picture it
Picking the tallest person in a room: there is no need to work out everyone’s share of the total height — the tallest is the tallest either way.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · The tallest stays the tallest
  1. Logits 3.0, 1.0, 0.5 → p = 82.1%, 11.1%, 6.7%.
  2. The largest logit is also the largest probability.
So: Greedy decoding can skip the softmax.
Example 2 · The tiny model, all 7 positions of sequence B
  1. argmax of each row: the cat is sleeping peac efully <EOS>.
  2. All 7 match the right next tokens.
So: Greedy on the trained model writes the sentence right.

The mathsSampling instead of argmaxtemperature, top-k and top-p, in the order generate() applies them3 formulas · 6 worked examples
pv∝exp(zvT)
Dividing the logits by T sharpens the probabilities (T < 1) or flattens them (T > 1).
In plain English
Temperature sets how bold the choice is. Dividing the scores by T < 1 stretches the gaps between them, so the top token gets even more likely; T > 1 shrinks the gaps, so rarer tokens get more of a chance. Example: scores 2 and 1 give 0.73 and 0.27; with T = 0.5 they become 0.88 and 0.12; with T = 2, 0.62 and 0.38.
Picture it
The contrast knob on a photo: low temperature sharpens the differences, high temperature washes them out.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Pizza 2, sushi 1, salad 0
  1. T = 1: 66.5% / 24.5% / 9.0%.
  2. T = 0.5: 86.7% / 11.7% / 1.6%.
  3. T = 2: 50.6% / 30.7% / 18.6%.
So: The temperature only rescales the gaps.
Example 2 · Cell 9’s temperature, 0.8
  1. Two words with logits 2.0 and 1.0: T = 1 gives 73.1%; T = 0.8 gives 77.7% to the first.
So: Slightly bolder than the plain probabilities.
keep v if zv≥z(k)
Top-k: only the k highest logits keep their chance; the rest are set to −∞.
In plain English
Top-k throws away every token outside the k best before drawing, so a very unlikely — often nonsensical — token can never be picked by bad luck. With k = 5 only the five highest-scored tokens remain, and their probabilities are shared out again to add up to 1.
Picture it
A shortlist: only the five finalists stay in the hat, so no long shot can be drawn by bad luck.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · A shortlist of two (k = 2)
  1. Pizza 2, sushi 1, salad 0 → keep the 2 best: shares 73.1% and 26.9%.
So: A long shot can never win by luck.
Example 2 · k = 5 among 7 candidates
  1. Probabilities 0.40, 0.20, 0.15, 0.10, 0.07, 0.05, 0.03; the 5 best hold 0.92.
  2. Shared again: 0.435, 0.217, 0.163, 0.109, 0.076.
So: The last two drop out completely.
yt∼p
Then a token is drawn at random by the probabilities. Top-p and the repetition penalty: deep dives 11 and 12.
In plain English
∼ means “draw at random with these chances”: a token with probability 0.6 is drawn about 6 times in 10. Unlike argmax, the same sentence can come out differently each time — good for variety, riskier for accuracy.
Picture it
Drawing a name from a hat in which each name appears as often as its probability says: the favourite usually wins, but not always.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · 100 dinners with pizza at 73%
  1. Drawing 100 times: about 73 pizza and 27 sushi.
So: The favourite usually wins.
Example 2 · Three draws
  1. The chance that sushi (27%) comes up at least once in 3 draws: 1 − 0.73³ = 61.1%.
So: Over a long sentence, less likely words do appear.

The model
GQA and QK-Norm · experts · the multi-token head · speculative decodingunchanged in v1.5
In one sentenceThe model itself, changed in six places: attention, the experts, the multi-token head, the cap — and a way to write two words per pass.
In plain words
Cell 2 is the model itself: every class the notebook defines. v3 changes it in six places — two about the scores (QK-Norm and a soft cap), two about attention’s cost (shared key/value heads, attention without a mask), one about the feed-forward (a mixture of experts) and one about writing (a multi-token head, whose guesses speculative decoding checks). The page has three parts: attention, then the experts and the head, then writing.
Picture it
Think of a workshop that already makes good furniture (v2.5). v3 changes six things about its machines and nothing about what they make: safety stops so no tool can run away, one tool rack shared by two benches, a request that lets a bought-in measuring machine skip laying every piece out on the floor, two specialists picked from four for each job, and an apprentice who prepares the next piece while the master checks the current one.
Each change sits in a different part of cell 2: attention (QK-Norm, the shared key/value heads, the causal call), the feed-forward (the experts), and the very end of the model (the cap, the multi-token head and speculative decoding).
Another way to see itOr a car given a speed limiter, a smaller fuel tank and a navigator who reads out the next turn: the same journey, made differently.
Where the picture stops workingA workshop’s improvements are sure; these were measured. On this small model the safety stops never had to act and the specialists did not help, while the shared racks and the apprentice did what they promise (deep dives 18–26).

What v3 changes here — and why it helps
  • QK-Norm — every query and key brought to the same size: a score can no longer grow with them
  • a soft cap on the output scores — nearly nothing changes, but no score can pass 30
  • grouped-query attention — half the keys and values to keep while writing
  • causal attention without a mask — the same numbers; PyTorch may then pick its built-in FlashAttention — only on a suitable GPU (deep dive 20)
  • a mixture of experts and a multi-token head — more to learn with, a second lesson per word
  • speculative decoding — two words per pass when the head’s guess is right, the same answers
A worked example, with this page’s real numbers
The tiny v3 model, on the last token of “the cat is sleeping peacefully”:
  1. Its query in head 0 is (5.08, 0.18) — RMS 3.596. After q_norm: (1.74, 0.07).
  2. Its largest score in that head would be 30.82 without the norm; with it, 2.25.
  3. At the end the cap moves its 15 output scores by at most 0.0227: the next token is the same.
  4. Writing for “the cat is running on the sof a”, a sentence it never saw, it needs 5 passes for 7 tokens: one guess was wrong.
Same answers, scores that stay in range, fewer passes.

The tokenizer
definitions · 5 rewritesunchanged since v2unchanged since v2unchanged in v1.5
What you’ll learn
How the BPE tokenizer was rebuilt to train on 50,000 words in seconds, why its vocabulary can now spell any word, and how each change was checked.
The big idea
Byte-pair encoding starts from single letters and repeatedly glues together the pair of neighbours that appears most often, until it has learned 16,000 such merges. The algorithm is unchanged. The bookkeeping is new: v1.5 recounted every pair in every word before each merge — fine for four sentences, painfully slow for 50,000 words. v2 counts once, keeps the counts in a priority queue (a heap), and after each merge updates only the words that contained the merged pair.
A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers
Measured here, on the real word list:
  1. v1.5’s loop takes 0.132 s per merge, about 35 minutes for all 16,000. v2’s heap takes 2.6 s for all of them.
  2. Encoding "peacefully" now takes 8 steps, each applying the earliest-learned merge present — instead of walking all 16,000 merges.
  3. Both ways of encoding give the same spelling for all 311 words checked.
  4. v1.5’s vocabulary rule would keep 15,764 tokens; v2 keeps 16,111, so 347 pieces — including two lone digits — can no longer fall out.
Same merges, same spellings, a fraction of the time — and nothing unseen becomes <UNK>.
What to look forSection A maps each method to the cell that calls it. Section B puts each rewritten method beside v1.5’s: counts from ranks, heap training with its timing, the vocabulary rule, rank-based encoding, and save / load.
In one sentenceThe tokenizer glues the most frequent neighbouring letters together, 16,000 times, until common words are single pieces.
In plain words
Cell 3 is the tokenizer: the code that learns word pieces from the word list and then cuts any text into them. Nothing in this cell changed in v2.5: its code is v2’s line for line (only v2’s own [NEW] comments are renamed [v2]), so the picture below is v2’s page, and still exact.
Picture it
Imagine inventing a shorthand from scratch. You start with single letters. You look through a huge pile of text for the two symbols that stand side by side most often — say “t” and “h” — and give that pair a symbol of its own, “th”. Then you look again: perhaps “th” and “e” are now the most common pair, so “the” gets a symbol. You repeat this 16,000 times.
At the end the common words are one symbol each, and rare or brand-new words can still be written from a few smaller pieces — “unbelievably” becomes “un” + “believ” + “ably_”. No word is ever impossible to write. That is byte-pair encoding (BPE). The list of all the symbols is the vocabulary, 16,111 tokens; each has a number, its id, and from here on the model sees only ids.
Another way to see itOr LEGO: common shapes come as ready-made pieces, but any rare shape can still be built from small bricks.
Where the picture stops workingThe tokenizer only counts. It has no idea that “cat” and “cats” are related — the model has to learn that later, from examples.

The mathsBPE encoding: the earliest-learned pair first_encode_word3 formulas · 6 worked examples
s=(c1,c2,…,cn</w>)
A word starts as its characters, the last one marked as the end of a word.
In plain English
Encoding starts from the smallest pieces: single letters. The last one is marked with </w> so the tokenizer knows where the word ends — “er</w>” at the end of “runner” is a different piece from “er” inside “very”. Example: “cat” starts as c, a, t</w>.
Picture it
Taking a word apart into single LEGO bricks, with a special end brick so you know where one word stops.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · “cat” and “sleeping”
  1. “cat” → c, a, t</w>.
  2. “sleeping” → s, l, e, e, p, i, n, g</w>: 8 pieces.
So: Every word starts as letters, the last one marked.
Example 2 · Why the end mark
  1. “er” at the end of “runner” becomes er</w>; inside “very” it is plain e, r.
  2. So er</w> and er are two different pieces.
So: The tokenizer knows where words end.
i*=argminirank(si,si+1)
Of all neighbouring pairs, take the one learned first (lowest rank)…
In plain English
Training learned its merges in order: merge 0 was the most frequent pair, merge 1 the next, and so on. To encode a word, the tokenizer looks at every pair of neighbouring pieces and takes the one learned earliest (the smallest rank). A pair never learned has rank ∞ and is never taken.
Picture it
Snapping bricks together in the order the instruction book lists the steps: the step learned earliest in training is done first.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · “cat” with the real ranks
  1. Pairs of c, a, t</w>: (c, a) rank 492, (a, t</w>) rank 28.
  2. argmin → (a, t</w>), the one learned earlier.
So: Rank = when the pair was learned.
Example 2 · The first choice in “sleeping”
  1. Among its 7 pairs the lowest rank is (i, n), rank 2 — the 3rd merge ever learned.
So: Common pairs merge first.
s←merge(s,i*)
…glue it into one symbol, and repeat until no neighbouring pair was ever learned.
In plain English
That pair is glued into one piece and the search starts again on the shorter list, until no neighbouring pair is a learned merge. A common word such as “cat” ends as a single token, cat</w>; a rare word stops earlier and stays split into a few pieces — so no word is ever completely unknown.
Picture it
Keep snapping until no listed step applies: common words end as one ready-made piece, rare words as a few smaller pieces.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · “cat”, to the end
  1. c a t</w> → (rank 28) c at</w> → (rank 6,591) cat</w>: one token.
So: A common word ends as one piece.
Example 2 · “peacefully”
  1. 8 merges, ranks 32, 46, 91, 153, 647, 1,199, 5,099, 6,410.
  2. It stops at peac + efully</w> — (peac, efully</w>) was never learned.
So: A rarer word is spelled from known pieces.
symbolwhat it isin the notebook
ckthe word’s characters
</w>end of word
rank(a,b)when the pair (a, b) was learned: 0 for the first merge; ∞ if never0 to 15,999
sthe symbols so far; at the end, the tokens
Ranks make encoding follow training: a pair learned early (frequent) always wins over one learned later.

two pairs · no splitunchanged since v2unchanged since v2unchanged in v1.5
What you’ll learn
Where the training pairs come from, how they are shuffled, and why — with only 2 pairs — the validation set is the training set.
The big idea
To know whether a model has learned or only memorised, you test it on examples it never trained on, like an exam with new questions. v2 can hold back a tenth of its pairs for that — but only when there are at least 20. With two, splitting would leave nothing to learn from, so validation re-reads the training pairs and the notebook prints a warning saying so.
A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers
What runs, in order:
  1. There is no pairs.tsv, so the two built-in pairs are copied into all_pairs.
  2. random.Random(0) shuffles them — and leaves them in their original order, so sequence A is still "the dog sat on the floor".
  3. 2 is less than 20: train_pairs and val_pairs become the same list.
Every "validation" number in cell 8 is therefore a measure of memorisation.
What to look forFrames 1 to 5 follow every branch and the lines it prints. Section B shows the two new features and a small table of what the split would do with more data.
In one sentenceTwo example pairs — a sentence and the answer it should get — split into practice and test.
In plain words
Cell 4 holds the training data — two sentence pairs — and splits it into training and validation. Nothing in this cell changed in v2.5: its code is v2’s line for line (only v2’s own [NEW] comments are renamed [v2]), so the picture below is v2’s page, and still exact.
Picture it
A teacher preparing flash cards: on the front a sentence, on the back the answer the model should write. This notebook has only two cards: “the dog sat on the floor” → “dog resting”, and “the cat is sleeping on the sofa” → “the cat is sleeping peacefully”.
A good teacher keeps some cards back for the exam, so the test shows whether the student learned the pattern and not just the cards. That is validation. With two cards there is nothing to spare, so the cell says so honestly and uses the same two cards for the test: here the exam can only show memory. Put thousands of pairs in a file called pairs.tsv and the cell holds back a tenth by itself.
Another way to see itOr a driving test taken on the same street you practised on: passing shows you learned that street, not how to drive.
Where the picture stops workingReal translation models learn from millions of pairs. Two are enough to show every line of code working, not to learn a language.

A teacher preparing flash cards: on the front a sentence, on the back the answer the model should write. This notebook has only two cards: “the dog sat on the floor” → “dog resting”, and “the cat is sleeping on the sofa” → “the cat is sleeping peacefully”.
A good teacher keeps some cards back for the exam, so the test shows whether the student learned the pattern and not just the cards. That is validation. With two cards there is nothing to spare, so the cell says so honestly and uses the same two cards for the test: here the exam can only show memory. Put thousands of pairs in a file called pairs.tsv and the cell holds back a tenth by itself.
Another way to see itOr a driving test taken on the same street you practised on: passing shows you learned that street, not how to drive.
Where the picture stops workingReal translation models learn from millions of pairs. Two are enough to show every line of code working, not to learn a language.

nval={max(1,⌊N/10⌋)if N≥20none: validation = trainingif N<20
One pair in ten is held back after a fixed shuffle (seed 0), and never trained on.
In plain English
To know whether the model has learned the task or only memorised its examples, some pairs are put aside and never trained on: the validation set. Here it is one pair in ten (at least one), chosen after a shuffle with a fixed seed, so every run holds back the same pairs. With fewer than 20 pairs there is nothing to spare, so the notebook validates on the training pairs — a score that can only show memorising.
Picture it
A teacher who keeps some exam questions back: if the students only memorised the practice sheet, the held-back questions will show it.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Three data sets
  1. 1,000 pairs → max(1, ⌊1,000 ÷ 10⌋) = 100 for validation, 900 for training.
  2. 25 pairs → max(1, 2) = 2 and 23. The notebook’s 2 pairs → below 20: validation = training.
So: Below 20 pairs the score shows memorising.
Example 2 · A teacher’s held-back questions
  1. Practise on 90 questions, test on 10 unseen ones: 90% on practice but 40% on the test means memorising.
So: Validation is the questions never practised.
