Train the tokenizer
cell 5 → cell 3 → cell 5unchanged since v2unchanged since v2unchanged in v1.5
What you’ll learn
How the tokenizer is actually trained: counts from ranks, the heap popping pairs, merges applied only where needed, the final vocabulary, and two sentences split with it.
The big idea
This is the first page where a call stack crosses cells: the lines run in cell 5, but most of the work happens inside cell 3’s train(). Think of the heap as a leaderboard of letter pairs, sorted by how often they occur. Each round the top pair is taken off, merged into one symbol everywhere it appears, and the scores of its neighbours are updated. An entry whose score changed after it was posted is stale; it is simply skipped when it comes up.
A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers
The first run, with no saved tokenizer:
  1. Starting from 107 distinct symbols, the heap’s first pop is t + h, counted 1,567,269 times across 1,313 words.
  2. Next it pops h + e</w>, posted at 1,072,363 — but most of those were inside "the", now merged, so its real count is 71,703: stale, skipped.
  3. After 16,000 merges (2.6 s here) the vocabulary has 16,111 tokens.
  4. "floor" becomes a single token in 4 merges.
The file it saves makes every later run skip all of this — and keeps the ids fixed.
What to look forThe strip at the top shows the stack moving between cells 5 and 3. Frame 4 is the sentence words’ counts. Then the merge loop, one pop per frame: merge 1, the stale entry it leaves behind, merge 2 — with a chart of how few words each merge touches against v1.5’s full recount. Then the vocabulary’s layout and two sentences split. Section B compares v1.5’s tokens.
In one sentenceBuild the tokenizer once and save it, so the same word always gets the same number.
In plain words
Cell 5 trains the tokenizer once and saves it, or loads it if it was saved before. Nothing in this cell changed in v2.5: its code is v2’s line for line (only v2’s own [NEW] comments are renamed [v2]), so the picture below is v2’s page, and still exact.
Picture it
You invented your shorthand once (cell 3). Now you write the list of symbols down, so tomorrow you use exactly the same ones — otherwise yesterday’s notes would become unreadable. Cell 5 does that: if tokenizer.json already exists it loads it; if not, it trains the tokenizer on the word list and saves it.
Before training it builds the counts: each of the 50,000 words gets a count from its rank (common words count more), and every word of the training pairs is added on top, so the notebook’s own words are sure to be covered. Afterwards it prints two test sentences cut into tokens, so you can see the result.
Another way to see itLike keeping the key to a code: a message written with one key can only be read with that same key.
Where the picture stops workingChange the word list and you must set RETRAIN_TOKENIZER = True — otherwise the old file is loaded and quietly keeps the old pieces.

The mathsTraining BPE: merge the most frequent pairBPETokenizer.train, on Zipf counts3 formulas · 6 worked examples
f(w)=max(1,round(106r(w)))+c(w)
Every word gets its Zipf count (cell 0) plus how often it appears in the sentence pairs.
In plain English
BPE needs to know how common each word is. Each word of the 50,000-word list gets its Zipf estimate (cell 0), and every time it appears in the sentence pairs adds 1 — so the task’s own words always count.
Picture it
Estimating how much each word is used from its place in a ranking, then adding the times it really appears in your own texts.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · “the”, “cat” and “sofa” in the notebook
  1. “the”: 1,000,000 from the list + 5 uses in the two sentence pairs = 1,000,005.
  2. “cat”: 309 + 2 = 311 · “sofa”: 90 + 1 = 91.
So: List counts and data counts simply add.
Example 2 · A word only in the data
  1. A made-up word used 3 times in the pairs but not in the list: 0 + 3 = 3.
So: The task’s own words always count.
count(a,b)=∑wf(w)·nw(a,b)
A pair of neighbouring symbols counts once for every time a word containing it is used.
In plain English
To find which pieces belong together, every pair of neighbouring pieces in every word is counted, weighted by how often the word is used. Example: “the” counts 1,000,000, so the pair (t, h) inside it gets 1,000,000 from that word alone.
Picture it
Counting which letter pairs turn up most often across everything you read, with popular words counted many times over.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · (t, h) in six common words
  1. the 1,000,000, this 52,632, their 28,571, there 24,390, other 20,408, then 12,987.
  2. Each has t, h once: 1,138,988 from these six alone; with all 1,313 words that contain it, 1,567,269.
So: A pair collects the counts of every word it is in.
Example 2 · A pair inside one word twice
  1. “banana” has (a, n) twice: a word used 50 times adds 2 × 50 = 100 to count(a, n).
So: n_w(a, b) counts every place the pair occurs.
(a,b)*=argmax(a,b)count(a,b)
Merge the most frequent pair into a new symbol, update the counts, and repeat — 16,000 times, or until no pair is seen twice.
In plain English
The most frequent pair becomes a new piece — (t, h) becomes th — every word is re-spelled with it, the counts are updated, and the next most frequent pair is merged: 16,000 times. Common words end up as single tokens; rare ones are spelled with a few common pieces.
Picture it
Inventing a shorthand: the pair you write most often gets its own symbol, then the next — like texting abbreviations, but chosen by counting.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · The notebook’s first merge
  1. Top counts at the start: (t, h) 1,567,269; (h, e</w>) 1,072,363; (i, n) 765,322.
  2. argmax → (t, h): merged into “th”.
So: The most frequent pair becomes a new piece.
Example 2 · The second merge — the counts have changed
  1. (h, e</w>) disappeared: its h was swallowed by “th”.
  2. Now: (th, e</w>) 1,000,660; (i, n) 765,322; (a, n) 698,452 → argmax (th, e</w>).
So: After every merge the counts are taken again.

r(w)the word’s rank in the list1 to 50,000
c(w)its count in the sentence pairs
nw(a,b)how often a is followed by b inside word w

Dataset and DataLoader
(2, 8) and (2, 8)unchanged since v2unchanged since v2unchanged in v1.5
What you’ll learn
How the two pairs become two padded rectangles of ids: encoding, the length limit, and padding that is decided one batch at a time.
The big idea
A tensor must be a rectangle, so shorter sentences are filled out with <PAD> (id 0). v1.5 padded everything to the longest sentence in the whole data set. v2’s DataLoader groups sentences into batches and pads each batch only to ITS longest sentence — like packing each box to fit what is in it rather than using one box size for everything.
A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers
With two pairs there is one batch:
  1. Sequence A’s source is 6 ids, B’s is 8: the batch is (2, 8), with A padded by 2.
  2. The targets gain <SOS> and <EOS>: the batch is (2, 8), with A padded by 4.
  3. Nothing is longer than 64 tokens, so nothing is cut.
With thousands of pairs of different lengths, dynamic padding is what keeps most of each batch real data rather than zeros.
What to look forThe first frames build the dataset (and call into cell 3 to encode). The collate frame, reached from cell 8’s loop, draws the two padded rectangles. Section B compares v1.5’s hand-made batch.
In one sentenceSentences become rectangles of ids, each batch padded only to its own longest sentence.
In plain words
Cell 6 turns the pairs into batches of token ids, padding each batch only as much as it needs. Nothing in this cell changed in v2.5: its code is v2’s line for line (only v2’s own [NEW] comments are renamed [v2]), so the picture below is v2’s page, and still exact.
Picture it
Imagine posting several letters together in one parcel. The parcel has to be a rectangle, so the shorter letters get a blank strip at the end until they are as long as the longest one. Cell 6 does this with sentences: it turns each pair into token ids and packs a few pairs into a batch; the shorter sentences are filled up with <PAD> tokens.
The trick, since v2, is dynamic padding: each parcel is only as long as its own longest letter, not as long as the longest letter in the whole post office. Less blank space means less wasted arithmetic. Later a mask tells attention to ignore every blank, so the padding changes nothing.
Another way to see itOr a row of seats at the cinema: a group of three next to a group of five, the shorter row left with empty seats that nobody looks at.
Where the picture stops workingPadding is pure bookkeeping. The model learns nothing from it — which is exactly why the mask has to hide it.

The mathsCut, add <SOS> and <EOS>, pad per batchSeq2SeqDataset and collate3 formulas · 6 worked examples
src=ids1:64
The sentence to read is cut to 64 tokens.
In plain English
ids₁:₆₄ means the first 64 token ids. Longer sentences are cut so that one very long example cannot blow up memory; 64 is plenty for the short sentences this notebook trains on.
Picture it
A word limit on an essay: anything beyond 64 tokens is cut, so one huge example cannot take all the room.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · A 70-token sentence
  1. ids₁:₆₄ keeps the first 64 tokens; 6 are cut.
So: One long example cannot blow up memory.
Example 2 · A 10-token sentence
  1. 10 ≤ 64: kept whole, all 10 tokens.
So: Short sentences are not touched.
tgt=(SOS,ids,EOS)
The answer gets its start and end tokens (if too long, the first 63 tokens and <EOS>).
In plain English
The answer gets <SOS> in front — the signal to start writing — and <EOS> at the end: the token the model must learn to produce to say “done”. A too-long answer is cut to 63 tokens and <EOS> is put back, so every answer still ends properly.
Picture it
Quotation marks around a sentence: <SOS> says the answer starts here, <EOS> says it is finished.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Sequence B in the tiny model
  1. “the cat is sleeping peac efully” → ids 14, 4, 8, 12, 10, 6.
  2. With <SOS> (1) and <EOS> (2): 1, 14, 4, 8, 12, 10, 6, 2.
So: The answer is framed by its start and end tokens.
Example 2 · A 70-token answer
  1. 1 + 70 + 1 = 72 > 64 → the first 63 and <EOS> = 64.
So: Even a cut answer still ends with <EOS>.
Lbatch=maxb∈batch|seqb|
Each batch is padded with <PAD> only up to its own longest sentence.
In plain English
A batch must be a rectangle, so shorter sentences are filled up with <PAD>. Padding only to the longest sentence of each batch, not always to 64, saves work: a batch of short sentences stays short. The masks then make sure the padding is ignored.
Picture it
Packing a box only as long as its longest item: short items get padding, and a box of short items stays small.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Three sentences of 5, 9 and 7 tokens
  1. L_batch = max(5, 9, 7) = 9 → 27 cells, 6 <PAD> (22%).
  2. Padded to 64 every time: 192 cells, 171 <PAD> (89%).
So: Padding per batch saves most of the wasted work.
Example 2 · The tiny model’s batch
  1. Sources of 8 and 4 tokens → L_batch = 8; the shorter gets 4 <PAD>.
So: Each batch is as wide as its longest sentence.

Building the model
The model built, weight decay aimed only at weight matrices, and an averaged copy of the weights.
Building the model
The model built, and two optimizers: Muon and AdamW.
CELL 7
Model, optimizer, AMP
22,979,823 parametersunchanged in v1.5
What you’ll learn
How the model is actually built: the constructor from cell 2 running for real, every weight drawn, the parameters counted, and the optimizer, schedule, loss and precision set up around it.
The big idea
Until now there were only blueprints. Transformer(**model_config) builds the model: it creates every layer and fills every weight matrix with small random numbers, sized by the Xavier rule so signals neither shrink nor explode as they pass through. Around the model, this cell sets up how it will learn: AdamW decides how each weight moves, the schedule decides how big the steps are over time, and the loss decides what counts as a mistake.
A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers
The numbers this cell produces:
  1. 22,979,823 parameters, of which the one tied embedding table is 8,248,832 (35.9%).
  2. That table is drawn from ±0.0190; its <PAD> row is then set to zero.
  3. The learning rate warms up to 5e-4 by step 9, glides down a cosine, and sits at its 5% floor from step 173.
  4. With 16,111 tokens and label smoothing 0.1, even a perfect model scores at least 1.2937.
On a current Colab T4, the precision code picks bf16 without a GradScaler — not the fp16 path the notebook’s comment describes.
What to look forFrames 3 to 8 are the constructor in cell 2; frame 8 shows real rows of the table. Then the parameter breakdown, the optimizer, the schedule chart (v2 against v1.5), the loss, and a table of which precision each machine gets. Section B compares the schedules.
CELL 7
Model, optimizer, EMA, mixed precision
decay on matrices only · an average of the weightsunchanged in v1.5
In one sentenceBuild the model, a tutor that decays only real weights, and a slow average of the weights for exams.
In plain words
Cell 7 builds everything training needs: the model from its settings, the optimizer that nudges the parameters, the learning-rate schedule, the loss, and — new in v2.5 — a second, slow-moving copy of the weights, the EMA.
Picture it
Think of a student preparing for an exam. Everything they know right now is the model’s weights. After each lesson a tutor corrects them a little — that is the optimizer, AdamW. The tutor also has a habit: at every lesson they gently trim whatever has grown too big, so no single habit takes over (weight decay). v2.5 teaches the tutor to trim only the real habits — the big tables of numbers — and to leave alone the few settings that must stay where they are: the volume dials of the normalisers (gains) and the small offsets (biases).
The student also keeps study notes that are rewritten only a little at a time. One bad lesson barely changes them, and they hold what was learned over many lessons. That is the EMA: a second copy of all 22,979,823 numbers that follows the weights slowly. At the exam — validation and saving — the notes are used, not the jittery latest state.
The same cell sets how big the corrections are over time (the learning-rate schedule) and how a wrong guess is judged (the loss); both are v2’s.
Another way to see itOr a pilot who steers by the heading averaged over the last minute, not by every gust of wind.
Where the picture stops workingAt the very start the notes would just be random numbers, so the EMA first follows fast — (1 + step) / (10 + step) — and only slowly settles at 0.999.

parameterweight decayEMAlearning rateloss
What v2.5 changes here — and why it helps
  • weight decay only on weight matrices — gains and biases are no longer shrunk toward 0 for no reason
  • an EMA of the weights, used for validation and the checkpoint — a smoothed model instead of one step’s snapshot
A worked example, with this page’s real numbers
On this model and this run:
  1. Decay acts on 22,945,280 numbers in 37 matrices; the 34,543 numbers in 37 gains and biases are left alone.
  2. Over this short run decay would shrink a gain only to ×0.9996; over a long run (100,000 steps) to ×0.74 — that is the harm avoided.
  3. The EMA starts as a copy of the random weights and follows training more slowly as steps accumulate: about the last 11 steps by the end of this run.
The model itself is v2’s size: 22,979,823 parameters.
Where to lookSection A is the stack: the count, the two groups, the EMA’s growing window. Section B puts each change beside v2’s line.
The mathsAdamW: one update of every weightoptim.AdamW(betas=(0.9, 0.98), eps=1e-9)4 formulas · 8 worked examples
θ←θ−ηλθ
Decoupled weight decay: shrink the weight a little (matrices only, deep dive 14).
In plain English
Weight decay pulls every weight a little towards 0 at each step, so no weight grows bigger than it needs to — a large weight has to keep earning its size. “Decoupled” (the W in AdamW) means this pull is applied directly, apart from the gradient step. With η = 5 × 10⁻⁴ and λ = 0.01, each step keeps 99.9995% of the weight.
Picture it
A small tax on every weight, paid at each step: a weight must keep earning its size, or it slowly shrinks.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · One step on a weight of 2.0
  1. ηλθ = 0.0005 × 0.01 × 2.0 = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ → θ = 1.99999.
So: A tiny pull towards 0 every step.
Example 2 · 10,000 steps on a weight of 0.5 that no gradient supports
  1. 0.5 × (1 − 5 × 10⁻⁶)^10,000 = 0.4756.
So: Tiny pulls add up.
m←β1m+(1−β1)g,v←β2v+(1−β2)g2
Running averages of the gradient and of its square.
In plain English
The gradient g says in which direction the loss would rise for this weight; it is noisy from batch to batch. m is a running average of g — momentum: it keeps rolling in a consistent direction — and v a running average of g², how big the gradients usually are. With β₁ = 0.9, m mostly reflects the last 10 steps or so; with β₂ = 0.98, v the last 50.
Picture it
A ball rolling downhill: m is its momentum, which carries it the same way through small bumps; v is a record of how bumpy the road usually is.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · A steady gradient of 1.0
  1. step 1: m = 0.100, v = 0.0200; step 2: m = 0.190, v = 0.0396; step 3: m = 0.271, v = 0.0588.
So: m and v build up slowly from 0.
Example 2 · A noisy gradient: +1, −1, +1
  1. step 1: m = 0.100; step 2: m = −0.010; step 3: m = 0.091.
  2. v still grows (0.0588): the gradients are big, but m stays small because they cancel.
So: Momentum averages the noise away.
m^=m1−β1t,v^=v1−β2t
Corrected for starting at 0.
In plain English
m and v start at 0, so in the first steps they are too small. Dividing by 1 − βᵗ fixes that: at step 1, 1 − 0.9 = 0.1, and since m is then 0.1·g, m̂ = g exactly. As t grows, βᵗ shrinks to 0 and the correction fades away.
Picture it
A new thermometer that starts at 0°: for the first readings you correct for the fact that it has not warmed up yet.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Step 1
  1. m = 0.1 → m̂ = 0.1 ÷ (1 − 0.9) = 1; v = 0.02 → v̂ = 0.02 ÷ (1 − 0.98) = 1.
So: The correction undoes the start at 0.
Example 2 · Step 100
  1. For m: 1 ÷ (1 − 0.9¹⁰⁰) = 1.00003. For v: 1 ÷ (1 − 0.98¹⁰⁰) = 1.153.
So: Later it fades away.
θ←θ−ηm^v^+ε
Step against the averaged gradient, scaled per weight by how large its gradients usually are.
In plain English
Each weight moves against its averaged gradient. Dividing by √v̂ gives every weight a step of about the same size, whether its gradients are tiny or huge: one with large gradients does not overshoot, one with tiny gradients still moves. ε = 10⁻⁹ only guards against dividing by 0; η sets the overall step size.
Picture it
Hikers each pacing themselves to their own terrain: short careful steps on a steep, rough path, longer ones on a gentle path — η is how fast the whole group walks.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Tiny and huge gradients
  1. g = 0.001: step = η × 0.001 ÷ 0.001 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴.
  2. g = 100: step = η × 100 ÷ 100 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴.
So: Adam sizes each step to the weight’s own gradients.
Example 2 · Steady against noisy, at step 3
  1. Steady: step 5.0 × 10⁻⁴. Noisy (+1, −1, +1): m̂ = 0.336 → step 1.7 × 10⁻⁴.
So: When the gradients disagree, Adam steps more carefully.

The mathsThe learning rate: warmup, then cosinelr_lambda — LambdaLR multiplies LR by it1 formula · 2 worked examples
η(s)=η0·{s+1Ws<Wmax(0.05,12(1+cos(πs−WS−W)))s≥W
Rise in a straight line for the first W steps, then follow half a cosine down — never below 5% of η₀.
In plain English
At the start the weights are random and Adam’s averages are empty, so big steps could throw training off course: the learning rate climbs in a straight line during the warmup, the first 5% of the steps. Then it follows half a cosine wave down — big steps while there is much to learn, ever smaller ones to settle into a good solution. It never drops below 5% of the peak, so learning never stops. Example: halfway through the decay, cos(π/2) = 0, so η = η₀ × ½ × (1 + 0) = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴.
Picture it
A runner’s session: warm up gently, run hard, then ease down into a jog — but never stop walking completely (the 5% floor).
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · The notebook’s own run: 2 pairs, 200 epochs
  1. One batch per epoch → S = 200, W = 10.
  2. η(0) = 5 × 10⁻⁴ × 1 ÷ 10 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁵ · η(9) = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ · η(105) = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ · η(199) = 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ (the floor).
So: A short climb, then half a cosine down.
Example 2 · A 10,000-step run
  1. W = 500. η(250) = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ · η(5,250) = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ · η(8,000) = 5.3 × 10⁻⁵ · η(9,999) = 2.5 × 10⁻⁵.
So: The same shape at any length.

dn=min(0.999,1+n10+n)
The decay, lowered at the start so the average is not stuck on the random first weights.
In plain English
The decay d says how much of the old average is kept: normally 0.999. But at the start the “old average” is just the random first weights; keeping 99.9% of them would make the average useless for thousands of steps. So d starts small: at step 1 it is (1 + 1) ÷ (10 + 1) = 0.18, at step 90 it is 0.91, and only after about 9,000 steps does it reach 0.999.
Picture it
A new weather station’s average: at first it trusts the latest readings heavily, and only after weeks does it settle into a slow, steady average.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · How d grows
  1. d₁ = 2 ÷ 11 = 0.182 · d₁₀ = 11 ÷ 20 = 0.550 · d₁₀₀ = 0.918 · d₉₀₀₀ = 0.999.
So: Small at first, 0.999 later.
Example 2 · What the warm-up saves
  1. With d = 0.999 from the start, after 100 updates the random first weights would still be 90.5% of the average.
  2. With d_n they are d₁ × d₂ × … × d₁₀₀ = 2.2 × 10⁻¹².
So: The random start is forgotten almost at once.
θ‾←dnθ‾+(1−dn)θ
After every update the average moves a little towards the weights.
In plain English
After every training step the average moves a small part of the way towards the current weights. The trained weights jump about from batch to batch; the average smooths that out and often scores better, which is why validation and the saved checkpoint use it.
Picture it
A slow camera following a jittery runner: the picture is smooth because it ignores each little jerk but follows the overall path.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · A jittery weight (1.2, 0.9, 1.1, 1.0) after a start at 1.0
  1. update 1: 0.182 × 1.000 + 0.818 × 1.2 = 1.164
  2. update 2: 0.250 × 1.164 + 0.750 × 0.9 = 0.966
  3. update 3: 0.308 × 0.966 + 0.692 × 1.1 = 1.059
  4. update 4: 0.357 × 1.059 + 0.643 × 1.0 = 1.021
So: The average moves less than the weight.
Example 2 · Much later (d = 0.999)
  1. Average 1.000, weight jumps to 1.5: 0.999 × 1.000 + 0.001 × 1.5 = 1.0005.
So: One odd step barely shows.

CELL 7
Model, two optimizers, EMA
Muon for the matrices · AdamW for the restunchanged in v1.5
In one sentenceThe model built with v3’s parts, and two optimizers: Muon for the layers’ matrices, AdamW for the rest.
In plain words
Cell 7 builds the model and what trains it. v3 builds its model with the new parts switched on, and trains it with two optimizers instead of one: Muon for the weight matrices inside the layers, AdamW — as in v2.5 — for the embedding table, the routers, the gains and the biases. One schedule drives both; the EMA is unchanged.
Picture it
A gym has two coaches. One looks at each muscle on its own and adjusts its effort by its own history — the classic way, and the right one for small, separate things.
The other looks at whole movements. When a lift is done mostly by one strong muscle, this coach evens it out, so every muscle in the movement does its share. Each trainee goes to the coach that suits them, and both coaches follow one plan: an easy start, a hard middle, a gentle end.
Another way to see itOr two teachers in one class: one corrects each pupil’s spelling word by word, the other makes sure every voice in a group project is heard.
Where the picture stops workingCoaches choose their trainees by judgement; here the split is a fixed rule — the matrices inside the layers go to Muon, everything else to AdamW. Whether the second coach made the difference, or only a harder plan, is measured in deep dive 24.

The tiny v3 model:
  1. Muon trains 4,736 of its numbers in 76 matrices; AdamW 248 in 5 matrices and 303 gains and biases.
  2. At training step 300, decoder layer 0’s W_q gets an update whose strongest direction is 182× its weakest; after Muon, 1.7×.
  3. Its first weight moves from -0.7659 to -0.7741.
Two coaches, one plan.

CELL 8
Training
4 parts · cell 8 → cell 2 → cell 8unchanged in v1.5
What you’ll learn
One complete training step, line by line: the batch going through the encoder and the decoder, the loss, the gradient, AdamW’s first step, and the bookkeeping that follows.
The big idea
Training shows the model a sentence pair, lets it guess every next token of the answer at once, measures how wrong the guesses were, and nudges every weight a little in the direction that would have made them less wrong. The trick that makes "all at once" possible is teacher forcing: the decoder is given the correct previous tokens, and the causal mask stops each position from peeking at the ones after it.
A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers
Epoch 0, both sentences, the untrained model:
  1. The decoder produces 225,554 scores: 16,111 for each of 14 positions.
  2. 10 positions have a real answer. Their mean loss is 9.6760 (smoothed) — against ln 16,111 = 9.6873, the score of a blind guess.
  3. For A’s first position the right token’s score gets a gradient of -0.0900: a strong push up.
  4. AdamW’s first step, at lr 5e-05, moves each output bias by exactly that much: up for the 9 target tokens, down for the other 16,102.
Then run_epoch counts accuracy, validation runs without dropout, the best model is saved, and the loop decides whether to keep going.
What to look forPart 1 follows the batch from cell 8 into cell 2 and through the encoder; part 2 is the decoder and the logits; part 3 the loss, the gradient and the step; part 4 accuracy, validation, the checkpoint and early stopping, with the v1.5 comparison.
CELL 8
Training
the v2.5 forward pass · the EMA stepunchanged in v1.5
In one sentenceGuess, measure the surprise, nudge every number, update the average — and check it once per epoch.
In plain words
Cell 8 is training: guess, measure, nudge, check — over and over. Three pages: the guess (one pass through the model), the nudge (gradients, the optimizer, the EMA), and the checks (validate the average, keep the best, stop in time).
Picture it
Practising a piece on the piano. You play it (the guess), hear the wrong notes (the loss), and adjust your fingers a little (the nudge). One run through all your practice pieces is an epoch. Every so often you record yourself to hear how you really sound (validation); you keep the best recording (the checkpoint); and if twenty recordings in a row are no better, you stop (early stopping).
Cell 8 is that loop. For each batch the model reads the input sentence and, shown the right answer so far, guesses every next token at once (teacher forcing). The loss says how surprised it was by each right token. The gradients say which way to move each of the 22,979,823 numbers; they are capped so no step is too big (clipping); the optimizer moves the numbers; the learning rate is updated; and — new in v2.5 — the averaged copy, the EMA, takes one small step after them.
At the end of each epoch the averaged weights are put in, validated, and saved if they are the best so far; then the working weights go back, so practice carries on where it was.
Another way to see itOr a thermostat: measure, compare with the target, adjust a little, measure again — thousands of times.
Where the picture stops workingWith two sentences the “recording” is made on the very pieces you practised, so it measures memory, not skill.
Who is who — the picture, then the code
in the picturein the notebook
playing the piecethe forward pass: logits = model(src, decoder_input)
being shown the right notes so farteacher forcing: decoder_input = tgt[:, :-1]
hearing the wrong notesloss = criterion(...), the cross-entropy
working out what to changebackward(): the gradients
not over-correctingclip_grad_norm_(..., max_norm=1.0)
adjusting your fingersscaler.step(optimizer), then scheduler.step()
updating your practice diaryema.update()
recording yourself from the diarywith ema.applied(): validate, save if best
giving up when nothing improvesPATIENCE = 20 epochs

A worked example, with this page’s real numbers
From the untrained trace and the real run:
  1. The untrained model’s first loss is 9.7040 — a blind guess among 16,111 tokens would score 9.6873.
  2. At epoch 20 the averaged weights score 2.56 and the latest 2.08: the average trails while the loss falls fast.
  3. The best epoch was 72 (validation loss 1.3002); training stopped at epoch 92.

The mathsThe loss: teacher forcing and label smoothingnn.CrossEntropyLoss(ignore_index=PAD, label_smoothing=0.1)3 formulas · 6 worked examples
input=y0:T−1,expected=y1:T
The decoder is fed the answer shifted right and must say the next token at every position.
In plain English
Teacher forcing: the decoder is given the correct answer as its input, shifted by one. Given “<SOS> the cat” it must say “the cat is” — at each position, the next word. Because the whole answer goes in at once, with the causal mask hiding the future, one forward pass trains every position.
Picture it
Learning to read aloud with the text in front of you: at every word you are shown the true words so far and asked only for the next one.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Sequence B
  1. Input: <SOS> the cat is sleeping peac efully.
  2. Expected: the cat is sleeping peac efully <EOS> — 7 lessons in one pass.
So: Each position predicts the next token.
Example 2 · “dog resting”
  1. tgt = <SOS> dog resting <EOS> → input (<SOS>, dog, resting), expected (dog, resting, <EOS>): 3 lessons.
So: Input and expected are the same answer, shifted by one.
qv=(1−α)[v=y]+αV
The target: 0.9 on the right token, the remaining 0.1 spread over all tokens.
In plain English
Instead of demanding 100% on the right token, label smoothing asks for 90% plus a tiny share for every token: 0.9 + 0.1 ÷ 16,111 on the right one and 0.1 ÷ 16,111 ≈ 0.0000062 on each other one. This keeps the model from becoming overconfident and usually helps it do better on sentences it has not seen.
Picture it
A teacher who never marks anything as 100% certain: the right answer is asked for at 90%, and a sliver goes to every other answer, so students do not learn to be overconfident.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · The tiny model (V = 15)
  1. Right token: (1 − 0.1) × 1 + 0.1 ÷ 15 = 0.9067; each other: 0.1 ÷ 15 = 0.0067.
  2. Check: 0.9067 + 14 × 0.0067 = 1.
So: The target is never 100%.
Example 2 · The real model (V = 16,111)
  1. Right token: 0.9 + 0.1 ÷ 16,111 = 0.9000062; each other: 6.2 × 10⁻⁶.
So: The 0.1 is spread very thin.
ℓ=−∑vqvlogpv,L=1|P|∑t∈Pℓt
Cross-entropy against that target, averaged over the positions that are not padding.
In plain English
Cross-entropy compares the target q with the model’s probabilities p: for every token, q × (−log p), all added up. Most of it comes from the right token: if the model gives it 0.9, that part is 0.9 × 0.105 ≈ 0.095. Positions holding <PAD> are left out (ignore_index), and the rest are averaged.
Picture it
A betting slip: you are scored on how much you bet on what really happened — and blank lines (padding) are not scored at all.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Humble against overconfident (tiny model)
  1. p equal to the target: ℓ = −Σ q log q = 0.556, the floor.
  2. p = 0.999 on the right token: ℓ = 0.892.
So: Too sure costs more.
Example 2 · A wrong guess, and the average
  1. p = 0.05 on the right token: ℓ = 2.967.
  2. A batch with 7 real positions and 2 <PAD>: L = (sum of the 7 losses) ÷ 7 — the padding is not counted.
So: Confident mistakes dominate the average.

Ppositions whose expected token is not <PAD>
The lowest possible loss is not 0: even a perfect model pays the entropy of q, −Σ q_v log q_v.

The mathsOne update: scale, clip, step, averagethe train branch of run_epoch3 formulas · 6 worked examples
g=1s∇(s·L)
With fp16, the loss is scaled up by s before backward() and the gradients scaled back (GradScaler).
In plain English
With 16-bit floats (fp16), very small gradients can round to 0 and be lost. GradScaler multiplies the loss by a large number s before the gradients are computed, so they stay in range, and divides them by s afterwards: the same gradients, computed safely. On a CPU, or with bf16, nothing is scaled.
Picture it
Weighing a feather on a kitchen scale: put a thousand on, read the weight, divide by a thousand — the tiny value is not lost to rounding.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · A gradient too small for fp16
  1. 10⁻⁸ is below fp16’s smallest number (about 6 × 10⁻⁸): it would be 0.
  2. × 65,536 (GradScaler’s start) = 6.6 × 10⁻⁴ — representable. ÷ 65,536 later → 10⁻⁸.
So: Scaling rescues tiny gradients.
Example 2 · A gradient too big
  1. 2 × 65,536 = 131,072 > 65,504, fp16’s largest number → inf.
  2. GradScaler skips that step and halves the scale to 32,768.
So: It adjusts itself in both directions.
g←g·min(1,c‖g‖+10−6)
Clipping: if all gradients together are longer than c, shrink them to length c.
In plain English
All the gradients together are seen as one long arrow, and ‖g‖ is its length. One unlucky batch can produce a huge gradient, and a step along it could undo much of the training. Clipping shrinks the arrow to length 1 at most and keeps its direction. Example: ‖g‖ = 4, so every gradient is multiplied by ¼.
Picture it
A speed limiter in a car: you can still steer anywhere, but you never go faster than the limit, however hard you press.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Gradients (3, 4)
  1. ‖g‖ = √(9 + 16) = 5 > 1 → × 1 ÷ 5 → (0.6, 0.8), length 1.
So: Only an oversized step is shortened.
Example 2 · Gradients (0.3, 0.4)
  1. ‖g‖ = 0.5 → min(1, 1 ÷ 0.5) = 1: unchanged.
So: Normal steps pass untouched.
θ←AdamW(θ,g,η(s)),θ‾←EMA(θ‾,θ)
Then the optimizer step, the schedule’s next learning rate, and the average (cell 7).
In plain English
Then the usual order: AdamW moves the weights, the scheduler sets the next learning rate, and the EMA follows the new weights. This happens once for every batch.
Picture it
One lap of the routine: take the step, set the next pace, update the slow average — once per batch.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · One lap on one weight
  1. θ = 1.0, clipped g = 0.8: AdamW’s first step → θ = 1.0 − 0.000005 (decay) − 0.0005 = 0.999495.
  2. EMA (d₁ = 0.182): 0.182 × 1.0 + 0.818 × 0.999495 = 0.999587.
So: Step, then the average follows.
Example 2 · How many laps
  1. The notebook (2 pairs, 1 batch per epoch): 200 updates in 200 epochs.
  2. 9,000 pairs at batch size 32: ⌈9,000 ÷ 32⌉ = 282 per epoch → 56,400 updates.
So: One lap per batch.

acc=#{t∈P:argmaxzt=yt}|P|
Token accuracy: the share of positions whose top-scored token is right.
In plain English
For every position that is not padding, check whether the token with the highest score is the right one; accuracy is the share of positions where it is. 90% means 9 tokens in 10 would be right if the model picked greedily — with the correct answer fed in so far, which is easier than writing on its own.
Picture it
A spelling test where you can see the correct letters so far: useful, but easier than writing the whole word yourself.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · 20 positions
  1. 17 have the right top token → acc = 17 ÷ 20 = 85%.
So: Token by token, with the right answer fed in.
Example 2 · Token accuracy is not sentence accuracy
  1. 90% of tokens right, 10 tokens a sentence: all 10 right only 0.9¹⁰ = 34.9% of the time.
So: A high token score can hide many imperfect sentences.
Lepoch=∑bLbnb∑bnb
The epoch’s loss, each batch weighted by its number of real tokens.
In plain English
Batches hold different numbers of real tokens. Weighting each batch’s loss by its token count gives the average over every token of the epoch, as if it were one big batch: a short batch counts less than a long one.
Picture it
Averaging test results by the number of questions in each test, so a 2-question quiz does not weigh as much as a 50-question exam.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Two batches of different size
  1. A: 0.5 over 100 tokens; B: 2.0 over 10 → (50 + 20) ÷ 110 = 0.636 (not 1.25).
So: Every token counts once.
Example 2 · Two batches of the same size
  1. A: 0.5 over 50; B: 2.0 over 50 → (25 + 100) ÷ 100 = 1.25, the plain average.
So: Equal batches weigh the same.
stop if there is no new best validation loss for 20 epochs
Early stopping (PATIENCE = 20); the best checkpoint is the one kept.
In plain English
If the validation loss has not improved for 20 epochs in a row, more training is unlikely to help and may only teach the model to memorise. Training stops, and the checkpoint saved at the best validation loss is the one used from then on.
Picture it
Ending an experiment after 20 rounds with no new best result, and keeping the best one reached.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Patience 20
  1. Best at epoch 37; 38 to 57 never beat it → stop after epoch 57, keep epoch 37.
So: The best checkpoint wins.
Example 2 · The earliest possible stop
  1. If epoch 0 were the best, training would stop after epoch 20 of the 200 allowed.
So: Patience sets a minimum run.

Training
two more losses · two optimizersunchanged in v1.5
In one sentenceOne forward pass, three losses — the main one, the token after next, the experts’ balance — and both optimizers step.
In plain words
Cell 8 trains the model. In v3 each step gets two sets of scores from one forward pass and trains on three losses: the main one, the multi-token head’s for the word after next, and the experts’ balance. Both optimizers step. The loss it reports is still the main one, so the numbers mean what they meant in v2.5.
Picture it
A teacher grades each exercise on three things: the answer, the step right after it, and whether everyone in the group took part. The extra grades push the pupils to think ahead and to share the work.
The report card still shows only the answer’s grade, so it means what it always meant. Then two tutors correct the pupils — each the ones they look after — following the same term plan.
Another way to see itOr a driving test scored on reaching the destination, signalling the next turn and sharing the road — with only the destination on the certificate.
Where the picture stops workingPupils see their extra grades; the model only feels them as extra pushes in its gradient. Whether those pushes improved the answers is measured in deep dive 26.

3 parts · the KV cache · sampling · beam searchunchanged in v1.5
What you’ll learn
How the model writes an answer on its own — one token per step with the KV cache — and the two new ways of choosing each token: sampling, and beam search.
The big idea
In training the right answer was always there to lean on. Here the model must use its own previous words. Each step it produces a score for every token, and a decoding strategy turns those scores into one word: greedy takes the best, sampling draws at random from the best few, and beam search keeps several partial answers alive at once. The KV cache is the reason all of this is affordable: each step processes only the newest token, because the keys and values of the past never change.
A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers
Measured on the untrained v2 model:
  1. 8 greedy steps take 8 position passes with the cache and 36 without — with identical scores.
  2. Sampling at T = 0.8 gives the top token 22.3% of the draw among five near-equal candidates.
  3. Beam search over 5 steps needs 17 passes with the cache and 57 without.
  4. After 5 steps beam search holds a sentence 0.030 more likely (in log-probability) than greedy’s — it grew from the SECOND-best first token.
An untrained model repeats one word; the mechanisms are what these pages show.
What to look forPart 1: exact_match, then generate() step by step — frames for steps 0, 1 and 2 show the cache being stored, appended to and reused, and a timeline draws five steps beside what v1.5 recomputed. Part 2: the four lines of sampling, with the shares and the draw. Part 3: beam search frame by frame, then the whole search as a tree with greedy’s path through it.
CELL 9
Evaluation and decoding
exact match and BLEU · four ways to writeunchanged in v1.5
In one sentenceReload the best weights, grade the answers strictly and fairly, and write them four different ways.
In plain words
Cell 9 uses the trained model: it reloads the best weights, grades the answers two ways — exact match and, new in v2.5, BLEU — and writes each sentence four ways.
Picture it
Exam day. First the saved notes come out of the drawer: the best checkpoint is reloaded, which also proves that saving works. Then every input sentence is answered and graded two ways. Exact match is a strict examiner: full marks for a perfect answer, zero for anything else. BLEU, new in v2.5, is a fairer one: it counts how many single words, pairs, triples and runs of four words in the answer also appear in the right answer, so “the is sleeping peacefully” gets partial credit instead of nothing.
Then the cell writes each answer four ways, to show the styles side by side: always the likeliest word (greedy); a weighted draw from the 5 best (top-k); a weighted draw from as many as it takes to cover 90% (top-p, with the repetition penalty); and four candidate answers kept at once (beam search). Last, it checks that beam search gives identical answers with and without the KV cache.
Another way to see itOr two teachers marking a translation: one crosses out any answer with a single mistake, the other gives a point for every phrase that is right.
Where the picture stops workingBLEU counts matching words, not meaning: a correct synonym scores nothing.

What v2.5 changes here — and why it helps
  • BLEU beside exact match — partial credit for partial answers
  • top-p sampling with the repetition penalty — a fourth way of writing that adapts to how sure the model is
A worked example, with this page’s real numbers
From the trained run:
  1. Both answers are exactly right: exact match 100%, BLEU 100.
  2. v2’s dropped-word answer, “the is sleeping peacefully”, would score 0 on exact match and 49.8 on BLEU.
  3. The model gives its best token about 93% at every step, so all four ways of writing agree.
The differences between the four ways appear when the model is unsure: cell 2, part 3.
Where to lookPart 1 grades, with BLEU worked out run by run; part 2 is the four ways of writing and the cache check.
The mathsExact match and BLEUevaluate() and bleu()2 formulas · 4 worked examples
exact=1N∑i[ŷi=yi]
The share of sentences written exactly right.
In plain English
[ŷᵢ = yᵢ] is 1 if the written sentence is exactly the reference, word for word, and 0 otherwise; the average is the share of perfect sentences. It is strict: one wrong word counts the same as a completely wrong sentence.
Picture it
A pass/fail exam: one mistake fails the sentence as surely as total nonsense.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Ten answers
  1. 7 exactly right → (7 × 1 + 3 × 0) ÷ 10 = 70%.
So: All or nothing.
Example 2 · One word short
  1. “the cat is sleeping” against “the cat is sleeping peacefully”: [ŷ = y] = 0.
So: Nearly right counts as wrong.
BLEU=100·BP·exp(14∑n=14logpn)
The geometric mean of four n-gram precisions, times a brevity penalty (deep dive 16).
In plain English
BLEU gives partial credit: how many of the written single words, word pairs, triples and runs of four also appear in the reference. Log, average, exp is a geometric mean, which falls sharply if any one of the four shares is low. The brevity penalty stops an answer from scoring well by writing only a few safe words. Example: an answer missing one word of five still scores about 50, where exact match gives 0.
Picture it
Grading by phrases instead of whole answers: matching words and word pairs earn partial credit, and a too-short answer is fined.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · One word short, by BLEU
  1. p₁…p₄ = 4/4 · 3/3 · 2/2 · 1/1; BP = 0.779 → BLEU = 100 × 0.779 × 1 = 77.9.
So: Partial credit.
Example 2 · A word dropped in the middle
  1. “the is sleeping peacefully”: p₁…p₄ = 4/4 · 2/3 · 1/2 · 0/1; BP = 0.779 → 49.8.
So: A gap breaks every longer run through it.

zPAD=zSOS=−∞
1 · _block_special.
In plain English
Before anything else, <PAD> and <SOS> are taken out of the race by setting their scores to −∞.
Picture it
Crossing two names off the ballot before counting.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · A row of logits
  1. <PAD> 1.0, <SOS> 0.5, the 1.9, cat 1.7, sofa 0.2 → <PAD> and <SOS> become −∞.
  2. They had 15.3% and 9.3%; now 0.
So: Removed before anything else.
Example 2 · Even when they score highest
  1. <PAD> 3.0, cat 2.0: <PAD> would win greedy; blocked, cat wins with 100% of the two.
So: The block cannot be outvoted.
zv←{zv/ρzv>0zv·ρzv≤0  for v already written
2 · the repetition penalty (ρ = 1.2 in cell 9’s top-p line; 1 = off).
In plain English
To stop the model repeating itself, every token already in the answer loses ground. A positive score is divided by 1.2 (3 becomes 2.5); a negative one is multiplied by 1.2 (−1 becomes −1.2). Dividing a negative score would move it towards 0 and make the token more likely — hence the two cases.
Picture it
A quiz that docks points for an answer already given: repeated tokens are pushed down, whether their score was positive or negative.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · “the” written already (positive score)
  1. the 1.9 > 0 → 1.9 ÷ 1.2 = 1.583.
So: A repeat loses ground.
Example 2 · A negative score
  1. sofa −0.5 written already → −0.5 × 1.2 = −0.6.
So: Negative scores are multiplied, so they also drop.
greedy: y=argmaxz ;  sampling: y∼softmax(z/T) over the top k or the top p
3 · pick: temperature 0.8 with k = 5, or with top-p 0.9.
In plain English
Then a token is picked: greedy takes the top score; sampling divides by the temperature and draws at random from the top k (or the top-p group).
Picture it
Then either take the favourite (greedy) or draw from a hat holding only the strongest few (sampling).
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Greedy
  1. After the penalty: the 1.58, cat 1.7, sofa 0.2 → greedy takes cat.
So: The penalty changed the choice.
Example 2 · Sampling at T = 0.8
  1. Shares: the 42.8%, cat 49.6%, sofa 7.6%.
So: Sampling keeps both in play.
beam: keep the B best by  Σlogp((5+n)/6)0.6
4 · beam search (B = 4) scores whole candidate answers instead.
In plain English
Beam search instead keeps 4 partial sentences alive, grows each by its best next tokens, and compares whole sentences by their total log-probability. Dividing by ((5 + n) ÷ 6)^0.6 makes up for longer sentences having more — always negative — log terms.
Picture it
Instead of one runner, send four scouts down different paths and compare where they end up.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · A short and a long answer
  1. A: Σ log p = −1.2, n = 3 → ÷ 1.188 = −1.010. B: −1.4, n = 6 → ÷ 1.439 = −0.973.
So: After the penalty the longer answer wins.
Example 2 · The penalty itself
  1. ((5 + n) ÷ 6)^0.6: n = 1 → 1, n = 5 → 1.359, n = 10 → 1.733, n = 20 → 2.354.
So: It grows slowly with length.

CELL 9
Evaluation and decoding
speculative decoding · 8-bit weightsunchanged in v1.5
In one sentenceThe scores, and three checks: speculative decoding writes what greedy writes, the 8-bit copy answers like the original, FlashAttention’s maths equals plain attention.
In plain words
Cell 9 scores the trained model. v3 adds three checks: speculative decoding must write exactly what greedy writes, in fewer passes; the model stored in 8 bits must answer like the original; and flash_attention, FlashAttention’s maths written out to read (the model itself calls PyTorch’s scaled_dot_product_attention), must equal plain attention.
Picture it
A bakery changes its oven, its recipe cards and its delivery van. Before reopening it does what it always does — tastes loaves against the reference — and adds one extra test for each change.
Does the faster van deliver exactly the same loaves? Does the smaller recipe card still make the same bread? Does baking in batches give the same crumb as the old oven? Each test runs old and new on the same input and compares the results.
Another way to see itOr a pilot’s checklist after a refit: the usual checks, plus one line for each new instrument.
Where the picture stops workingTasting proves sameness only for the loaves tasted: these checks use the notebook’s own sentences (deep dives 23 and 25 add many unseen ones). “The same” also has a size: the block-by-block attention differs by about 6.0e-07 — rounding, not a different answer. And on this CPU the van’s trip went from 0.034 s to 0.041 s: slower, for the reasons in deep dive 23.

CELL 10
Attention heatmap
a row per generated tokenunchanged in v1.5
What you’ll learn
How the attention heatmap is built: one row per generated token, collected step by step from the cached decoder, averaged over heads, trimmed and plotted.
The big idea
Cross-attention is where each output word looks at the source sentence. Its weights say how much each source word contributed to each output word — and a heatmap turns that table into a picture. With the KV cache, each generation step computes just one row of that table, so generate() collects the rows as it goes and stacks them at the end.
A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers
For sequence A, alone:
  1. Each step adds a (1, 4, 1, 6) slice: one row, four heads, 6 source tokens.
  2. The heads are averaged; the <SOS> label is dropped because row i predicts token i + 1.
  3. No <EOS> is ever written, so the full map would have 63 rows; the first 8 are drawn.
  4. Every row spreads about 0.167 to each source word — flat, as an untrained model must be.
After training each row would light up the source word its output word comes from.
What to look forFrames 3 to 5 are the collection inside generate(); frames 7 to 9 are the plotting function, ending with the map itself. Section B explains why v2 has to collect rows at all.
CELL 10
Attention heatmap
the trained model’s own attentionunchanged in v1.5
In one sentenceA heatmap of where the model looked in the input while it wrote each word of the answer.
In plain words
Cell 10 draws where the trained model looked: for each token it wrote, how its attention was shared among the input words. The code is v2’s, unchanged; the model is v2.5’s, trained here.
Picture it
Imagine an eye-tracker on a translator. While they write each word of the translation, it records where on the original sentence their eyes rest, and for how long. Cell 10 draws that record for the model: one row for every token it wrote, one column for every input word, and each square’s brightness is a share of attention — the shares in a row add up to 100%.
The shares come from the cross-attention of the last decoder layer, averaged over its 4 heads. A model trained on millions of sentences usually looks at the word it is translating. This one learned from two sentences, so any pattern that tells them apart is enough — which is why it can look at “on” and “floor” while writing “dog”.
Another way to see itOr a spotlight operator in a theatre: for every line spoken, which actors on stage get light, and how much.
Where the picture stops workingAttention shows where the model looked, not why it decided: a bright square is a clue, not an explanation.

Row t: how much of its cross-attention the step that wrote token t gave to source token s, averaged over the heads of the last decoder layer.
In plain English
At every step, each cross-attention head spreads 100% of its attention over the source words — that is where it looked. The map averages the 4 heads of the last decoder layer: one row per written token, one column per source token. A bright cell means “while writing this word, the model looked mostly at that source word”.
Picture it
An eye-tracking heatmap: for each word the model wrote, where on the source sentence its eyes rested.

Example 1 · Four heads, one written word
  1. Heads over “the cat is sleeping”: (0.1, 0.1, 0.1, 0.7); (0.0, 0.2, 0.1, 0.7); (0.2, 0.2, 0.2, 0.4); (0.1, 0.0, 0.1, 0.8).
  2. A = (1/4) × their sum = (0.100, 0.125, 0.125, 0.650).
So: The average look of the 4 heads.
Example 2 · Reading the row
  1. 0.100 + 0.125 + 0.125 + 0.650 = 1 — the row adds up to 1.
  2. Its brightest cell, 0.65, is on “sleeping”.
So: Each row is 100% of one step’s attention.

Greedy decoding, under the hood
generate() line by linegenerate() line by linegenerate() line by lineunchanged in v1.5
What you’ll learn
How greedy decoding actually runs inside generate(): what goes into the decoder each step, why <PAD> and <SOS> are removed, how argmax picks, how a batch keeps a finished sentence in place — and why the best step is not always the best sentence.
The big idea
Greedy decoding writes the answer one token at a time and always takes the single most likely next token. It is like choosing a route by always taking the road that looks best at each junction: quick, and often fine, but a slightly worse turn early on can lead to a much better road later — and greedy never goes back to try it.
A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers
On the hand-set model, traced with the notebook’s own loop:
  1. Step 0: row 0’s raw second choice is <SOS>; _block_special removes it, and argmax takes "the" (0.50) over "a" (0.40).
  2. Step 1: row 1 writes <EOS> and is marked finished; from then on masked_fill writes <PAD> in its place while row 0 goes on.
  3. The loop stops after 4 steps, when every row is finished.
  4. Greedy’s sentence has P = 0.0630; the most likely sentence has P = 0.1344 — 2.1 times as likely, and greedy dropped its first word at step 0.
Deep dive 2 shows how beam search keeps that first word alive long enough to find it.
What to look forSection A is the table that stands in for the network. Section B is generate() one line at a time, with the probability bars and the growing batch at every line. Section C puts greedy’s sentence beside the best one; D is the sampling branch of the same loop; E is the real v2 model; F the pros, cons and claims.
In one sentenceGreedy decoding always writes the single likeliest next token, and never looks back.
In plain words
Deep dive 1 takes greedy decoding apart: always writing the single most likely token. It is v2’s page: generate() works the same way in v2.5 when temperature is 0 and the new repetition penalty is left at 1.0.
Picture it
Picture a hiker who, at every fork, takes whichever path looks best right now, without looking any further ahead. That is greedy decoding: at each step the model writes the single most likely token, adds it to the answer, and moves on.
It is fast and needs no randomness, and when the model is sure of every word — as the trained model here is — it is exactly right. Its weakness shows when an early choice looks good but leads somewhere worse: greedy never goes back. In the table on this page it writes “the cat sat”, because “cat” beats “dog” by 0.36 to 0.34, although a better sentence existed.
Another way to see itOr answering a multiple-choice test by ticking the first answer that sounds right, without reading the others.
Where the picture stops workingGreedy is not always worse. When the model is confident it gives the same answer as slower methods — deep dive 5 compares them on the same numbers.

The mathsGreedy decodingthe highest score, one token at a time1 formula · 2 worked examples
y0=SOS,yt=argmaxv∉{PAD,SOS}p(v|y<t,x)
Take the most likely token, feed it back, repeat — until <EOS> or max_len.
In plain English
Greedy decoding is the simplest way to write: start from <SOS>, ask the model for the probabilities of the next token, take the most likely one, add it, and ask again — until <EOS> is chosen or the length limit is reached. It is fast and always gives the same answer, but it never goes back: one weak early choice stays for good.
Picture it
Finding your way through a maze by always taking the corridor that looks best right now: quick, but you cannot turn back from a dead end.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Greedy’s short-sighted route
  1. Step 1: “the” 0.5, “a” 0.4 → “the”. Step 2: “dog” 0.4 → 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.20.
  2. Not taken: “a” then “cat” 0.9 → 0.36.
So: The best first step was not the best sentence.
Example 2 · The tiny model, sequence B
  1. Each step’s best token has about 0.91: greedy writes “the cat is sleeping peac efully” — exactly the expected answer.
So: When the model is sure, greedy is enough.

Beam search, under the hood
beam_search() line by linebeam_search() line by linebeam_search() line by lineunchanged in v1.5
What you’ll learn
How beam search actually runs inside beam_search(): how beams propose candidates, how the candidates are ranked and kept, what happens when one says <EOS>, why the cache has to be re-sorted, and how the length penalty picks the final answer.
The big idea
Instead of one partial answer, beam search keeps the B best at once — its "beams". Every step each beam proposes its B most likely next tokens, all the proposals are ranked by the probability of the WHOLE sequence, and the best B survive. Think of it as exploring several routes in parallel and dropping the worst ones at every junction, instead of committing to one road.
A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers
On the same hand-set model as deep dive 1, beam_size = 2:
  1. Step 0 keeps "the" and "a". Step 1: "a dog" is the best candidate of all, so the beams swap — parents [1, 0] — and the cache rows are swapped to match.
  2. Step 2: "a dog <EOS>" finishes and moves to completed; step 3: two more finish, and the search stops.
  3. Raw, "a dog" scores best (-2.007); after the length penalty "a dog sat" wins (-2.101 before the penalty).
  4. Greedy wrote "the cat sat" (-2.765): beam search’s answer is 1.9 times as likely. On the real v2 model beam search also beats greedy, by 0.030.
Every candidate, every decision and every cache row is drawn at the line that produced it.
What to look forSection A is the whole search as a tree — read it first. Section B is the same search on a board: four steps, each with the beams going in, every token they proposed and the arithmetic behind its score, the ranked list with the dropped branches struck out, and the cache rows being moved. Section C is the call stack, six frames per step: what is fed, the log-probabilities, the candidates, the ranking and selection, the state, and the cache reorder. D compares with greedy and shows the real model’s search; E is the length penalty; F the pros, cons and claims; G is a trained run that dropped "cat" — why the stopping rule did it, and the fix; H is the recap — greedy and beam search side by side, and when to use which.
In one sentenceBeam search keeps the four best partial answers at every step and returns the best finished one.
In plain words
Deep dive 2 takes beam search apart: keeping several candidate answers at once. It is v2’s page. One thing differs in v2.5: the stopping rule that section G shows going wrong — and fixes — is the real code in v2.5, not a tutorial patch.
Picture it
Instead of one hiker, send four groups out. At every fork each group looks at its best next paths; of all those options, only the four most promising — judged by the whole route so far — go on, and the rest go home. A group that reaches the hut (<EOS>) is set aside as a finished answer. At the end the best finished route wins.
This fixes greedy’s short-sightedness: a path that starts a little worse can still win if it goes on much better. On this page greedy writes “the cat sat”, while beam search finds “a dog sat”, about twice as likely overall. The KV cache keeps each group’s notes, and when groups are replaced the notes are re-ordered to follow them.
Another way to see itOr a chess player who thinks a few moves ahead along the four most promising lines, instead of playing the move that looks best this instant.
Where the picture stops workingBeam search is not sure to find the very best answer either — only the best among the lines it kept.

The mathsBeam searchkeep the B most likely partial answers3 formulas · 6 worked examples
score(y1:n)=∑t=1nlogp(yt|y<t,x)
A candidate’s score: the log of its probability, a sum of one log per token (always ≤ 0).
In plain English
The probability of a whole sentence is the product of its tokens’ probabilities: 0.9 × 0.8 = 0.72. Multiplying many small numbers gets tiny fast, so beam search adds their logs instead: log 0.9 + log 0.8 = −0.105 − 0.223 = −0.329 = log 0.72. Every log is at most 0, so a sentence’s score can only go down as it grows.
Picture it
The cost of a journey: the chance of the whole route is the chance of each turn multiplied together; adding the logs is adding up a cost for each turn instead.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · A two-token sentence
  1. 0.9 × 0.8 = 0.72 → log 0.9 + log 0.8 = −0.105 + −0.223 = −0.329 = log 0.72.
So: Adding logs is multiplying probabilities.
Example 2 · The tree, beam of 2
  1. “a cat”: log 0.36 = −1.022 beats “the dog”: log 0.20 = −1.609.
So: Keeping two options finds the better sentence.
lp(n)=(5+n6)α
The length penalty (GNMT): it grows with the length…
In plain English
Because every token adds a negative term, short answers would always win. The length penalty divides the score by a number that grows with the length — with α = 0.6: lp(1) = 1, lp(5) = 1.36, lp(10) = 1.73, lp(20) = 2.35 — so long and short answers are compared more fairly.
Picture it
A golf handicap: longer courses get a bigger allowance, so a long, good round can beat a short, mediocre one.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Penalties for three lengths
  1. lp(3) = (8 ÷ 6)^0.6 = 1.188 · lp(6) = 1.439 · lp(20) = 2.354.
So: A 20-token answer’s score is divided by 2.35.
Example 2 · α = 0 and α = 1
  1. α = 0: lp = 1 always (no penalty). α = 1: lp(20) = 25 ÷ 6 = 4.167.
So: α = 0.6 sits in between.
best=argmaxfinishedscorelp(n)
…and the final answer is the finished candidate with the highest score per penalty, so short answers are not favoured just for being short.
In plain English
When the search ends, of all the finished sentences — those that reached <EOS> — the one with the best score ÷ length penalty is the answer.
Picture it
The finish line: of all the hikers who reached a summit (<EOS>), the one with the best handicapped score wins.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · The length penalty flips a choice
  1. Short: −1.0 ÷ 1.188 = −0.841. Long (6 tokens): −1.15 ÷ 1.439 = −0.799.
So: The longer one wins after the penalty.
Example 2 · Equal raw scores
  1. Both −1.2: 4 tokens → −0.941; 8 tokens → −0.755.
So: At equal probability, the longer answer is preferred.

The KV cache, under the hood
the real keys, scores and weightsthe real keys, scores and weightsthe real keys, scores and weightsunchanged in v1.5
What you’ll learn
What the KV cache is, what exactly it stores, how attention reads it at every step, and why the answer comes out identical to recomputing everything — on the real v2 model.
The big idea
Attention needs a key and a value for every earlier token. In a decoder an earlier token can never see a later one, so its key and value are final the moment they are computed. The cache keeps them in a list of dicts — one per layer, with a "self" drawer that gains a row every step and a "cross" drawer holding the encoder’s rows — so each step computes only the newest token.
A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers
The real v2 model, layer 0, head 0, sequence A:
  1. Step 0 stores one key; the new token attends only to itself (weight 1).
  2. Step 1 appends a second key with torch.cat; the query weighs the two 0.4034 and 0.5966, and the context matches the model’s own to the last digit.
  3. Recomputed from scratch, the cached keys differ by 0: the cache is exact.
  4. Without start_pos the same cached decoder drifts by 0.344 by step 5.
The cross drawer is filled once with the encoder’s 6 rows and read at every step.
What to look forSection A is the cache object. Section B follows four steps inside attention, with the real numbers. C checks exactness, D counts cost and memory, E is start_pos, F the cache re-sorted for beams, G the claims.
In one sentenceThe KV cache remembers each written token’s key and value, so every step works only on the newest token.
In plain words
Deep dive 3 takes the KV cache apart: keeping the keys and values of the tokens already written. It is v2’s page. In v2.5 the cached keys are stored already turned by RoPE — cell 2, page 2, section C shows that part.
Picture it
Imagine writing a story one word at a time and, before each new word, re-reading the whole story from the beginning. That is what the decoder would do without a cache. The KV cache is a notebook: after each word the model writes down that word’s key and value (what it advertises, and what it would hand over), so the next step only has to work on the newest word and can look the rest up.
The result is exactly the same — the page checks that the scores match — but the work shrinks: writing 8 tokens pushes 8 positions through the decoder instead of 36. In v2.5 the keys are written into the notebook already turned by RoPE to their own positions, so they never need to be touched again.
Another way to see itLike a running total at a till: each new item is added to the total, instead of adding up the whole receipt again.
Where the picture stops workingThe notebook costs memory: it grows with every token written, which is why long texts need a lot of it.

The mathsThe KV cacheone new row per step instead of all of them3 formulas · 6 worked examples
K≤t=[K≤t−1;kt],V≤t=[V≤t−1;vt]
The keys and values of earlier tokens never change, so each step appends the new token’s and keeps the rest.
In plain English
While the model writes, each step adds one token. The keys and values of earlier tokens are exactly what they were the step before (they depend only on earlier tokens), so computing them again is wasted work. The cache keeps them, and each step adds one new row.
Picture it
Keeping notes as you read instead of re-reading the whole book before every new sentence.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Writing “<SOS> the cat is”
  1. Call 1: the cache holds 1 row · call 2: 2 · call 3: 3 · call 4: 4 rows of keys (and of values), per head and layer.
So: Each call adds one row, keeps the rest.
Example 2 · The tiny model’s cache, head 0
  1. After call 3, cache["k"] holds 3 rows of 4 numbers; the newest is (0.76, −1.70, 2.02, −2.33).
  2. Call 4 appends (−0.74, −2.03, 1.07, 0.14) and leaves those 3 rows untouched.
So: Old keys never change.
ot=softmax(qtK≤t⊤dk)V≤t
Only the newest token needs a query.
In plain English
Only the newest token asks a question: its query is compared with every stored key, and the stored values are mixed by the resulting shares. The result is exactly what recomputing everything would give — just much faster.
Picture it
Only the newcomer asks the room a question; everyone else’s name tags (keys) and contributions (values) are already on the table.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · One query against three cached keys
  1. q = (1, 0); keys (0.5, 0), (1, 1), (2, 0); d_k = 2 → shares 0.188, 0.268, 0.544.
  2. Values 1, 2, 3 → output 2.355.
So: Only the newest token asks.
Example 2 · The tiny model: the same as the full call
  1. Call 5’s output for “sleeping” starts (−0.4205, 0.7088, 0.1383).
  2. Row 4 of the whole-sentence call starts (−0.4205, 0.7088, 0.1383) — identical.
So: The cache changes the speed, not the answer.
work:  T  instead of  ∑t=1Tt=T(T+1)2
Writing T tokens processes T token rows instead of recomputing the whole answer at every step.
In plain English
Without the cache, step t runs all t tokens again: for 64 tokens that is 1 + 2 + … + 64 = 2,080 token rows. With it, 64 — about 32 times less work for the projections over a whole sentence.
Picture it
Writing a 64-word story: re-reading everything before each word means 2,080 word-readings; keeping notes means 64.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · 64 tokens and 200
  1. 64: 64 × 65 ÷ 2 = 2,080 rows against 64 → 32.5× less.
  2. 200: 20,100 against 200 → 100.5× less.
So: The longer the answer, the more it saves.
Example 2 · What it costs
  1. Per token: a key and a value of 512 numbers in each of 2 decoder layers = 2,048 numbers.
  2. 64 tokens → 131,072 numbers = 512 KB at 4 bytes each.
So: A little memory buys a lot of speed.

Warmup + cosine decay
the learning-rate schedule, step by stepthe learning-rate schedule, step by stepthe learning-rate schedule, step by stepunchanged in v1.5
What you’ll learn
What a learning-rate schedule is, how v2’s warmup + cosine decay is built and stepped, why it has the shape it has, and — measured — why shrinking the steps late in training helps.
The big idea
The learning rate is the size of every training step. Early on the weights are far from good values but the optimizer’s estimates are still noisy, so v2 starts small and climbs for 10 steps (the warmup). Then it follows half a cosine down: it stays near the peak for a while, falls fastest in the middle of training, and eases into a small floor at the end — like braking smoothly before a stop instead of slamming the brakes or never braking at all.
A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers
The notebook’s own schedule, computed for its 200 steps:
  1. Step 0 uses 5e-5 — a tenth of the peak. Step 9 reaches the peak, 5e-4.
  2. Half way through the decay the cosine crosses 0 and the rate is exactly half the peak, 2.5e-4.
  3. From step 173 the max(0.05, …) floor holds the rate at 2.5e-5 until the end.
  4. In a noisy toy problem the cosine ends 3.9 times closer to the minimum than a constant rate.
The schedule never changes the direction of an update — only how big it is.
What to look forA is the whole schedule; B the call stack, with every lr_lambda worked out; C the shape, on a half circle; D the alternatives; E why warm up; F the experiment; G what else the schedule touches; H the claims.
In one sentenceThe learning rate starts small, rises quickly, then glides down a cosine curve so training settles.
In plain words
Deep dive 4 takes the learning-rate schedule apart: a short warm-up, then a slow decrease shaped like a cosine curve. It is v2’s page; v2.5 uses the same schedule.
Picture it
Think of a coach who decides how big each correction to your technique should be. At the very start they are careful — the first attempts are wild, and a big push could send you the wrong way (the warm-up). Then come the biggest corrections, while there is most to learn. Towards the end the corrections get smaller and smaller, so you settle into what you have learned instead of overshooting it (the cosine decay).
The size of the correction is the learning rate. Here it climbs to its peak over the first 5% of the steps, then follows half a cosine curve down to 5% of the peak — never all the way to zero.
Another way to see itOr parking a car: quick across the empty car park, slowing smoothly as you get close to the space.
Where the picture stops workingThe best shape is found by trying. Warm-up and cosine decay are a common, safe choice, not a law.

η(s)=η0·{s+1Ws<Wmax(0.05,12(1+cos(πs−WS−W)))s≥W
A straight climb to η₀, then half a cosine wave down to a floor.
In plain English
Example with 1,000 steps in all: W = 50. At step 0 the rate is η₀ ÷ 50; at step 49 it reaches η₀. Halfway through the decay (step 525) cos(π/2) = 0, so η = η₀ ÷ 2. At the last step the cosine reaches −1 and the formula would give 0 — the 0.05 floor keeps it at 5% of η₀. Warmup protects the start, when the weights are random and Adam’s averages are still empty; the cosine takes big steps while there is much to learn and small ones to settle in.
Picture it
A car journey: pull away gently, cruise at speed, then slow down smoothly as you near the destination — never quite coming to a full stop.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · A 1,000-step run
  1. W = 50. η(0) = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ · η(25) = 2.6 × 10⁻⁴ · η(49) = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴.
  2. η(525) = 5 × 10⁻⁴ × ½(1 + cos(π × 0.5)) = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ · η(999) = 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ (floor).
So: Up in a straight line, down along a cosine.
Example 2 · Without the warmup
  1. The first step would use 5.0 × 10⁻⁴; with warmup it uses 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ — 50× smaller.
So: Warmup protects the fragile start.

Greedy, top-k sampling and beam search
the same scores, three waysthe same scores, three waysthe same scores, three waysunchanged in v1.5
What you’ll learn
How the model’s raw scores become probabilities, and how greedy, top-k sampling and beam search each read the same row of numbers — with every calculation shown, and the pros and cons of all three.
The big idea
The decoder never writes a word. At each step it gives one number per token, a logit, and softmax turns those numbers into probabilities: exp() makes them positive, dividing by their sum makes them add up to 1. What happens next is a choice. Greedy takes the largest. Top-k sampling keeps the k best, reshapes them with a temperature and rolls a weighted die. Beam search keeps the B best partial sentences and judges whole sentences later. A sentence’s probability is just the product of the probabilities of its tokens — which is why the scores are added in logs, and why longer sentences need a length penalty.
A tiny example, with this page’s real numbers
One hand-set row of six scores, and the same three strategies run to the end:
  1. The top logit, 4.0, becomes a probability of 0.5471 once the whole row is summed.
  2. Greedy always writes the same sentence: P = 0.0630.
  3. Beam search always returns P = 0.1224 — twice as likely, because it kept a second candidate.
  4. Top-k sampling can return 15 different sentences: the best one 19% of the time, greedy’s 14% of the time.
Same model, same scores — three different answers.
What to look forA is the softmax arithmetic, worked out. B reads one row three ways, side by side. C runs all three to the end of a sentence. D is how a sentence’s probability is calculated and compared. E is the pros and cons of all three, F the usual misunderstandings.
In one sentenceGreedy, sampling and beam search read the same probabilities and make different choices from them.
In plain words
Deep dive 5 compares three ways of choosing the next token — greedy, top-k sampling and beam search — on the same scores, with every calculation shown. It is v2’s page; v2.5 adds a fourth way, top-p, and a repetition penalty (deep dives 11 and 12, and cell 2, page 3).
Picture it
Three travellers read the same weather forecast: 60% sun, 30% cloud, 10% rain. The first always packs for the single likeliest weather — sun, every time (greedy). The second rolls a die weighted by the forecast, so usually packs for sun but sometimes for cloud or rain (sampling; top-k first crosses out all but the few likeliest). The third packs a few different bags and keeps the best combination as the trip goes on (beam search).
The model gives the same kind of forecast before every token: a probability for each of its 16,111 tokens. The three strategies read that one forecast and make different choices from it. Greedy is steady but cannot recover from a poor early choice; sampling is varied but can wander; beam search looks further ahead but costs more work.
Another way to see itOr three chess players: one plays the best-looking move, one sometimes tries a surprising one, one calculates several lines before moving.
Where the picture stops workingThe forecast here is made up for the picture. Which strategy is best depends on the job: one right answer (translation) favours greedy or beam; varied writing favours sampling.

DEEP DIVE 6
RoPE — positions as turning clock hands
order is invisible without it · the score against distanceunchanged in v1.5
In one sentenceRoPE turns each word’s hands by its seat, so comparing two words reveals only how far apart they are.
In plain words
Attention on its own cannot tell word order: shuffle a sentence and every word comes out the same. This deep dive shows that, then takes RoPE apart — the way v2.5 tells the model where each word sits, by turning pairs of numbers inside attention.
Picture it
Everyone at a long dinner table wears a watch. Before the meal, each person’s watch hands are turned forward by an amount that depends on their seat: seat 1 a little, seat 10 ten times as much. Nobody is told a seat number. But when two people compare watches, the difference between their hands tells them exactly how many seats apart they sit — and that difference is the same at seats 5 and 15 as at seats 40 and 50.
In RoPE each word’s query and key are cut into 64 pairs of numbers, and each pair is a watch hand. Every pair turns at its own speed: pair 0 like a second hand (57.3° per word), the last like an hour hand that barely moves. The fast hands tell near neighbours apart, the slow ones far-apart words. When attention compares a query with a key, only the angle between their hands counts — so the score depends on how far apart the words are, not on where they are.
v2 did it differently: it printed a seat-number pattern, made of the same sines and cosines, straight onto every word’s card. The card then carried where the word sat mixed in with what it meant, and “ten seats apart” looked different at every place in the sentence.
Another way to see itOr two clocks in different time zones: whatever time it is, the difference between them stays the same all day.
Where the picture stops workingThe hands turn only inside self-attention: the values (what words hand over) and the comparison with the other sentence (cross-attention) are never turned.

The mathsRoPE, in fullthe tables, the turn, and why only the distance counts3 formulas · 6 worked examples
θi=base−2i/dk,anglep,i=pθi
rope_tables: one speed per pair, one angle per position and pair (cos and sin are stored).
In plain English
rope_tables builds two tables once: for every position p (0 to 65) and every pair i (0 to 63), the angle p × θ_i, stored as its cos and its sin. Every self-attention call then just reads the rows it needs.
Picture it
Printing a table of clock-hand angles once — for every minute and every hand — so nobody has to work them out again.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · The first rows of the tables
  1. Pair 0 (θ = 1): angles 0, 1, 2, 3 rad = 0°, 57°, 115°, 172°.
  2. Pair 63 (θ ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻⁴): at position 3, 0.0198°.
So: 64 very different speeds.

  1. θ₀ = 1 → 5 rad = 286°; θ₁ = 0.01 → 0.05 rad = 2.86°.
So: One hand races, one barely moves.
