apply_rope: x1 · cos − x2 · sin and x1 · sin + x2 · cos.
In plain English
apply_rope splits each head’s numbers into x1 (numbers 0, 2, 4, …) and x2 (1, 3, 5, …) — the two coordinates of every pair — and turns each pair by its angle with the rotation formula. Example: the pair (1, 0) turned by 90° becomes (0, 1); its length is still 1.
Picture it
Turning a compass needle by a set angle: the needle (the pair) keeps its length; only its direction changes.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · (3, 4) by 90°
  1. (3 × 0 − 4 × 1, 3 × 1 + 4 × 0) = (−4, 3); length 5 before and after.
So: Direction changes, length stays.
Example 2 · (1, 0) by 45°
  1. (cos 45°, sin 45°) = (0.707, 0.707).
So: The point moves around the circle.
(Rmq)⊤(Rnk)=q⊤Rm⊤Rnk=q⊤Rn−mk
Turning back by m and forward by n is turning by n − m: the score sees the distance only.
In plain English
R_m means “turn by m steps”. Turning back by m and then forward by n is the same as turning forward by n − m. So the dot product of a query at position m and a key at position n depends only on n − m — the distance between the two words.
Picture it
Two ships, each turned by its own number of steps: the angle between them depends only on the difference of the steps.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · q = (1, 2), k = (2, 1), θ = 1
  1. m = 3, n = 1: score −4.3925 · m = 10, n = 8: −4.3925 — the same.
So: Both pairs are 2 apart.
Example 2 · Changing the distance
  1. m = 3, n = 2 (distance 1): −0.3632 · m = 3, n = 0 (distance 3): −4.3833.
So: The distance decides the score.

DEEP DIVE 7
RMSNorm
LayerNorm in 5 steps, RMSNorm in 3 · the cost, measuredunchanged in v1.5
In one sentenceRMSNorm brings every word’s numbers to the same size before each move, in fewer steps than LayerNorm.
In plain words
RMSNorm, the normaliser in front of every move in v2.5: why vectors need rescaling at all, LayerNorm’s five steps against RMSNorm’s three on the same word, what the gain and the float32 conversion are for, and what it costs — measured.
Picture it
A sound engineer at a mixing desk. Voices come in at very different volumes — one singer whispering, another shouting. Before the next part of the song the engineer turns each voice to the same overall loudness, then applies a personal setting per channel. That is normalisation: each word’s 512 numbers are brought to a steady size before every move of every layer, so no move is flooded by huge numbers or starved by tiny ones.
v2’s LayerNorm took five steps: it first moved each voice so its average sat at zero (subtract the mean), then scaled it, then applied a gain and a bias. v2.5’s RMSNorm skips the centring and the bias: it only divides by the root mean square — the typical size of the numbers — and applies the gain. The page shows the vectors here were nearly centred already, so the result barely differs.
Another way to see itOr photos taken in different light, all brought to the same brightness before they are compared.
Where the picture stops workingFewer steps did not mean faster here: on this CPU PyTorch’s optimised LayerNorm was quicker (section F). The gain is simplicity.

in the picturein the notebook
a voice’s loudnessthe vector’s RMS: √(mean of its squared numbers)
turning every voice to the same loudnessx × rsqrt(mean(x²) + eps)
the per-channel settingself.weight: one gain per number, starting at 1
the step RMSNorm skipsLayerNorm’s subtracting the mean, and its bias
a safety margin for silenceeps = 1e-6: an all-zero vector never divides by 0
measuring carefullyx.float(): the statistics in 32-bit, even in 16-bit training

The mathsLayerNorm against RMSNormwhat each computes, symbol by symbola comparison · 2 worked examples
LayerNorm (v2)RMSNorm (v2.5)
FormulaLN(x)=x−μσ2+ε⊙γ+βRMSNorm(x)=xRMS(x)⊙γ
Centreμ=1d∑jxjnone — the row keeps its offset
Sizeσ2=1d∑j(xj−μ)2RMS(x)=1d∑jxj2+ε
Learnedγ,β:  2d numbersγ:  d numbers
ε10−510−6
Ignoresthe row’s scale and its offsetthe row’s scale only
In plain English
Centre
LayerNorm first finds the row’s average μ and subtracts it, so every row is centred on 0. RMSNorm leaves the average in.
Size
LayerNorm measures the spread around the average; RMSNorm the size around 0. They are linked: mean square = variance + mean². When the mean is near 0 — as is usual inside a trained network — they are almost equal.
Learned
Both learn a gain per column; LayerNorm also a bias per column. RMSNorm has half as many learned numbers.
Ignores
Multiply a row by 2: neither output changes. Add 1 to every number: LayerNorm’s output stays the same, RMSNorm’s changes. That is the one real difference in what they do.
Picture it
Two volume levellers: LayerNorm also re-centres every track around silence and adds a learned offset; RMSNorm only levels the loudness — and in a trained network the tracks already sit near the centre.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Exam scores (70, 80, 90)
  1. LayerNorm: mean 80, spread 8.165 → (−1.22, 0.00, 1.22).
  2. RMSNorm: size 80.42 → (0.87, 0.99, 1.12).
So: LayerNorm shows above and below average.
Example 2 · Everyone gets 10 bonus points: (80, 90, 100)
  1. LayerNorm: (−1.22, 0.00, 1.22) — unchanged. RMSNorm: (0.885, 0.996, 1.107) — changed.
So: Only LayerNorm ignores a shift.

GELU — v2’s feed-forward bend
why a bend · the curve · on real numbersunchanged in v1.5
In one sentenceGELU is v2’s smooth dimmer: it lets strong values through and fades weak or negative ones.
In plain words
GELU, the bend in v2’s feed-forward — the part v2.5 replaces. Why a feed-forward needs a bend at all, what the curve is, how it differs from the older ReLU, and what it does to real numbers.
Picture it
Inside v2’s feed-forward each word’s 512 numbers are spread out into 2,048 “units”, and each unit decides how much of its value to pass on. If every unit simply passed its value unchanged, two layers in a row would collapse into one plain multiplication — the network could only draw straight lines. The bend is what lets it draw curves.
An older bend, ReLU, is a light switch: positive values pass, negative ones are cut to zero. GELU is a dimmer: large positive values pass almost fully, large negative ones are dimmed almost to zero, and in between the change is smooth — a small negative value still lets a little through. That smoothness makes training steadier.
Another way to see itOr a door that opens further the harder you push, instead of one that is either locked or wide open.
Where the picture stops workingIn GELU each unit decides from its own value only — exactly what v2.5’s gate changes (deep dive 9).
Who is who — the picture, then the code
in the picturein the notebook
a unitone of 2,048 hidden numbers after fc1
the light switchReLU: max(0, z)
the dimmerGELU: z × Φ(z)
how far the dimmer is turnedΦ(z): the chance a normal random number is below z
passing the result onfc2: 2,048 back to 512

The curve and the real numbers:

  2. Its lowest point is -0.170: unlike ReLU, it lets small negative values through a little.

Where to lookA explains why the bend is needed; B draws it against ReLU; C runs it on “cat”.
The mathsGELUv2’s bend: a number times the chance it is above a random normal one2 formulas · 4 worked examples
GELU(z)=z·Φ(z)=12z(1+erf(z2))
nn.GELU() computes this exact form.
In plain English
GELU lets a number through in proportion to how likely a random normal number is to be smaller than it, Φ(z). Large positive numbers pass almost whole (Φ(3) ≈ 0.999), large negative ones are almost blocked (Φ(−3) ≈ 0.001), and around 0 it bends smoothly. Example: GELU(1) = 1 × 0.841 = 0.841, GELU(−1) = −1 × 0.159 = −0.159.
Picture it
A doorman who lets people in according to how sure he is they are above average: almost everyone clearly above gets in, almost nobody clearly below, and borderline cases partly.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Five inputs
  1. GELU(−2.0) = −2.0 × 0.023 = −0.046 · GELU(−0.5) = −0.5 × 0.309 = −0.154 · GELU(0.0) = 0.0 × 0.500 = 0.000 · GELU(0.5) = 0.5 × 0.691 = 0.346 · GELU(2.0) = 2.0 × 0.977 = 1.954.
So: Big positives pass almost whole.
Example 2 · Against a hard switch (ReLU)
  1. At −0.5: ReLU 0, GELU −0.154. At 2: ReLU 2, GELU 1.954.
So: GELU is ReLU with the corner smoothed.
Φ(z)=12π∫−∞ze−u2/2du
Φ is the normal distribution’s cumulative curve: from 0 far left to 1 far right.
In plain English
Φ(z) is the area under the bell curve to the left of z: the chance that a random number from the standard normal distribution is below z. It rises from 0 to 1 in an S shape; erf is the standard function that computes it.
Picture it
Walking along the bell curve from the far left and counting how much of its area you have passed: that share is Φ.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Φ at three points
  1. Φ(0) = 0.5, Φ(1) = 0.841, Φ(−1) = 0.159.
So: Half the bell curve lies left of 0.
Example 2 · Heights in a town
  1. Heights normal with mean 170 cm and spread 10 cm: 180 cm is z = 1 → Φ(1) = 84.1% of people are shorter.
So: Φ is “what share is below”.
symbolwhat it isin the notebook
zone hidden number (after fc1)
Φ(z)how much of z passes, between 0 and 1
erfthe error function
A common shortcut, ½ z (1 + tanh(√(2/π)(z + 0.044715 z³))), is GELU(approximate="tanh"); v2 used the exact one.
DEEP DIVE 9
SwiGLU — a feed-forward with a gate
SiLU · five steps · the gate at workunchanged in v1.5
In one sentenceSwiGLU gives every hidden unit a learned gate that decides how much of its value passes.
In plain words
SwiGLU, v2.5’s feed-forward: two views of the same word, one of which decides — unit by unit — how much of the other passes. Its switch (SiLU), its five steps on real numbers, what the gate does, and why its width is two thirds.
Picture it
Imagine 1,368 musicians, each with a partner holding a volume knob. The musician plays what they have worked out from the word (the value, from w_up). The partner listens to the same word from a different angle and decides how far to open the knob (the gate: w_gate, then SiLU) — shut, a little, or wide open. What reaches the audience is the music times the knob. A last mixer (w_down) blends all 1,368 back into the word’s 512 numbers.
In GELU each unit set its own volume from its own value. In SwiGLU the decision and the content come from two separate, learned views of the word — so a unit can carry a large value that its gate still shuts, or a small one that its gate opens wide. That is the extra freedom. To keep the size equal to v2’s, the width is two thirds of 2,048, rounded to 1,368, because there are three matrices instead of two.
Another way to see itOr a tap and a valve on one pipe: the tap sets how much water there is, the valve how much of it gets through.
Where the picture stops workingThe gates start random. Until training teaches them when to open, they are just noise.
Who is who — the picture, then the code
in the picturein the notebook
the musiciansu = w_up(x): 1,368 values
the partners’ judgementg = w_gate(x): 1,368 gate values
the knobSiLU(g) = g × sigmoid(g): near 0 shuts, large opens
music × knobSiLU(g) × u, unit by unit
the mixerw_down: 1,368 back to 512
the same size of stage1,368 = two thirds of 2,048, rounded to a multiple of 8

The mathsSwiGLUa gated linear unit with the Swish (SiLU) gate3 formulas · 6 worked examples
SwiGLU(x)=Wdown(SiLU(Wgatex)⊙Wupx)
Shazeer (2020): two projections of the same input; one, bent, multiplies the other.
In plain English
Instead of one wide layer and a bend, SwiGLU makes two projections of the token and multiplies them unit by unit. The bent one acts as a gate that decides, unit by unit, how much of the other passes. This gated linear unit lets the network switch features on and off depending on the input, and works noticeably better in large language models (LLaMA uses it).
Picture it
A mixing desk worked with two hands: one sets each fader (the gate), the other supplies the sound (the values); what you hear is the faders times the sounds.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · One unit, two gates
  1. Value 3, gate a = −2: SiLU(−2) × 3 = −0.238 × 3 = −0.715.
  2. Value 3, gate a = 3: SiLU(3) × 3 = 2.858 × 3 = 8.573.
So: The same value, muted or amplified.
Example 2 · “sleeping” in the tiny model
  1. 7 of its 16 units have an open gate (above 0.5); the output row starts (0.11, 1.37, 1.53).
So: Each token opens its own units.
SiLU(a)=a·σ(a),σ(a)=11+e−a
SiLU is Swish with β = 1: a times how open its own sigmoid says it is.
In plain English
Swish is a · σ(βa); with β = 1 it is SiLU. Next to GELU it is almost the same curve, a little simpler to compute, and dips a little lower below 0 — its lowest point is about −0.28, at a ≈ −1.28.
Picture it
A dimmer whose own setting decides how open it is: a · σ(a) is the signal times its own switch.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · σ at five points
  1. σ(−4) = 0.018 · σ(−1) = 0.269 · σ(0) = 0.500 · σ(1) = 0.731 · σ(4) = 0.982.
So: A soft switch from 0 to 1.
Example 2 · SiLU’s dip
  1. Its lowest point: SiLU(−1.278) = −1.278 × σ(−1.278) = −0.278.
So: It goes a little below 0 before rising.
hidden=8·⌊⌊2dff/3⌋+78⌋

v2 had two matrices of 512 × 2,048 plus biases: 2,099,712 numbers. SwiGLU has three; at width 1,368 they hold 3 × 512 × 1,368 = 2,101,248 — the same budget, so the comparison with v2 is fair.
Picture it
Repacking into three smaller suitcases with the same total volume as v2’s two.

Example 2 · LLaMA-7B

So: The same idea in large models.

GELU against SwiGLU
the pipelines · the curves · the same input · trainingunchanged in v1.5
In one sentenceSame size, same curve shape — the real difference is SwiGLU’s gate from a second view of the word.
In plain words
GELU against SwiGLU, side by side: the two pipelines, the two curves, the same word through both, and what training showed.
Picture it
Two ways to run a band. In the first (GELU) every musician plays and sets their own volume by how loud their part is. In the second (SwiGLU) every musician has a partner with a volume knob who decides separately. The stage is the same size — about the same number of numbers — but the second band can say “this part is loud, but not now”.
The curves themselves, GELU and SiLU, are almost the same shape; the page shows it. The real difference is structural: GELU bends one view of the word, SwiGLU multiplies two. On large models that gating has been found to train to a lower loss at the same size, which is why modern models use it. On this notebook’s small tasks, deep dive 17 shows what happened.
Another way to see itOr one person both writing and editing their essay, against a writer with a separate editor.
Where the picture stops working“Trains better” is a finding on large models with a lot of data; small tasks do not always show it.

DEEP DIVE 11
Top-p (nucleus) sampling
the cut, line by line · two real modelsunchanged in v1.5
In one sentenceTop-p shortlists as many tokens as it takes to reach 90% — few when sure, many when not.
In plain words
Top-p (nucleus) sampling: how many candidate tokens deserve a chance when the model samples its next one — the fewest that together hold 90% of the probability.
Picture it
Choosing where to eat. Top-k always shortlists exactly five restaurants, whether you already know you want pizza or have no idea at all. Top-p shortlists however many it takes to cover 90% of what you would plausibly enjoy: if you are sure, that is one place; if you are undecided, it might be twenty. Then you pick from the shortlist at random, the likelier places more often.
The model is sometimes sure and sometimes not. A fixed shortlist is too wide when it is sure — it lets poor choices in — and too narrow when it is unsure. Top-p follows the model’s own confidence: sort the tokens from likeliest down, add up their probabilities, and cut as soon as the total reaches 0.9. The untrained model here keeps 13,438 tokens; the trained one keeps 1.
Another way to see itOr packing for a trip: as many outfits as it takes to be ready for 90% of the weather — one if the forecast is certain, more if it is not.
Where the picture stops workingTop-p only acts when sampling (temperature above 0); greedy decoding ignores it.

in the picturein the notebook
your list of places, best firstnext_logits.sort(descending=True)

stopping once 90% is covereddrop = cumsum − probs ≥ top_p

The mathsTop-p (nucleus) samplingkeep the fewest tokens that hold p of the probability3 formulas · 6 worked examples
p(1)≥p(2)≥…
Sort the probabilities from largest to smallest.
In plain English
First the tokens are sorted from the most to the least likely.
Picture it
Lining up the candidates from most to fewest votes.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Four probabilities
  1. (0.10, 0.50, 0.15, 0.25) sorted → (0.50, 0.25, 0.15, 0.10).
So: Largest first.
Example 2 · The tiny model after “<SOS> the cat is”
  1. Its 4 largest: 0.9047, 0.0090, 0.0087, 0.0086.
So: One token towers over the rest.
keep token (j)  if  ∑i<jp(i)< top_p
Keep a token while the tokens before it hold less than p — so the one that crosses p is kept too.
In plain English
Then they are taken in that order until their probabilities reach top_p = 0.9. When the model is sure (one token at 0.95), only that token is kept; when it is unsure, dozens may be. Unlike top-k’s fixed 5, the shortlist follows the model’s confidence. Example: 0.5, 0.3, 0.15 and 0.05 — keep 0.5 (nothing before it), 0.3 (0.5 before it), 0.15 (0.8 before it, still under 0.9), and drop 0.05 (0.95 before it).
Picture it
Taking candidates from the top of the list until they hold 90% of the votes: a landslide leaves one finalist, a close race many.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · A confident model
  1. 0.95, 0.03, 0.02: before the first, 0 < 0.9 → keep; before the second, 0.95 ≥ 0.9 → stop. 1 kept.

The repetition penalty
the signs · the probabilities · four strengthsunchanged in v1.5
In one sentenceTokens already written lose a little score, which breaks loops but cannot replace training.
In plain words
The repetition penalty: a brake on writing the same token again. Why positive scores are divided and negative ones multiplied, what that does to probabilities, and how strong a brake is enough.
Picture it
A teacher reading your essay who gently marks down any word you have already used. It stops “very very very very”: the second “very” already costs a little, and a word that keeps winning by a hair soon loses to the runner-up. But it is also a little unfair to words like “the”, which a good sentence needs again and again — so the brake must be gentle (1.2 here).
The untrained model shows the problem: it writes “resort_” eight times in a row, because the same word stays on top. With the penalty “resort_” loses its lead at step 4 — and then the model loops on a new word instead. The brake nudges; it does not teach. The cure for loops is training: the trained model is so sure of each word that the penalty changes nothing.
Another way to see itOr a DJ who will not play a song again soon after playing it — good for variety, bad if the crowd really wants that song.
Where the picture stops workingIt punishes any repeat, right or wrong: set it high and the model starts avoiding words the answer genuinely needs twice.

A positive score is divided by ρ, a negative one multiplied — either way the token loses ground.
In plain English
Language models like to repeat themselves (“the the the”). The penalty makes every token already written less attractive. With ρ = 1.2: a score of 3 becomes 2.5, 0.6 becomes 0.5, −1 becomes −1.2. It works with greedy decoding too, and ρ = 1 turns it off. Too strong a penalty would forbid words that should repeat, such as “the”.

A quiz show that docks points for an answer already given: the repeated answer is still allowed, just less attractive.

DEEP DIVE 13
The beam-search stop, fixed
both trained models, step by stepunchanged in v1.5
In one sentenceBeam search now stops only when no unfinished answer could still beat the best finished one.
In plain words
The beam-search stop, fixed: v2 stopped as soon as four answers had finished, and could throw away a better one a step before its end. v2.5 stops only when nothing left can win — shown on both trained models, step by step.
Picture it
A quiz where four teams race to write the best answer, and answers are judged on quality, not speed. v2’s rule ended the quiz the moment four teams had handed in — even when a fifth team, one sentence from finishing, was on course to beat them all. v2.5’s rule keeps going until it is certain that no team still writing can beat the best answer already handed in.
How can it be certain? A beam’s score is a sum of log-probabilities, and each new word adds a negative number: the score can only fall as the answer grows. The length penalty softens that by dividing it by at most penalty(max_len). So a live beam can never end up better than its score now divided by penalty(max_len); if even that cannot beat the best finished answer, stopping is safe. On v2’s trained weights the old rule answered “the is sleeping peacefully”, the new one “the cat is sleeping peacefully”.
Another way to see itOr closing an auction: you do not stop at the fourth bid, you stop when nobody left could outbid the highest one.
Where the picture stops workingThe safe stop can cost a step or two of extra work — and only when those steps could still change the answer.

A live beam’s score can only fall as it grows (each log p ≤ 0), and the penalty divides by at most lp(max_len): so this is the best it could ever reach.
In plain English
Beam search keeps both finished answers and still-growing ones; the question is when growing is pointless. Each extra token adds log p ≤ 0, so a live beam’s score can only fall. The best it could possibly do is keep its present score and get the largest length penalty, lp(max_len). If even that hopeful value cannot beat the best finished answer, nothing can improve and it is safe to stop. v2 stopped as soon as 4 answers had finished — sometimes one step before a better, longer answer.
Picture it
Calling off the search once even the most hopeful outlook for every hiker still out cannot beat the best one already home.

Example 1 · Not yet

  2. Live beam −1.5: at best −1.5 ÷ lp(64) = −1.5 ÷ 4.33 = −0.346 > −1.472 → keep searching.
So: A better answer is still possible.
Example 2 · Now it can stop
  1. Live beam −9.0: at best −9.0 ÷ 4.33 = −2.079 < −1.472 → stop.
So: Safe once even the best case cannot win.

DEEP DIVE 14
Weight decay, only where it helps
decay against a gain · the two groupsunchanged in v1.5
In one sentenceWeight decay shrinks the big weight tables a little every step, but leaves gains and biases alone.
In plain words
Weight decay, applied only where it helps: what decay does, AdamW’s decoupled kind, what it would do to a normaliser’s gain, and the two groups v2.5 splits the parameters into.
Picture it
Weeding a garden. A little weeding every day keeps any one plant from sprawling over the others — that is weight decay: at every step each number is pulled a little towards zero, so the model does not come to lean on a few huge numbers. But you would not weed the fence posts. Some numbers are meant to sit at a particular value: an RMSNorm gain is the volume dial of a normaliser and should stay near 1; a bias is a small offset. Pulling them towards zero does harm and no good.
v2 weeded everything. v2.5 splits the garden into two beds by shape: tables of numbers (the real plants — embeddings, attention, SwiGLU) are decayed; single rows (gains and biases) are not. AdamW applies the decay separately from the gradient step (“decoupled”), so it is a clean, steady pull.
Another way to see itOr a budget that trims every expense by 1% a month — sensible for spending, silly for the rent, which is fixed.
Where the picture stops workingOver this short run the harm avoided is tiny (a gain shrunk only to ×0.9996); it matters on long runs (×0.74 over 100,000 steps).

Every step, each decayed weight is pulled a little towards 0, before the Adam step.

(1 − ηλ) is a number just below 1 — 0.999995 here — so every step shrinks the weight very slightly. A weight the training keeps pushing up stays large; one that is not needed slowly fades towards 0. This stops the model leaning on a few huge weights and helps it do well on new sentences.
Picture it
A small tax on savings: each step a sliver is taken, so only the weights the training keeps paying for stay large.

Taxing savings, but not the thermostat setting: a gain that should stay near 1 is not wealth to be shrunk.

DEEP DIVE 15
The EMA — an average of the weights
the warm-up · applied() · unseen sentencesunchanged in v1.5
In one sentenceThe EMA is a slow average of the weights that smooths training’s jitter; exams and saving use it.
In plain words
The EMA: a slowly-moving average of the weights that v2.5 validates and saves. The formula and its warm-up, the with-block that borrows it, the real run, and the experiment on unseen sentences.
Picture it
A long-exposure photograph of a tree in the wind. Each single snapshot catches the branches wherever the last gust blew them; the long exposure shows the tree’s real shape. Training is windy: every step moves the weights towards what the last batch wanted, noise included. The EMA is the long exposure — a running average of the weights that moves only a small part of the way towards them after each step.
The formula is one line: average = decay × average + (1 − decay) × weights. With decay 0.999 the average remembers roughly the last 1,000 steps. At the start, though, the average would still be mostly the random starting weights, so the decay is lowered at first — (1 + step) / (10 + step) — and the average catches up quickly. To validate and save, v2.5 swaps the average into the model for a moment, with ema.applied(), then puts the working weights back.
Another way to see itOr your average speed on a journey, which does not jump every time you brake.
Where the picture stops workingThe average only follows: it never knows anything the weights did not. On a run as short as this one it ends up almost the same as them.

BLEU — grading with partial credit
seven answers, two scoresunchanged in v1.5
In one sentenceBLEU gives partial credit for every matching run of one to four words, minus a penalty for missing words.
In plain words
How BLEU grades an answer with partial credit: runs of 1 to 4 words, counted with a cap, combined, and lowered for answers that are too short — worked out on seven answers.
Picture it
Marking a copy of a poem. You give a point for every word that is also in the original, then for every pair of words in the right order, every triple, and every run of four. Nobody gets points for repeating a line more often than the original has it. And if half the poem is missing, you take marks off, however good the half that is there.
That is BLEU. The four shares — 1-word to 4-word runs — are combined into one number by a geometric mean, so one poor share pulls the whole score down, and multiplied by a brevity penalty for answers shorter than the right one. v2’s real beam answer, “the is sleeping peacefully”, loses a word: exact match gives it 0, BLEU gives 49.8 — it is nearly right, and BLEU can say so.
Another way to see itOr a spelling test marked letter by letter instead of word by word: “recieve” is wrong, but not as wrong as “xyz”.
Where the picture stops workingBLEU checks words, not meaning: “the cat is asleep” loses points against “the cat is sleeping”, though it means the same.

pn=∑runsmin(counthyp,countref)∑runscounthyp
Of the n-word runs written, the share that also appear in the reference (each counted at most as often as there).
In plain English
For each n from 1 to 4, list every run of n words in a row in the output and check whether the reference has it. A run counts at most as often as the reference has it: “the the the” against a reference with one “the” gets 1 of 3. Example: output “the cat is sleeping”, reference “the cat is sleeping peacefully” — all 4 single words match (p₁ = 4/4), all 3 pairs (p₂ = 3/3), both triples, the one run of four.
Picture it
Checking a translation phrase by phrase against a model answer, counting each phrase at most as often as the model answer uses it.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Counting with a cap
  1. “the the the the the”: 5 single words, the reference has “the” once → p₁ = 1/5.
So: Repeating a safe word earns nothing.
Example 2 · One word short
  1. “the cat is sleeping”: p₁…p₄ = 4/4 · 3/3 · 2/2 · 1/1 — every run matches.
So: Precision alone is perfect here.
BP={1c>re1−r/cc≤r
Brevity penalty: an output shorter than the reference loses points.
In plain English
Precision alone rewards short answers — writing only “the” gets 1/1. The brevity penalty corrects that: with c words written and a reference of r > c words, the score is multiplied by e^(1 − r/c). Example: 4 words against 5 gives e^(1 − 1.25) = e^(−0.25) = 0.78.
Picture it
A fine for an essay that is too short: you cannot score well by writing only the few words you are sure of.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · 4 words against 5
  1. c = 4 ≤ r = 5 → BP = e^(1 − 5 ÷ 4) = e^(−0.25) = 0.779.
So: Too short is fined.
Example 2 · 6 words against 5
  1. c = 6 > r = 5 → BP = 1.
So: Longer is not fined — precision catches extra words.
BLEU=100·BP·exp(14∑n=14logpn)
The geometric mean of the four precisions; a precision of 0 is smoothed to 1 / (2^k · total).
In plain English
The four precisions are combined by a geometric mean (log, average, exp), which is low if any one of them is low — word order counts through the longer runs. Then × BP and × 100. In the example above every precision is 1 and BP is 0.78: BLEU 77.9.
Picture it
A chain is as strong as its weakest link: the geometric mean drops if any one of the four phrase lengths matches badly.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · One word short
  1. 100 × 0.779 × exp(¼ × (log 1 + log 1 + log 1 + log 1)) = 77.9.
So: Only the length is fined.
Example 2 · Right words, wrong order
  1. “peacefully sleeping is cat the”: p = 5/5 · 0/4 · 0/3 · 0/2 → BLEU 16.0.
So: Order counts through the longer runs.

Attention scores multiply a query by a key, so they grow when the vectors grow. This page shows how far they grow without QK-Norm, how the norm stops it, what the soft cap does to the output scores, and what both did in training — measured, not assumed.
Picture it
Imagine a debate club where any member can shout. A question gets answered by whoever is loudest, not by whoever points to the right answer. As the season goes on, some members learn to shout louder and louder, until one voice drowns out the whole room.
QK-Norm hands everyone a microphone set to the same volume before they speak: each query and each key is brought to the same size, keeping only the direction it points in. A match between a question and an answer is now decided by how well they agree, not by volume. The soft cap is a limiter on the room’s loudspeakers: ordinary voices pass untouched, and no single voice can go past 30.
Another way to see itOr compasses instead of speeding cars. Comparing two compasses only asks where each needle points; comparing two cars asks how fast each one goes — and speeds can run away.
Where the picture stops workingA limiter’s setting is fixed; QK-Norm’s gains are learned, so its ceiling can move a little during training. And on this small model training never ran away without it either: the protection pays off in large, long training runs.

What v3 changes here — and why it helps
  • QK-Norm — a score has a ceiling, √d_k times the learned gains
  • the soft cap — scores below about 10 barely move; none passes 30
A worked example, with this page’s real numbers
Real numbers:
  1. One attention of the real model’s code, its input ×100: v2.5’s largest score 8,818, v3’s 2.38.
  2. While the tiny models train, v2.5’s largest score climbs to 10.7; v3’s stays at 2.46.
  3. In the experiment, v3 without QK-Norm and the cap gets 94.7% on the reverse task; v3 96.5%.
A thermostat costs almost nothing — and matters most in the runs that would otherwise break.

The mathsQK-Norm and the soft capevery query and key brought to the same size; every output score held under 303 formulas · 6 worked examples
q̂=qRMS(q)⊙gq,k̂=kRMS(k)⊙gk
One head’s query and key, each divided by its own size and multiplied by learned gains.
In plain English
RMSNorm, the same 3 steps as before every block, now applied to each head’s query and each key on its own: square the d_k numbers, average, take the root, divide by it, multiply by the gains. What is left is the vector’s direction (and the gains’ fixed stretch); its length, which training could otherwise let drift up, is gone.
Picture it
Like comparing two compasses instead of two cars: only the direction each needle points matters, not how fast either car is going. QK-Norm swaps the cars for compasses.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · The last query of the tiny model, head 0
  1. “efully” asks q = (5.0827, 0.1836).
  2. RMS(q) = √((5.0827² + 0.1836²) ÷ 2 + ε) = 3.5964.
  3. q ÷ RMS(q) = (1.4133, 0.0511); times the gains g_q = (1.2303, 1.3502): q̂ = (1.7388, 0.0689).
So: The query keeps its direction and loses its length: only where it points still counts.
Example 2 · The same query, ten times longer
  1. 10 q = (50.827, 1.836).
  2. RMS(10 q) = 35.9636 — exactly 10 × 3.5964 (the tiny ε aside).
  3. q̂ = (50.827, 1.836) ÷ 35.9636 ⊙ g_q = (1.7388, 0.0689): the same as before.
So: Scaling a query (or a key) up or down changes nothing after QK-Norm.
score=q̂·k̂dk,|score|≤dk·max|gq|·max|gk|
After QK-Norm a score has a ceiling set by the gains alone.
In plain English
A score multiplies two vectors number by number and adds up. Normalised, each has length about √d_k (times its gains), and two vectors can never multiply to more than their lengths’ product. So with d_k = 128 and gains near 1, no score passes about 11 — however big the activations get. Without the norm, a score grows with the square of the vectors’ size, and one runaway score swallows the whole softmax.
Picture it
Two people pushing on a door can do at most as much as their two strengths combined. Normalising both caps their strengths, so the door can only swing so far, however hard training shouts.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · The ceiling of the tiny model
  1. d_k = 2, the largest gains are max|g_q| = 1.3502 and max|g_k| = 1.3414.
  2. √d_k · max|g_q| · max|g_k| = 1.4142 × 1.3502 × 1.3414 = 2.561.
  3. One score: “efully” → “cat” = q̂·k̂ ÷ √2 = −1.9726; the largest of all its scores is 2.3655.
So: Every score of this attention is below 2.56, whatever its input — the gains alone set the limit.
Example 2 · The real model’s heads, with and without
  1. d_k = 128 and the gains start at 1, so a score starts out below √128 = 11.31.
  2. check3.py feeds one attention vectors 1, 10 and 100 times bigger. v2.5’s largest score: 0.9 → 87.7 → 8,818.4.
  3. v3’s: 2.16 → 2.37 → 2.38.
So: Without the norm a score grows with the square of the size; with it, it stays put.
z̃=c·tanh(zc)
The soft cap on every output score z: nearly z when small, never past c.
In plain English
tanh bends a number into the range −1 to 1 and is nearly a straight line near 0. Stretched by c = 30 on both axes, it leaves every score below about 10 within 4%, keeps their order, and squeezes anything larger toward 30. The gradient through it is 1 − tanh²(z ÷ c): a runaway score also stops being pushed further.
Picture it
A volume limiter on a microphone: quiet speech passes untouched, and a shout comes out loud but never deafening. Where the picture stops: the limiter here also changes how training pushes on the loudest score.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Small, medium and runaway scores, cap 30
  1. z = 5: 30 · tanh(5 ÷ 30) = 30 × 0.1651 = 4.954 (−0.9%).
  2. z = 30: 30 · tanh(1) = 22.85 — a quarter lower.
  3. z = 100: 30 · tanh(3.33) = 29.92; z = 1,000 gives 30.00.
So: Scores far below the cap pass almost unchanged; no score can pass 30.
Example 2 · The tiny model’s last position
  1. Its highest raw score is “<EOS>” at 3.9542; capped, 30 · tanh(3.9542 ÷ 30) = 3.9315.
  2. The largest change over all 15 scores is 0.0227.
  3. The next word stays “<EOS>”: the cap keeps the order of the scores.
So: In a healthy model the cap is a guard rail, not a change: it only acts when a score runs away.

DEEP DIVE 19
Grouped-query attention
fewer key/value heads · half the cacheunchanged in v1.5
In one sentenceFour query heads, two key/value heads: half the cache, the same number of questions.
In plain words
While a model writes, it keeps the keys and values of every token so far — the KV cache. This page shows what that cache holds, how sharing key/value heads halves it, what the shared heads still do differently, and what it does and does not buy on this machine.
Picture it
Four detectives question witnesses about one case. In v2.5 each detective has a witness of their own and keeps a full notebook of what that witness said: four notebooks to carry, and every new statement written four times.
In v3 the detectives work in pairs, and each pair shares one witness and one notebook. Each detective still asks their own questions, so they still notice different things. But only two notebooks are kept and re-read whenever a new question comes: half the paper, half the reading.
Another way to see itOr a library keeping one copy of a book for every pair of readers instead of one each: the shelves hold half as much, and each reader still underlines different lines.
Where the picture stops workingTwo detectives sharing a witness cannot hear different answers, so sharing can cost a little quality — here v3 with 2 key/value heads scored 96.5% and with 4, 94.7%. And half the notebooks only means faster work when reading them is the slow part: true on a GPU, not on this CPU (3.38 ms with 4 heads, 4.54 ms with 2).

What v3 changes here — and why it helps
  • 2 key/value heads for 4 query heads — half the numbers cached per token, the same number of questions
A worked example, with this page’s real numbers
Real numbers:
  1. The real model caches 1,024 numbers per written token, where v2.5 cached 2,048.
  2. W_k and W_v lose 1,575,936 numbers across the model’s 6 attentions.
  3. On this CPU one attention step against an 8,192-token cache takes 3.38 ms with 4 key heads and 4.54 ms with 2, computed without copies: memory halves, time does not.
  4. In the experiment, 2 key/value heads did as well as 4: 96.5% against 94.7% exact on the reverse task.
A sure saving in memory; a speed-up where reading memory is the bottleneck — on GPUs, for long texts.
Where to lookA sizes the cache; B compares the three ways to share; C shows four maps from two sets of keys; D the parameters; E the speed, measured; F the experiment. G v2.5 against v3: pros and cons.
The mathsGrouped-query attentionH query heads, H_kv key/value heads, G = H ÷ H_kv queries per group3 formulas · 6 worked examples
headh=softmax(QhKg(h)⊤dk)Vg(h),g(h)=⌊h÷G⌋
Every query head keeps its own question; head h reads key/value head g(h).
In plain English
Each of the 4 query heads still multiplies its own queries by keys and mixes values — but there are only 2 sets of keys and values, one per group of 2 query heads. ⌊h ÷ G⌋ is just “which group am I in”: heads 0 and 1 → 0, heads 2 and 3 → 1. In code the sharing is a copy (repeat_interleave) on the manual path and done inside the kernel (enable_gqa) on the fast one.
Picture it
Four detectives questioning two witnesses: each detective asks their own questions, but two of them share a witness. Where the picture stops: here the witnesses’ answers are fixed numbers, not people who tire.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · The tiny model: 4 query heads, 2 key/value heads
  1. G = H ÷ H_kv = 4 ÷ 2 = 2 query heads per group.
  2. g(0) = ⌊0 ÷ 2⌋ = 0, g(1) = ⌊1 ÷ 2⌋ = 0, g(2) = g(3) = 1.
  3. Head 1, “efully” → “the”: q·k ÷ √2 = (−1.595×0.849 + 0.700×−1.232) ÷ 1.414 = −1.5681, using key head 0.
So: Heads 0 and 1 read the same keys, yet “efully” gives “the” 36% in head 0 and 1% in head 1: the questions differ, the answers are shared.
Example 2 · A large model: Llama 3 8B
  1. H = 32 query heads, H_kv = 8: G = 4.
  2. g(h) = ⌊h ÷ 4⌋: heads 0–3 read key/value head 0, heads 4–7 head 1, … heads 28–31 head 7.
  3. With H_kv = H (as v2.5) every head would have its own; with H_kv = 1 all would share one (multi-query attention).
So: Grouped-query attention sits between the two: as many questions, a quarter of the answers to keep.
cachepertoken=2·NL·Hkv·dk
Keys and values, in every layer: it shrinks with H_kv, not with H.
In plain English
While writing, every layer keeps the key and value of every token so far, one row per key/value head. So the cache grows with H_kv, and halving it halves the memory every new token must read. For long texts on a GPU, that reading is the slow part of writing.
Picture it
A library that keeps one copy of each answer sheet per group of readers instead of one per reader: half the shelf space, and half the walking to fetch them.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · The real v3 model, writing 64 tokens
  1. Per token: 2 × 2 layers × 2 heads × 128 = 1,024 numbers (v2.5: 2 × 2 × 4 × 128 = 2,048).
  2. In 16-bit floats: 2 KB per token against 4 KB.
  3. After 64 tokens: 128 KB against 256 KB, per sentence.
So: Tiny either way here — the notebook writes short answers; the saving is the same half at any length.
Example 2 · Llama 3 8B, a long conversation
  1. Per token: 2 × 32 layers × 8 heads × 128 = 65,536 numbers = 128 KB in 16-bit.
  2. With 32 key/value heads it would be 512 KB.
  3. At 8,192 tokens: 1.0 GB against 4.0 GB — for one conversation.
So: At this scale the cache, not the weights, decides how many conversations fit on one GPU.
|Wk|=|Wv|=d·Hkv·dk+Hkv·dk
The two projections that make keys and values shrink by the same factor.
In plain English
W_k and W_v used to produce d = 512 numbers per token; now they produce H_kv × d_k = 256. W_q and W_o are unchanged, so the model asks as many questions and gives as many outputs; only what is stored shrinks.
Picture it
Printing half as many answer sheets: the questions on the exam stay the same.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · W_k and W_v of the real model
  1. v2.5: 512 × 512 + 512 = 262,656 numbers each.
  2. v3: 512 × (2 × 128) + 256 = 131,328 each.
  3. Saved: 2 × 131,328 per attention × 6 attentions (2 encoder, 2 decoder self, 2 cross) = 1,575,936.
So: About 1.6 million fewer numbers — while the experts (deep dive 21) add more elsewhere.
Example 2 · The tiny model
  1. W_k: 8 × (2 × 2) + 4 = 36 numbers (it would be 8 × 8 + 8 = 72 with 4 key heads).
  2. W_q keeps its 8 × 8 + 8 = 72.
  3. The 4 query heads still get 4 different questions per token.
So: Only the side that is stored and shared gets smaller.

DEEP DIVE 20
FlashAttention — how it works, and when PyTorch uses it
built into PyTorch · a block at a time · the conditionsunchanged in v1.5
In one sentenceHow PyTorch’s built-in FlashAttention works — a block at a time, the same answer, no full table — and when it runs.
In plain words
FlashAttention is a way of computing attention that PyTorch has built in: F.scaled_dot_product_attention uses it by itself when the call and the GPU allow. This notebook does not implement it. Plain attention builds the table of every query against every key; FlashAttention reads the keys a block at a time instead, keeping only a running largest score, a running sum and a running output per query — and gets exactly the same answer. This page is for understanding it: it computes one row both ways, then shows when PyTorch actually uses it.
Picture it
A teacher has to grade every exam relative to the class. The plain way: pile every exam on the desk, add up all the marks, then go back through the pile and divide each mark by the total. With a thousand exams, the desk overflows.
The FlashAttention way: grade the exams as they arrive, a few at a time, and keep only three things on a sticky note — the highest mark so far, a running total and a running weighted answer. When a new exam beats the highest mark, rescale the note once to the new reference and carry on. At the end, one division gives exactly the result of the full pile.
Another way to see itOr a till that keeps a running total instead of listing every purchase: if the price list changes halfway through the day, it multiplies the total once and keeps counting.
Where the picture stops workingThe sticky note saves desk space, not grading: FlashAttention does the same arithmetic, plus a few rescales. Its speed comes from a GPU keeping each block in fast on-chip memory. On this CPU, is_causal alone was faster (34.6 against 63.5 ms at 2,048 words) with PyTorch’s CPU version of FlashAttention; v3’s real call, with grouped-query attention, runs the plain kernel here: 139.3 ms. And the note is PyTorch’s, not yours: it decides to work this way, on a suitable GPU.

  2. The online result (2.5877, 4.4112) equals the plain one (2.5877, 4.4112).

The mathsFlashAttention’s mathsthe online softmax: attention a block of keys at a time3 formulas · 6 worked examples
softmax(s)j=esj−cΣkesk−cforanyc
Subtracting the same number from every score changes no weight.
In plain English
Softmax turns scores into weights by e^ and dividing by the sum. Multiply every e^ by the same factor e^−c and the sum is multiplied by it too: the factor cancels. So any c gives the same weights; the largest score is the natural choice, because then every e^ lies between 0 and 1.
Picture it
Like measuring heights from the tallest person in the room instead of from the floor: the differences between people stay the same, and nobody’s number gets huge.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · “efully”’s 7 scores, two ways
  1. c = 0: e^s sums to 11.1408; “peac” gets e^1.4209 ÷ 11.1408 = 0.3717.
  2. c = m = 1.4209: e^(s − m) sums to 2.6903; “peac” gets 1 ÷ 2.6903 = 0.3717.
  3. Every other weight agrees as well.
So: The e^c cancels top and bottom: any reference point gives the same weights.
Example 2 · Why the largest score is the safe choice
  1. Scores of 100 and 99: e^100 ≈ 2.7 × 10⁴³, past what 16-bit numbers hold (6.6 × 10⁴).
  2. Subtract m = 100: e^0 = 1 and e^−1 = 0.3679; weights 1 ÷ 1.3679 = 0.731 and 0.269.
  3. With 32-bit floats e^89 already overflows; with m subtracted no e^ ever exceeds 1.
So: Subtracting the largest score is free and always safe.
m′=max(m,maxjsj),ℓ′=em−m′ℓ+Σjesj−m′,o′=em−m′o+Σjesj−m′vj
After each block of keys: the largest score, the running sum and the running output, brought to the new largest score.
In plain English
Read the keys a block at a time. Keep m, the largest score so far. If a block brings a larger one, m′, the sums you already have were measured against the old m: multiplying them by e^(m − m′) re-measures them against m′. Then add the block’s own e^(s − m′) terms. The block’s scores are never needed again.
Picture it
Like a running tally in a currency that keeps being re-valued: when the reference changes, you convert the whole tally at once with one exchange rate, then keep adding.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Block 2 of “efully”: no larger score
  1. Before: m = 1.3796, l = 1.0430; the block’s scores −1.9726, 0.0592.
  2. m′ = max(1.3796, 0.0592) = 1.3796: rescale e^(1.3796 − 1.3796) = 1.
  3. l′ = 1 × 1.0430 + 0.0350 + 0.2670 = 1.3450.
So: When the maximum does not change, the sums just grow.
Example 2 · Block 3: a larger score arrives
  1. Before: m = 1.3796, l = 1.3450; the block’s largest score is 1.4209.
  2. m′ = 1.4209: rescale = e^(1.3796 − 1.4209) = 0.9595.
  3. l′ = 0.9595 × 1.3450 + 0.3743 + 1.0000 = 2.6648; o is rescaled the same way.
So: One multiplication moves everything kept to the new reference.
output=oℓ,memory∝L·(2+dk)insteadofL2
Divide once at the end: exactly softmax(s) · V, without the L × L table.
In plain English
After the last block, ℓ is the full sum of e^(s − m) and o the full weighted sum of the values, both against the true largest score. Their ratio is the attention output. Only m, ℓ and o are kept per query — 2 + d_k numbers — never the table.
Picture it
Like averaging exam marks as the papers arrive instead of piling them all on the desk first: a running total and a count are enough.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · The last division
  1. After the last block: o = (6.9618, 11.8676), l = 2.6903.
  2. o ÷ l = (2.587690, 4.411210).
  3. The plain way, weights × V: (2.587690, 4.411210).
So: The same output, the table never built.
Example 2 · The memory, one head at 8,192 tokens
  1. The plain way: 8,192 × 8,192 = 67,108,864 scores.
  2. FlashAttention: 8,192 × (1 + 1 + 128) = 1,064,960 numbers (m, l and o per query).
  3. About 63 times less — and the gap grows with the length.
So: Memory that grows with the length, not its square: long contexts become possible.

DEEP DIVE 21
A mixture of experts
the router · top-2 · the balance lossunchanged in v1.5
In one sentenceA router sends each word to the best 2 of 4 small feed-forwards: more to learn with, about the same work per word.
In plain words
A mixture of experts splits each layer’s feed-forward into several smaller ones and lets a tiny router send every token to the best 2. The layer can hold more knowledge while each token costs about the same. This page follows the router on real tokens, blends two experts’ answers, explains the balance loss, and measures what it costs and what it did here.
Picture it
A small clinic has one family doctor who sees every patient. To know more, it could hire a doctor who knows twice as much — but then every visit would take twice as long.
Instead it hires four specialists, each half as broad, and puts a triage nurse at the door. The nurse looks at each patient, sends them to the best two specialists and says how much to trust each one. The clinic now knows twice as much, and each patient still gets about one doctor’s worth of time. A rota makes sure no specialist sits idle while another is swamped.
Another way to see itOr a newsroom with four section editors and a chief who passes each story to the two best placed to edit it: more know-how in the building, the same work per story.
Where the picture stops workingA nurse knows what each specialist is for; the router is never told, and its experts seldom specialise along lines a person would name. The specialists also cost time here — a training step about 1.6× slower on this CPU — and did not help these small tasks: 96.5% exact on unseen reverse sentences with experts, 97.6% with one feed-forward.

Real numbers:

The mathsA mixture of expertsa router, 4 SwiGLU experts, the best 2 per token4 formulas · 8 worked examples
p=softmax(Wrx)∈ℝN
The router: one probability per expert, for this token.
In plain English
The router is the smallest layer in the model: one row of weights per expert, and a token’s score for an expert is the dot product of the two. Softmax turns the 4 scores into probabilities. Nobody tells the router what each expert is for: the specialisation is learned.
Picture it
A hospital triage nurse: one quick look at each patient decides which specialists to call.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · The router on “sleeping”
  1. Scores for the 4 experts: (−2.823, 1.985, −1.434, −1.046).
  2. e^ of each: (0.059, 7.281, 0.238, 0.351); their sum 7.930.
  3. p = (0.007, 0.918, 0.030, 0.044).
So: The router is sure: expert 1 gets 92% of the vote.
Example 2 · The router on “the”
  1. p = (0.179, 0.086, 0.024, 0.711).
  2. Two experts close together: 71% and 18%.
  3. The other two share the rest.
So: Some tokens are clear-cut, some need two specialists.
T=topk(p),ge=peΣe′∈Tpe′fore∈T
Keep the k = 2 most likely experts; their gates add up to 1.
In plain English
Only the k = 2 most likely experts run on the token; dividing their probabilities by their sum makes them shares of a whole. The other experts cost nothing for this token — that is what keeps the arithmetic per token flat while the layer grows.
Picture it
Two specialists are called, and their opinions are weighted by how sure the nurse was about each.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · “the”: top 2 and their gates
  1. top_2(p) = experts 3 and 0 (0.7105 and 0.1793).
  2. g = 0.7105 ÷ 0.8898 = 0.7985, and 0.1793 ÷ 0.8898 = 0.2015.
  3. The gates add up to 1.
So: The 2 shares are rescaled to a whole; the other 2 experts never see this token.
Example 2 · “sleeping”: nearly one expert
  1. top_2 = experts 1 and 3.
  2. Gates 0.9540 and 0.0460.
  3. The second expert is computed but barely counts.
So: With a confident router, top-2 behaves almost like top-1.
y=Σe∈Tge·Ee(x)
The answer: the chosen experts’ answers, weighted by their gates.
In plain English
Each chosen expert is a full SwiGLU feed-forward, half as wide as v2.5’s. The token’s output is their two answers blended by the gates; the shape is exactly what a dense feed-forward returns, so nothing else in the layer changes.
Picture it
The diagnosis is a weighted blend of the two specialists’ reports; the rest of the hospital never hears about this patient.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · “the”’s output, number 0
  1. Expert 3 says −41.2549; expert 0 says −7.0088.
  2. y[0] = 0.7985 × −41.2549 + 0.2015 × −7.0088 = −34.3533.
  3. The same for all 8 numbers of the row.
So: Each token’s answer is a weighted blend of its 2 experts.
Example 2 · The real model’s arithmetic per token
  1. One expert: 3 × 512 × 688 = 1,056,768 numbers (d_ff ÷ 2 = 1,024 → hidden 688).
  2. Two experts + the router (4 × 512): 2,115,584 — v2.5’s one feed-forward: 2,101,248.
  3. The layer holds 4 experts + the router: 4,229,120.
So: Twice the knowledge, the same work per token — the reason experts exist.
balance=N·Σe=1Nfe·Pe
f_e: the share of choices that went to e; P_e: e’s mean probability. 1 when even.
In plain English
f_e counts where tokens actually went; P_e says how much the router wanted to send there. Their product summed over experts, times N, is 1 for an even split and up to N if one expert took everything. Added to the loss, it stops a few experts from hoarding the tokens.
Picture it
A rota that keeps any one doctor from being sent every patient: an even workload keeps everyone learning.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · The tiny model’s decoder layer 0
  1. Shares f = (0.286, 0.214, 0.214, 0.286) (2 choices × 7 tokens = 14).
  2. Mean probabilities P = (0.107, 0.252, 0.426, 0.216).
  3. 4 × (0.0304 + 0.0540 + 0.0912 + 0.0617) = 0.9493.
So: Close to 1: the work is spread almost evenly.
Example 2 · If the router collapsed onto 2 experts
  1. Every token picks experts 0 and 1: f = (0.5, 0.5, 0, 0).
  2. Suppose the router gives them P = (0.45, 0.45, 0.05, 0.05).
  3. 4 × (0.5 × 0.45 + 0.5 × 0.45) = 1.8.
So: Lopsided routing costs extra loss, so training spreads the tokens out again.

DEEP DIVE 22
Multi-token prediction
guessing the token after nextunchanged in v1.5
In one sentenceA small extra head that also learns the word after next — and whose guesses speculative decoding checks.
In plain words
Every position of an answer teaches the model what comes next. Multi-token prediction adds a small head that also learns what comes after that, from the same sentence. This page follows the head step by step, shows what it guesses, follows both losses through training, and measures what it did.
Picture it
A chess coach replays a famous game with a student. At every position the usual question is: what is the next move? The student learns to look one move ahead.
Now the coach adds a second question: given the next move, what comes after it? To answer, the student must understand the position well enough to see further. It is the same game, but every position now teaches two things. Later, while playing, a quick guess at the move after next can be checked against what really happens.
Another way to see itOr dictating a letter while already thinking of the word after next: you say one word at a time, but your mind runs a step further along.
Where the picture stops workingA student plays better for thinking ahead; on these small tasks the extra lesson moved the accuracy little (96.5% exact on unseen reverse sentences with the head, 95.0% without). And the head never plays a move itself: generate() still writes one token per pass; only speculative decoding uses its guesses.

the replayed gamea training sentence, run through the decoder

and the move after it?the multi-token head: position t also learns the token at t + 2
given the next moveteacher forcing: the real token at t + 1 is fed in, next to the state at t
the same board and notationthe shared output layer: the head adds only 2,627,072 numbers in the real model

What v3 changes here — and why it helps
  • a small head for the token after next — a second lesson per position; drafts for speculative decoding
A worked example, with this page’s real numbers
Real numbers:
  1. On the tiny model’s five sentences the head guesses the token after next right 27 of 27 times.
  2. In the real model the head adds 2,627,072 numbers — it shares the output layer.
  3. In the experiment, 100 unseen sentences took 404 passes of the model for 650 tokens with the head’s drafts.
  4. Accuracy on the reverse task: 96.5% with the head, 95.0% without.
A helping lesson in training, a time-saver at writing time.
Where to lookA shows what each position is taught; B follows the head on one position; C the two losses; D the experiment. E v2.5 against v3: pros and cons in every condition.
The mathsMulti-token predictionan extra head that guesses the token after next3 formulas · 6 worked examples
zt=Wp [ RMSNormh(ht);RMSNorme(et+1) ]
The decoder’s state at t and the embedding of the token at t + 1, normalised, joined and mixed.
In plain English
The head reads two things about position t: everything the decoder worked out there (h_t), and which token really comes next (e_{t+1}, given during training). Each is normalised, the two lists are laid end to end, and one matrix mixes them: z_t says “knowing this, and that this token follows”.
Picture it
A chess student told the next move and asked for the one after: the position and the move just played, considered together.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Position 2, “cat”: the two inputs
  1. h_t = (1,385.410, −918.578, 912.772… — size (RMS) 1,004.084.
  2. e_{t+1} (the embedding of “is”, × √8) — size 1.560.
  3. After their norms both have size about 1 (times their gains): (1.352, −1.126, 0.856… and (1.781, −0.050, 1.972….
So: The norms put the state and the next token on the same footing before they are mixed.
Example 2 · Joined and projected
  1. [norm_h(h) ; norm_e(e)]: 8 + 8 = 16 numbers.
  2. W_p (8 × 16, no bias) mixes all 16 into 8: z = (0.143, 3.106, −1.733….
  3. The real model: W_p is 512 × 1,024 = 524,288 numbers.
So: One small matrix merges “what I know” with “what comes next”.
ut=RMSNorm(zt+SwiGLU(zt)),p̃t=softmax(cap(Eut+b))
A miniature layer, then the model’s own output layer: p̃_t scores the token at t + 2.
In plain English
z_t goes through a SwiGLU with a shortcut and a final RMSNorm — a one-layer model in miniature — and is scored by the model’s own output layer, so the head adds only 2,627,072 numbers in the real model.
Picture it
The student answers on the same scoresheet as the teacher: no new notation to learn, only a little extra thinking.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · What the head predicts at position 2
  1. u = norm_out(z + SwiGLU(z)) = (0.804, 0.216, −2.310….
  2. Through the shared output layer and the cap: its highest score is “sleeping” with 4.462.
  3. p̃(“sleeping”) = 0.9074 — the truth after next is “sleeping”.
So: From “cat” plus “is”, the head sees “sleeping” coming.
Example 2 · Every position of the sentence
  1. The head’s guesses: “cat”, “is”, “sleeping”, “peac”, “efully”, “<EOS>”.
  2. The truth two ahead: “cat”, “is”, “sleeping”, “peac”, “efully”, “<EOS>”.
  3. Right on all five training sentences: 27 of 27.
So: A tiny model learns its five sentences two tokens ahead too; unseen text is where guesses go wrong (deep dive 23).
L=Lmain+λ·Lmtp+0.01·balance,Lmtp=1T−1ΣtCE(p̃t,xt+2)
Training learns both lessons at once; λ = 0.3 keeps the extra one a helper.
In plain English
Every position now teaches twice: the next token through the main head, the token after it through the extra one. The extra loss is weighted 0.3, so it guides without taking over; its gradient flows back into the decoder and pushes the state to plan further ahead.
Picture it
Homework with a bonus question: the main grade counts most, but practising two moves ahead makes the main answers better too.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · This sentence’s total
  1. Main loss (mean over 7 positions): 0.5633.
  2. Head loss (6 positions): 0.5663; balance 0.9979.
  3. Total = 0.5633 + 0.3 × 0.5663 + 0.01 × 0.9979 = 0.7432.
So: Training minimises the total; the loss it reports is the main one alone.
Example 2 · Why 0.56 is the floor
  1. Label smoothing 0.1 over 15 tokens: the best possible target puts 0.9 + 0.1 ÷ 15 on the right token.
  2. p(right) = 0.9067, every other 0.0067: loss = −(0.9067 ln 0.9067 + 14 × 0.0067 ln 0.0067) = 0.5565.
  3. The tiny model’s losses (0.556 to 0.576) sit right on it.
So: Both heads are as sure as label smoothing allows.

DEEP DIVE 23
Speculative decoding
two tokens per pass · the same answersunchanged in v1.5
In one sentenceThe head guesses the next word, one pass checks it: up to two words per pass, never a different answer.
In plain words
A model writes one token per pass, and passes are what writing costs. Speculative decoding lets the multi-token head guess the next token and checks the guess inside a pass that was needed anyway: right, and the pass writes two tokens; wrong, and it writes the model’s own one. This page follows it pass by pass, shows why the answer cannot change, explains the rule that keeps sampling exact, and measures passes and time.
Picture it
In a busy kitchen the head chef plates every dish personally, one at a time, and each dish needs a full trip to the pass. The trips are what make service slow.
So an apprentice prepares the next dish ahead of time. On each trip the chef checks the apprentice’s plate against the one the chef would have made. If it matches, both dishes go out on the same trip. If not, the chef’s own dish goes out, the apprentice’s plate is scrapped, and the apprentice starts on the next one. Diners always get exactly the chef’s food.
Another way to see itOr a fast lane at a supermarket: shoppers with a pre-scanned basket pass after a quick spot check; if the check fails, they rejoin the normal queue at the same place, and nobody leaves with the wrong items.
Where the picture stops workingA chef’s trip costs the same for one plate or two. On this CPU it does not: a pass with 2 tokens costs 1.99× a pass with 1, so even with every guess right a token cost 2.91 ms against 2.41 ms. The kitchen picture holds on a GPU writing for one reader, which was not measured here. And with sampling the check is a weighted coin, not a match: a guess is kept as often as the model agrees with it.
Who is who — the picture, then the code
in the picturein the notebook
the head chefthe whole model: one pass of the decoder
a trip to the passone pass, reading the last token and the guess together
the apprenticethe multi-token head: guess_after() guesses the next token from the state
checking the platethe model’s own pick at the guess’s place (row 0) equals the guess
both dishes on one tripa right guess: 2 tokens in one pass — 7 tokens in 4 passes on a sentence it knows
the scrapped platea wrong guess: its row is cut from the cache — 5 passes on a sentence it never saw
always the chef’s foodthe same tokens as greedy: 3,000 sentences identical in the experiment

What v3 changes here — and why it helps
  • speculative_generate(): the head guesses, one pass checks — fewer passes, identical answers; the time saved depends on the hardware
A worked example, with this page’s real numbers
Real numbers:
  1. On a sentence the tiny model knows, 7 tokens take 4 passes instead of 7; on one it never saw, 5: one guess was wrong.
  2. With sampling, the head’s over-bet on “cat”, where the model wants “dog”, is kept with chance 0.0169.
  3. In the experiment, 100 unseen sentences took 404 passes for 650 tokens — identical answers in all 3,000 sentences checked.
  4. On this CPU a pass of 2 tokens costs 1.99× a pass of 1, so a token costs 2.91 ms instead of 2.41 ms: fewer passes, no time saved.
A sure saving in passes, never a different answer; a saving in time where a pass of 2 tokens is nearly free — on GPUs.
Where to lookA and B follow every pass on two sentences; C shows why the answer cannot change; D the sampling rule; E passes and time; F the experiment. G what it costs and saves against v2.5.
The mathsSpeculative decodingguess with the head, check with one pass — the same answers4 formulas · 8 worked examples
d=argmaxxqt(x) ;   kept if  d=argmaxxpt(x)
Greedy: the head’s guess is kept only if it is the model’s own pick at that place.
In plain English
The head proposes its likeliest token d for the next place. The next pass reads the last token and d together; its first row of scores, p_t, belongs to the place where d goes and cannot see d (attention only looks back). If greedy’s pick there is d, the guess is exactly what greedy would have written — and the second row, computed with d in place, gives the token after it.
Picture it
An apprentice plates the next dish while the chef finishes this one. The chef glances at it: if it is what she would have made, it goes out with hers; if not, she makes her own as usual.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Pass 2 on “the cat is sleeping on the sof a”
  1. The head’s best guess after “the”: d = “cat” (q 0.8953).
  2. The pass reads “the” and “cat”; row 0’s best: “cat” (p 0.9195) — the same: kept.
  3. Row 1’s best, “is” (p 0.9203), is written too.
So: Two tokens, one pass of the model.
Example 2 · Pass 2 on “the cat is running on the sof a”, never seen
  1. The head is unsure: “cat” q 0.6817, “dog” q 0.2044; d = “cat”.
  2. Row 0’s best: “dog” (p 0.9229) ≠ d: not kept.
  3. The pass writes “dog” only; row 1, computed after the wrong guess, is dropped.
So: A wrong guess costs the check, never a wrong token.
P(kept)=min(1,p(d)q(d)) ;   if not: x∼max(0,p−q)1−β
Sampling: keep a guess with chance p ÷ q (at most 1), otherwise draw from what the guess left out.
In plain English
With sampling, an exact match is too strict: d was drawn at random. So d is kept with chance p(d) ÷ q(d): always when the model likes d at least as much as the head did, less often when the head over-bet. If d is dropped, the token is drawn from max(0, p − q), the part of p that q did not cover, rescaled to add up to 1.
Picture it
A quality check that keeps an item with chance “how much we want it ÷ how often the supplier sends it”: over-supplied items are thinned, under-supplied ones always pass, and the gap is ordered directly.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · A drawn “cat” at the place after “the”
  1. p(“cat”) = 0.0115, q(“cat”) = 0.6817 (temperature 1, the unseen sentence).
  2. P(kept) = min(1, 0.0115 ÷ 0.6817) = 0.0169.
So: The head bets on “cat” far more than the model does: the rule cuts that bet back.
Example 2 · A drawn “dog”
  1. p = 0.9229, q = 0.2044: p ÷ q = 4.515, so P(kept) = min(1, 4.515) = 1.
  2. A dropped “cat” is replaced from max(0, p − q) ÷ (1 − β): “dog” gets 0.9901 of it.
So: Where the head under-bets, its guess always survives, and the leftover makes up the rest.
P(x)=min(p(x),q(x))+(1−β)·max(0,p(x)−q(x))1−β=p(x),β=Σxmin(p(x),q(x))
Every token’s chance in all is exactly the model’s p(x).
In plain English
Add the two ways a token can come out: as a kept guess, min(p, q); as a redraw, (1 − β) times its share of the leftover. The (1 − β) cancels, and min(p, q) + max(0, p − q) = p. The guesser changes how many passes are needed, not what is written.
Picture it
Two routes into the same queue, a fast lane and the regular one: whoever is turned away from the fast lane joins the regular one, and the queue ends up exactly as it would have been.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · “dog” in all
  1. min(p, q) = 0.2044; β = Σ min(p, q) = 0.2743, so 1 − β = 0.7257.
  2. 0.2044 + 0.7257 × 0.9901 = 0.9229 = p(“dog”).
So: Kept guesses and redrawn tokens add up to exactly p.
Example 2 · How often a guess survives
  1. β = Σ min(p, q) = 0.2743 at this place of the unseen sentence.
  2. At the same place of the sentence the model knows, p and q agree: β = 0.9720.
So: The output never depends on q; only the number of passes does.
time a token = c2+ch1+α   against   c1
The pay-off: fewer passes, worth it when a 2-token pass is cheap.
In plain English
Plain writing costs c_1 a token. Speculative writing costs a 2-token pass and a guess per pass, and writes 1 + α tokens a pass on average. It wins when c_2 + c_h < (1 + α) c_1 — on a GPU, where c_2 ≈ c_1, but not on this CPU, where c_2 ≈ 2 c_1.
Picture it
Carrying two plates per trip saves walking only if two plates are no heavier to carry than one. On this CPU they are twice as heavy; on a GPU they barely weigh more.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · This CPU, every guess right (α = 1)
  1. c_1 = 2.41 ms, c_2 = 4.79 ms, c_h = 1.04 ms (the real-size model, bench3.py).
  2. (4.79 + 1.04) ÷ 2 = 2.91 ms a token, against 2.41 ms plain.
So: Here a 2-token pass costs 1.99× one: fewer passes, but no time saved.
Example 2 · The experiment, translate (mean of 3 seeds)
  1. 650 tokens in 404 passes: 1.61 tokens a pass; every guess kept, α = 1.
  2. Below 1 + α = 2: the first pass of each of the 100 sentences has nothing to check, and 58 checking passes wrote only <EOS>.
So: Short answers cap the gain: the ends of an answer write one token.

Leviathan et al. (2023) and Chen et al. (2023) prove the rule: the output follows p exactly, whatever q is — a better guesser only means fewer rejected guesses.

DEEP DIVE 24
Muon
Newton–Schulz · every direction the same stepunchanged in v1.5
In one sentenceAn optimizer that gives every direction of a matrix’s update the same strength — and a check of whether it is only a bigger step.
In plain words
A weight matrix is a map from one vector to another, and its gradient pushes along a few main directions with very different strengths. Muon keeps those directions and evens out their strengths with five cheap matrix products. This page follows one real update step by step, explains the polynomial that does it, compares it with Adam, and checks whether its gain is only a bigger step.
Picture it
A choir rehearses a song. After each run-through the director hears what went wrong — but the loudest section drowns out the rest. A director who only corrects what is loudest gives the quiet sections almost no feedback at all.
So this director listens to each section, then gives every section a correction of the same strength: the loud sopranos get a little less than their volume suggests, the quiet basses much more than theirs. Each section still hears what it got wrong; none is ignored. That is Muon: keep what the correction says, give every direction of it the same weight.
Another way to see itOr a coach who trains every muscle, not only the strongest: the same effort spread over the whole body, so the weak ones catch up.
Where the picture stops workingA choir has one director; in v3 Muon trains only the matrices inside the layers, and AdamW the rest. And the picture says nothing about how strong the corrections are overall: Muon’s steps are also larger than AdamW’s, and here that mattered — AdamW alone reached 56.9% on unseen reversals at its usual step and 97.4% exact at ten times it, against v3’s 96.5%.

in the picturein the notebook
a correction after a run-throughthe gradient of one batch, for one weight matrix
the choir’s sectionsthe matrix’s main directions
how loud each section isits strength (singular value): the strongest direction gets 76.2% of a plain step
what each section got wrongthe direction itself — kept as it is
the same strength for every sectionNewton–Schulz, five matrix products: the largest share falls to 17.2%
the quietest section, finally heardthe weakest direction: strength 0.0048 before, 1.1715 after five steps

What v3 changes here — and why it helps
  • Muon for the weight matrices in the layers — every direction of an update moves about the same amount
A worked example, with this page’s real numbers
Real numbers:
  1. One real update of the tiny model: its strongest direction takes 76.2% of the step; after Muon the largest share is 17.2%.
  2. Five steps lift its weakest strength from 0.0048 to 1.1715; the strongest stays near 0.83.
  3. The reverse task at the notebook’s learning rates: v3 with Muon 96.5% exact, with AdamW only 56.9%.
  4. AdamW given a 10× larger learning rate: 97.4% exact.
Muon spreads every update evenly — but here a 10× larger AdamW step matched it on unseen sentences; longer ones stay unsettled.

The mathsMuonmomentum, then Newton–Schulz: every direction of an update about the same strength4 formulas · 8 worked examples
mt=0.95mt−1+0.05gt,G=0.05gt+0.95mt
Momentum, then a look-ahead mix: a smoothed gradient for each weight matrix.
In plain English
Like SGD with momentum: keep a running average of each matrix’s gradients, moved 5% toward every new one, and use a mix that leans 95% toward that average — Nesterov’s look-ahead. One noisy batch cannot swing the direction much.
Picture it
A ship’s heading, steered by the average of many wind readings rather than the latest gust: the course holds, the noise fades.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · The running average, one number (× 10⁻⁵)
  1. m_{t−1}[0,0] = 1.8233, g_t[0,0] = −9.8534.
  2. m_t = 0.95 × 1.8233 + 0.05 × (−9.8534) = 1.2395.
So: The average moves only 5% of the way toward the new gradient.
Example 2 · The look-ahead mix, the same number
  1. G[0,0] = 0.05 × (−9.8534) + 0.95 × 1.2395 = 0.6849 (× 10⁻⁵).
  2. This mix, not the raw gradient, is what Newton–Schulz receives.
So: Nesterov looks one step ahead along the average.
X0=G‖G‖F,‖G‖F=ΣijGij2=Σiσi2
Divide by the matrix’s size: every strength σ falls below 1.
In plain English
The matrix G is divided by the root of the sum of all its squares. That same sum is the sum of its squared strengths, so afterwards the strengths’ squares add up to exactly 1 and none can exceed 1. Directions and ratios are untouched.
Picture it
Turning a recording’s master volume down until the loudest instrument is just under the limit: the mix is unchanged, nothing clips.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · The tiny model’s update
  1. ‖G‖_F = √(sum of its 64 squares) = 7.864 × 10⁻⁵.
  2. X_0 = G ÷ ‖G‖_F; its strengths run from 0.8719 down to 0.0048.
So: All below 1: in the range the polynomial is built for.
Example 2 · Why the largest is at most 1
  1. The squared strengths add up to ‖G‖²: after the division they add up to 1.
  2. Here 0.7602 + 0.1460 + 0.0696 + … = 0.9974 — just under 1: the code adds ε = 10⁻⁷ to ‖G‖, which shows when ‖G‖ is this small.
So: A sum of squares of at most 1 cannot hold a term above 1.
Xk+1=aXk+(bAk+cAk2)Xk,Ak=XkXkT⇔σ↦aσ+bσ3+cσ5
Five steps of the same polynomial lift weak directions, hold strong ones.
In plain English
Each step multiplies X by itself twice, X Xᵀ then again, and mixes: three matrix products. Written in X’s own directions this is the polynomial aσ + bσ³ + cσ⁵ applied to every strength separately. Near 0 it multiplies by 3.4445; from about 0.6 to 1.2 it maps back into the same band. After five steps every direction has a strength near 1.
Picture it
A choir director who brings up the quiet voices and holds back the loud ones, rehearsal after rehearsal, until every part is heard about equally — without changing what anyone sings.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · The weakest direction, one step
  1. σ = 0.0048: a σ = 0.0165, b σ³ = −5.3 × 10⁻⁷, c σ⁵ = 5.2 × 10⁻¹².
  2. f(σ) = 0.0165 — ×3.444.
So: Near 0 the cubic and quintic vanish: a weak direction grows ×3.4 a step.
Example 2 · The strongest direction, one step
  1. σ = 0.8719: 3.4445 × 0.8719 − 4.775 × 0.8719³ + 2.0315 × 0.8719⁵
  2. = 3.0033 − 3.1650 + 1.0236 = 0.8619.
So: Near 1 the terms cancel: a strong direction stays where it is.
W←W(1−ηλ)−ηmax(1,m/n)·X5
The step: weight decay, then the update at a fixed size set by η.
In plain English
Weight decay shrinks the matrix by ηλ = 0.0002, then the orthogonalized update is subtracted, times η. Its size no longer depends on the gradient’s, so η alone sets how far every direction moves. Tall matrices get a little more, so each number moves alike.
Picture it
Every team member gets the same budget of effort per week, whatever they shouted about: effort set by the manager, not by the loudest voice.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · One weight of W_q
  1. W = −0.7659, update = 0.4199, η = 0.02, λ = 0.01; the matrix is square: √max(1, 8 ÷ 8) = 1.
  2. −0.7659 × (1 − 0.02 × 0.01) − 0.02 × 0.4199 = −0.7741.
So: A step of −0.0084 — set by η, not by the gradient’s size.
Example 2 · A tall matrix of the real model
  1. An expert’s w_up maps 512 numbers to 688: its weight is 688 × 512 — taller than wide.
  2. Its update is multiplied by √(688 ÷ 512) = 1.1592.
So: So each of its numbers moves as much as in a square matrix.

DEEP DIVE 25
8-bit weights
a scale per row · a quarter of the bytesunchanged in v1.5
In one sentenceWeights as whole numbers from −127 to 127 with a scale per row: a quarter of the memory, the same answers.
In plain words
A trained model is mostly weight matrices stored as 4-byte floats. Stored instead as whole numbers from −127 to 127 with one scale per row, they take about a quarter of the memory. This page quantizes one real row step by step, shows why each row gets its own scale, counts the bytes, and measures what it changes in the answers — and what it does not buy.
Picture it
A workshop measures every part with a laser to seven digits and keeps a notebook full of those long numbers. Most of the digits never matter: a part works just as well a hair longer or shorter.
So every shelf gets its own ruler, marked in 127 steps from zero to the longest part on that shelf, and each part is written down as a whole number of steps. The notebook shrinks to a quarter. A shelf of small parts gets a ruler with small steps, so its parts stay precise. To use a part, read its step count and multiply by the shelf’s step size.
Another way to see itOr prices in whole coins instead of fractions of a cent: each price moves by at most half a coin, and the shopping still adds up the same.
Where the picture stops workingA ruler is only as fine as its steps: one very long part makes the steps coarse for the whole shelf. And a shorter notebook is not a faster workshop — here each weight is turned back into a float whenever it is used, so the copy saves memory, not time. The experiment’s reverse task, 3 seeds: 96.6% exact as float32, 96.6% as the 8-bit copy.

A worked example, with this page’s real numbers
Real numbers:
  1. One row of the tiny model: scale 0.02996; weight 0.2502 is stored as 8 and comes back as 0.2397.
  2. The real model: 130.2 MB as floats, 32.9 MB in 8 bits.
