A quarter of the memory with the same answers — not, with this simple version, more speed.
Where to lookA quantizes one row; B shows why a scale per row; C counts the bytes; D what changes in the answers; E the experiment; F what large models do beyond this. G what it costs and saves against v2.5.
The maths8-bit weightsone scale per row, whole numbers from −127 to 127, back to floats when used4 formulas · 8 worked examples
si=maxj|Wij|127
Each row’s step size, set by its largest weight.
In plain English
For every row, find the largest weight by size and divide it by 127. That is the row’s step: the 255 levels −127 × s … 127 × s cover the row exactly, and the largest weight lands on level 127.
Picture it
Choosing a ruler for each shelf: the tallest book on the shelf decides the markings, so short shelves get fine ones.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · The row with one large weight
  1. Its largest |w| is 3.8051 (weight 5).
  2. s = 3.8051 ÷ 127 = 0.02996: the row’s 255 levels are 0.02996 apart.
So: The largest weight sets the ruler for the whole row.
Example 2 · A row of smaller weights
  1. Row 7 of decoder_layers.1.cross_attn.W_o: largest |w| 1.3466, so s = 0.01060.
  2. One scale for the whole matrix would be 0.03536: 3.33× coarser for this row.
So: A scale per row keeps small rows precise.
qij=clamp(round(Wij/si),−127,127)
Each weight, counted in whole steps and stored as one byte.
In plain English
Divide every weight by its row’s step and round to the nearest whole number: how many steps it is. The clamp is a guard; with this s no weight goes past 127. That integer is all that is kept, one byte instead of four.
Picture it
Writing a price as a whole number of coins instead of an exact amount: a coin is the step, and the change is never more than half a coin.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Weight 4
  1. w ÷ s = 0.2502 ÷ 0.02996 = 8.3507.
  2. round → 8, stored in one byte.
So: The weight, counted in whole steps.
Example 2 · Weight 1, a negative one
  1. w ÷ s = (−1.1223) ÷ 0.02996 = −37.4582.
  2. round → −37; the largest, weight 5, becomes exactly 127.
So: Every weight of the row lands between −127 and 127.
Ŵij=qij·si,|Wij−Ŵij|≤si2
Back to float when the layer runs: never off by more than half a step.
In plain English
When the layer runs, QuantLinear multiplies the integers back by the scale. The true weight was between two levels and the nearer one was kept, so the error is at most half a step. The layer then computes as before, on very slightly rounded weights.
Picture it
A photo saved with fewer colours: from close up each pixel is slightly off, but the picture is the same picture.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Weight 4 back to float
  1. Ŵ = 8 × 0.02996 = 0.2397.
  2. |w − Ŵ| = |0.2502 − 0.2397| = 0.01051 ≤ s ÷ 2 = 0.01498.
So: Off by 0.70 of a half step — never more than one half step.
Example 2 · The worst in the whole tiny model
  1. Over all 4,984 weights, the largest |w − Ŵ| ÷ (s ÷ 2) is 0.998.
  2. Its logits for sequence B change by at most 0.0216.
So: Small errors in, small changes out.
bytes:4mn→mn+4m
An m × n matrix in 8 bits plus one float scale per row: about a quarter.
In plain English
Each weight goes from 4 bytes to 1, and each row adds one 4-byte scale; gains and biases stay float. With rows of 512 the scales cost under 1%, so the model shrinks almost 4×; with the tiny model’s rows of 8, much less.
Picture it
Packing a suitcase: each item folded to a quarter of its size, plus one label per row of items — the labels only matter when rows are short.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · A row of 512 weights
  1. As float32: 512 × 4 = 2,048 bytes.
  2. As int8: 512 × 1 + 4 (its scale) = 516 bytes: ÷ 3.97.
So: Wide rows make the scales almost free.
Example 2 · The tiny model and the real one
  1. Tiny: 21,148 → 8,624 bytes (÷ 2.45): rows of 8 pay 4 bytes per scale.
  2. Real: 130.2 → 32.9 MB (÷ 3.96).
So: Big models get close to the full 4×.

Rounding to the nearest step is the simplest choice. 4-bit methods such as GPTQ and AWQ choose the rounding using real activations, so the outputs, not the weights, stay closest.

DEEP DIVE 26
Does v3 learn better? The experiment
two tasks · seven variants · three seedsunchanged in v1.5
In one sentencev2.5, v3 and v3 without each part, three seeds each, at several learning rates — what each change really did here.
In plain words
Every v3 change was shown to help in large models. This page measures what each does here: v2.5 and v3 trained side by side on two tasks, then v3 with each part taken out, three seeds each — and the same models again with larger learning rates, because a bigger step can look like a better model.
Picture it
A cook wants to know which of several new tricks really improve a recipe. Tasting the new dish against the old one is not enough: if it is better, which trick did it?
So the cook makes the full new recipe, then the same recipe with one trick left out at a time — three batches each, because no two batches turn out quite alike. And since one trick also means a hotter oven, the old recipe gets a hotter oven too: otherwise the oven, not the trick, would take the credit.
Another way to see itOr a fair race: the same track, three heats each, and every runner allowed to pick their own pace — otherwise the fastest shoes win for the wrong reason.
Where the picture stops workingA test kitchen is only as good as its kitchen: this one is small (d_model 128, two layers, a few thousand sentences, a CPU), and the tricks were made for far bigger ones. With the same chance at a good learning rate, v3’s lead on unseen sentences disappears here; its parts are built for scale this experiment does not reach.

Real numbers, the reverse task:
  1. At the notebook’s learning rates: v3 96.5% exact on unseen reversals, v2.5 81.7%.
  2. v2.5 with a 10× larger learning rate: 96.5% exact.

The mathsReading the experimentthree seeds, what a part adds, and when two results cannot be told apart4 formulas · 8 worked examples
x‾=13(x0+x1+x2),range=[minsxs,maxsxs]
Each result is the mean of three runs, with the lowest and highest beside it.
In plain English
Training involves chance — the first random weights and the order of the batches — so every variant is trained three times, with seeds 0, 1 and 2. The page shows the mean, and the lowest and highest run in brackets.
Picture it
Timing a runner over three races, not one: the average and the spread tell you more than a single lucky day.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · v3 on unseen reversals
  1. Seeds 0, 1, 2: 97.4%, 96.4%, 95.6%.
  2. Mean (97.4 + 96.4 + 95.6) ÷ 3 = 96.5%, range 95.6–97.4%.
So: One number, and how far the runs spread.
Example 2 · v3 on longer sentences
  1. Seeds 0, 1, 2: 93.0%, 75.6%, 51.6%.
  2. Mean 73.4%, range 51.6–93.0%: 41.4 points between the best and the worst seed.
So: The same model, three seeds, very different results: small gaps here mean nothing.
Δpart=x‾_v3−x‾_v3withoutthepart
What a part adds inside v3: positive means it helped.
In plain English
Taking one part out of v3 and retraining isolates that part. The difference of the two means is what the part adds; it can be negative when a part does not suit the task.
Picture it
Taking one ingredient out of a recipe and tasting again: the difference is that ingredient’s share.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · What grouped-query attention adds
  1. v3 96.5%, v3 without GQA 94.7% (means).
  2. Δ = 96.5 − 94.7 = +1.8 points.
So: Taking the part out shows what it does inside v3.
Example 2 · What the experts add
  1. v3 96.5%, v3 without the experts 97.6%.
  2. Δ = 96.5 − 97.6 = −1.1 points: negative, v3 did better without them.
So: A part can cost accuracy on a task that does not need it.
[a,b]and[c,d]overlap⇔c≤banda≤d
If the two ranges overlap, three seeds cannot tell the variants apart.
In plain English
Two ranges overlap when neither lies wholly above the other. Then the order of the means could flip with other seeds, so the page calls it no clear difference.
Picture it
Two runners whose best and worst times overlap: who is faster is not settled by three races.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · GQA: apart
  1. v3 [95.6, 97.4], without GQA [94.6, 94.8].
  2. 94.6 ≤ 97.4 and 95.6 ≤ 94.8? no: no overlap.
So: No overlap: three seeds agree on the direction.
Example 2 · The experts: overlapping
  1. v3 [95.6, 97.4], without the experts [97.2, 98.4].
  2. 97.2 ≤ 97.4 and 95.6 ≤ 98.4? yes: they overlap.
So: Overlapping ranges: the difference may be luck.

The share of sentences written exactly right, every word.
In plain English
A sentence counts only if every word is right and in the right place, so exact match is strict; BLEU gives partial credit.
Picture it
A spelling test marked by whole sentences: one slip, no mark.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · v3, seed 0, unseen reversals
  1. 487 of the 500 written answers equal the reference exactly.
  2. 487 ÷ 500 = 97.4%.
So: One wrong word makes a whole sentence wrong.
Example 2 · The same model on longer sentences
  1. 465 of 500 sentences of 13–16 words written exactly right.
  2. 465 ÷ 500 = 93.0%.
So: Longer than anything it trained on: the hardest test here.

DEEP DIVE 27
AdamW against Muon
per number or per direction · step by step · the costunchanged in v1.5
In one sentenceAdamW against Muon on the same gradient, step by step: per number or per direction, and what each costs.
In plain words
v3 trains with two optimizers. AdamW, as in v2.5, divides each number’s step by that number’s own typical size; Muon, new in v3, treats a weight matrix as one map and gives every one of its directions a step of the same size. This page runs both on a task small enough to draw, step by step, then weighs what each costs in the real model.
Picture it
A sound engineer mixes a song on a desk of sliders. After each take the producer says what is off — mostly that the drums are too loud, only a little that the harmony is too quiet.
One engineer moves every slider by about the same small amount, each in the direction the note says: every slider is judged on its own. Another listens for the parts of the song — the beat, the harmony — and corrects each part by the same amount, whatever combination of sliders that takes. The first is AdamW; the second is Muon.
Another way to see itOr two teachers marking an essay: one corrects every word a little; the other corrects every argument by the same amount, so the weak argument gets as much attention as the strong one.
Where the picture stops workingAn engineer who corrects every part by the same amount also overcorrects the parts that were nearly right: Muon’s loss climbed back to 3.49 at step 10. Muon is not free either: one optimizer step took 406 ms against AdamW’s 31 ms on this CPU. And the desk has knobs that are not sliders of a matrix — the embedding table, the gains — which stay with AdamW.
Who is who — the picture, then the code
in the picturein the notebook
the slidersthe numbers of one weight matrix
the producer’s note after a takethe gradient: strengths 8.71 and 0.093 along its two directions
every slider moved about the same amountAdamW: each number divided by its own typical size — its first step had strengths 2 and 0
every part of the song corrected alikeMuon: every direction about the same strength — 0.74 and 0.70
the quiet harmony, finally fixedthe weak direction: its error halved at step 12 with AdamW, step 4 with Muon

What v3 changes here — and why it helps
  • Muon for the weight matrices in the layers — every direction of an update moves about the same amount
  • AdamW for the embedding table, the routers, the gains and the biases — as in v2.5, for every number Muon cannot take
A worked example, with this page’s real numbers
Real numbers:
  1. In v3, Muon trains 24,252,416 numbers in 76 matrices; AdamW trains 8,291,567.
  2. The same gradient (strengths 8.71 and 0.093): AdamW’s first step has strengths 2 and 0, Muon’s 0.74 and 0.70.
  3. The race, each at its best learning rate: loss below 0.1 at step 15 (AdamW) and 5 (Muon); after 60 steps 8.6 × 10⁻⁴ and 7.0 × 10⁻⁴.
  4. The real model: optimizer memory 65,087,966 against 40,835,550 numbers; one optimizer step 31 ms against 406 ms on this CPU.
Muon reaches the directions a gradient barely mentions and keeps less state; AdamW is cheaper, steadier and works on any shape — v3 uses each where it fits.

The mathsAdamW against Muonthe same gradient, two steps: every number by its own size, or every direction alike4 formulas · 8 worked examples
mt=β1mt−1+(1−β1)gt,vt=β2vt−1+(1−β2)gt2
AdamW keeps two running means per number: of the gradient and of its square.
In plain English
Both means start at 0 and move a little toward each new gradient: m by 10%, v by 2%. So m says where this number’s gradient has been pointing lately, and √v how big it usually is — one pair for every single weight.
Picture it
A diary per player of how they have been doing and how big their swings usually are: two notes for each.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Step 1, number [0, 0]
  1. g = −4.8434; m and v start at 0.
  2. m = 0.1 × (−4.8434) = −0.4843,  v = 0.02 × (−4.8434)² = 0.4692.
So: Both start at 0, so step 1 sees only this gradient.
Example 2 · Step 2, the same number
  1. g = 5.7872.
  2. m = 0.9 × (−0.4843) + 0.1 × 5.7872 = 0.1428,  v = 0.98 × 0.4692 + 0.02 × 5.7872² = 1.1296.
So: v keeps step 1’s large value: √v remembers how loud this number was.
W←W(1−ηλ)−ηm̂_tv̂_t+ε
AdamW’s step: every number divided by its own typical size.
In plain English
Dividing m by √v makes every number’s step about η, however loud its gradient. The hats undo the start at 0 (on step 1, m̂ = g and v̂ = g², so the update is sign(g)). It evens out the numbers, not the directions: four numbers leaning the same way give one direction.
Picture it
Every slider on a mixing desk moved by about the same amount: fair to each slider, blind to the song’s parts.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Step 1: sign(g)
  1. m̂ = m ÷ (1 − 0.9) = −4.8434 = g, and v̂ = v ÷ (1 − 0.98) = 23.4588 = g².
  2. m̂ ÷ √v̂ = g ÷ |g| = −1; all four of the gradient’s numbers are negative, so all four are −1.
So: One step of η per number, all one way: strengths 2 and 0.
Example 2 · Step 2, number [0, 0]
  1. m̂ = 0.1428 ÷ (1 − 0.9²) = 0.7516,  v̂ = 1.1296 ÷ (1 − 0.98²) = 28.5260.
  2. update = 0.7516 ÷ (√28.5260 + 10⁻⁹) = 0.1407.
So: Smaller than 1: the gradient changed its mind, and v remembers step 1.
W←W(1−ηλ)−η·NS5(G),NS5(USVT)≈UVT
Muon’s step: the gradient’s directions, every strength about 1.
In plain English
Muon smooths the gradient, then Newton–Schulz keeps its directions U and V and sets every strength near 1. η alone sets how far each direction moves — the weak ones as far as the strong.
Picture it
Every part of the song — beat, harmony — corrected by the same amount: fair to each part, whatever sliders it takes.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Step 1, the strengths
  1. G ÷ ‖G‖ has strengths 0.9999 and 0.0107.
  2. After 5 Newton–Schulz steps: 0.7396 and 0.6965.
So: The weak direction grew ×65: both now about the same.
Example 2 · Step 1, one weight
  1. η = 0.10 (the warm-up’s first step), λ = 0.01, W[0, 0] = 0.
  2. W = 0 × (1 − 0.10 × 0.01) − 0.10 × (−0.6685) = 0.0669.
So: The step’s size is set by η, not by how loud the gradient was.
ratio=σ1(Δ)σ2(Δ)
How unevenly a step Δ moves a matrix’s two directions: 1 means alike.
In plain English
The ratio of a step’s two strengths. The first gradient of the task on this page has a ratio of 94; AdamW’s steps follow that stretch in part, Muon’s stay near 1.
Picture it
A ratio of 1 is a round ball; a large one a cigar: how lopsided the step is.
Worked examples — with numbers
Example 1 · Step 1
  1. The gradient: 8.710 ÷ 0.0930 = 94.
  2. AdamW: 2 ÷ 0 — one direction only.  Muon: 0.7396 ÷ 0.6965 = 1.062.
So: Muon’s step is nearly round from the very first step.
Example 2 · All 60 steps
  1. The median ratio from step 2 on: AdamW 7.3, Muon 1.09.
So: AdamW follows the gradient’s stretch in part; Muon stays near 1.

GLOSSARY
Glossary
49 words, each in a sentence or twounchanged in v1.5
Every word the introductions mark with a dotted line, in alphabetical order. Tap or hover over a marked word anywhere on the page for the same explanation.
attentionEach word gathering information from other words, with shares (weights) that add up to 100%.
batchThe examples worked on together in one training step.
beam searchKeeping several candidate answers at once, extending each, and returning the best-scoring one.
BLEUA score from 0 to 100 for how many of the answer’s word runs also appear in the reference answer.
BPEByte-pair encoding: a tokenizer that builds its tokens by gluing together, again and again, the pair of neighbouring pieces seen most often.
checkpointThe parameters saved to a file at some point in training.
decoderThe half of the model that writes the answer, one token at a time.
EMAExponential moving average: a copy of the weights that follows training slowly, smoothing its jitter.
embeddingThe table that turns each token id into its vector. Its numbers are learned.
encoderThe half of the model that reads the input sentence.
epochOne pass over all the training examples.
exact match1 if the answer is exactly the reference, 0 otherwise — no partial credit.
feed-forwardThe “think” move: each word’s vector goes through a small network on its own.
gradientFor every parameter: which way, and how much, to nudge it to lower the loss.
greedyAlways writing the single most likely token.
headOne of several attentions running side by side in a layer; here 4 heads of 128 numbers each.
idA token’s number in the vocabulary. From the tokenizer on, the model sees only these numbers.
keyWhat a word advertises about itself, to be matched against queries.
KV cacheThe keys and values of the tokens already written, kept so each new step only works on the newest token.
layerOne round of the model’s moves — look around, then think. Layers are stacked.
learning rateHow big each nudge is.
logitA token’s raw score before softmax: higher means more likely.
lossHow surprised the model was by the right answer. Training makes it smaller.
maskA yes/no table saying which words may look at which: padding and future words are hidden.
normalisationRescaling a vector to a steady size, so no layer is flooded by big numbers or starved by tiny ones.
overfittingLearning the training examples by heart instead of the pattern behind them.
paddingFiller tokens (<PAD>) that make short sentences as long as the longest one in a batch.
parameterOne number the model learns. This model has 22,979,823 of them.
positionWhere a token sits in its sentence: 0, 1, 2, …
probabilityA share between 0 and 1 — 0% to 100%.
queryWhat a word is looking for. It is compared with every other word’s key.
repetition penaltyPushing down the score of tokens already written, so the model repeats itself less.
residualThe shortcut: each move’s result is ADDED to what went in, instead of replacing it.
RMSNormA normalisation that divides a vector by its root mean square (its typical size) and scales it.
RoPERotary position embedding: pairs of numbers are turned by an angle that grows with the token’s position.
samplingDrawing the next token at random, in proportion to its probability.
softmaxTurns any list of scores into probabilities that are all positive and add up to 1.
SwiGLUA feed-forward with a gate: one copy of the input decides, unit by unit, how much of the other passes.
temperatureA knob applied before drawing: below 1 it sharpens the probabilities, above 1 it flattens them.
tokenA piece of a word that the model reads or writes. “sofa” is two tokens here: “sof” and “a_”.
tokenizerThe part that cuts text into tokens and glues tokens back into text.
top-kSampling only among the k most likely tokens.
top-pSampling only among the most likely tokens that together reach probability p.
trainingShowing the model examples with their answers and nudging its parameters after each.
validationChecking the model on examples kept aside, to see if it learned the pattern rather than the examples.
valueWhat a word hands over when a query matches its key.
vectorA list of numbers. Every token becomes a vector of 512 numbers.
vocabularyThe full list of tokens the model knows — 16,111 in this notebook.
weight decayPulling weights a little toward 0 at every step, to keep them from growing needlessly large.

attentionEach word gathering information from other words, with shares (weights) that add up to 100%.
batchThe examples worked on together in one training step.
beam searchKeeping several candidate answers at once, extending each, and returning the best-scoring one.
BLEUA score from 0 to 100 for how many of the answer’s word runs also appear in the reference answer.
BPEByte-pair encoding: a tokenizer that builds its tokens by gluing together, again and again, the pair of neighbouring pieces seen most often.
checkpointThe parameters saved to a file at some point in training.
decoderThe half of the model that writes the answer, one token at a time.
EMAExponential moving average: a copy of the weights that follows training slowly, smoothing its jitter.
embeddingThe table that turns each token id into its vector. Its numbers are learned.
encoderThe half of the model that reads the input sentence.
epochOne pass over all the training examples.
exact match1 if the answer is exactly the reference, 0 otherwise — no partial credit.
expert newOne of the small feed-forwards of a mixture of experts.
feed-forwardThe “think” move: each word’s vector goes through a small network on its own.
FlashAttention newA way of computing attention a block at a time that never holds the whole table of scores — the same result, far less memory. It is built into PyTorch: F.scaled_dot_product_attention uses it by itself, only on a recent NVIDIA GPU, in fp16 or bf16, with no mask tensor (deep dive 20). This notebook does not implement it.
gradientFor every parameter: which way, and how much, to nudge it to lower the loss.
greedyAlways writing the single most likely token.
grouped-query attention newAttention in which several query heads share one key/value head, so the KV cache holds fewer numbers.
headOne of several attentions running side by side in a layer; here 4 heads of 128 numbers each.
idA token’s number in the vocabulary. From the tokenizer on, the model sees only these numbers.
int8 newAn 8-bit whole number, from −128 to 127: a quarter of the 32 bits of a float.
keyWhat a word advertises about itself, to be matched against queries.
KV cacheThe keys and values of the tokens already written, kept so each new step only works on the newest token.
layerOne round of the model’s moves — look around, then think. Layers are stacked.
learning rateHow big each nudge is.
logitA token’s raw score before softmax: higher means more likely.
lossHow surprised the model was by the right answer. Training makes it smaller.
maskA yes/no table saying which words may look at which: padding and future words are hidden.
mixture of experts newSeveral small feed-forwards (experts) and a router that sends each token to a few of them.
momentum newA running average of past gradients, so that one noisy batch cannot swing the step much.
multi-query attention newAttention in which all query heads share a single key/value head.
multi-token prediction newTraining an extra head to guess the token after next, not only the next one.
Muon newAn optimizer that turns each weight matrix’s update into one that moves every direction by the same amount.
Newton–Schulz newA few matrix products that bring every singular value of a matrix close to 1 without turning any of its directions.
normalisationRescaling a vector to a steady size, so no layer is flooded by big numbers or starved by tiny ones.
online softmax newSoftmax computed piece by piece, keeping a running largest score and a running sum, rescaled whenever a larger score turns up.
optimizer newThe part of training that turns the gradients into changes of the weights — AdamW, Muon.
overfittingLearning the training examples by heart instead of the pattern behind them.
paddingFiller tokens (<PAD>) that make short sentences as long as the longest one in a batch.
parameterOne number the model learns. This model has 22,979,823 of them.
positionWhere a token sits in its sentence: 0, 1, 2, …
probabilityA share between 0 and 1 — 0% to 100%.
QK-Norm newBringing every head’s query and key to the same size before they are compared, so a score cannot grow just because the vectors grew.
quantization newStoring numbers with fewer bits: here each weight as one of 255 whole numbers times a scale per row.
queryWhat a word is looking for. It is compared with every other word’s key.
repetition penaltyPushing down the score of tokens already written, so the model repeats itself less.
residualThe shortcut: each move’s result is ADDED to what went in, instead of replacing it.
RMSNormA normalisation that divides a vector by its root mean square (its typical size) and scales it.
RoPERotary position embedding: pairs of numbers are turned by an angle that grows with the token’s position.
router newA tiny layer that scores the experts for each token and picks the best few.
samplingDrawing the next token at random, in proportion to its probability.
singular value newHow strongly a matrix stretches along one of its main directions.
soft cap newcap × tanh(score / cap): small scores pass almost unchanged, none can go past the cap.
softmaxTurns any list of scores into probabilities that are all positive and add up to 1.
speculative decoding newWriting faster by checking a cheap guess of the next token in the same pass as the token before it; a right guess gives two tokens per pass.
SwiGLUA feed-forward with a gate: one copy of the input decides, unit by unit, how much of the other passes.
temperatureA knob applied before drawing: below 1 it sharpens the probabilities, above 1 it flattens them.
tokenA piece of a word that the model reads or writes. “sofa” is two tokens here: “sof” and “a_”.
tokenizerThe part that cuts text into tokens and glues tokens back into text.
top-kSampling only among the k most likely tokens.
top-pSampling only among the most likely tokens that together reach probability p.
trainingShowing the model examples with their answers and nudging its parameters after each.
validationChecking the model on examples kept aside, to see if it learned the pattern rather than the examples.
valueWhat a word hands over when a query matches its key.
vectorA list of numbers. Every token becomes a vector of 512 numbers.
vocabularyThe full list of tokens the model knows — 16,111 in this notebook.

1# ============================================================2# Masks  (True = may attend)3# ============================================================45def make_padding_mask(seq: torch.Tensor, pad_idx: int = 0) -> torch.Tensor:6    return (seq != pad_idx).unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(2)            # (B, 1, 1, L)78def make_causal_mask(size: int, device=None) -> torch.Tensor:9    return torch.tril(torch.ones(size, size, device=device, dtype=torch.bool))[None, None]1011def make_tgt_mask(tgt: torch.Tensor, pad_idx: int = 0) -> torch.Tensor:12    return make_padding_mask(tgt, pad_idx) & make_causal_mask(tgt.size(1), tgt.device)131415# ============================================================16# Model17# ============================================================1819class RMSNorm(nn.Module):20    """[v2.5] Replaces nn.LayerNorm. Divides each vector by its root mean square21    and multiplies by a learned gain: no mean to subtract and no bias to add, so fewer22    operations for the same job (keeping every vector at a steady size)."""23    def __init__(self, d_model: int, eps: float = 1e-6):24        super().__init__()25        self.eps = eps26        self.weight = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(d_model))2728    def forward(self, x):29        x32 = x.float()                                   # the statistics in float32, even under AMP30        rms = x32.pow(2).mean(-1, keepdim=True).add(self.eps).rsqrt()31        return (x32 * rms).type_as(x) * self.weight323334def rope_tables(head_dim: int, max_len: int, base: float = 10000.0):35    """[v2.5] Rotary position embedding (RoPE) replaces the table v2 ADDED to the input.36    The d_k numbers of a head are read as d_k / 2 pairs, and pair i of the token at37    position p is turned by the angle p * base ** (-2i / d_k): the first pair turns fast,38    the last one very slowly. Returns cos and sin of every angle, (max_len, d_k // 2) each."""39    speed = base ** (-torch.arange(0, head_dim, 2, dtype=torch.float) / head_dim)40    angle = torch.outer(torch.arange(max_len, dtype=torch.float), speed)41    return angle.cos(), angle.sin()424344def apply_rope(x, cos, sin):45    """[v2.5] Turn every pair (x[..., 2i], x[..., 2i+1]) of x (B, H, L, d_k) by its angle;46    cos, sin: (L, d_k // 2) for the L positions x holds. Turning Q and K this way makes47    q . k depend on how far apart two tokens are, not on where they are."""48    x1, x2 = x[..., 0::2].float(), x[..., 1::2].float()49    turned = torch.stack([x1 * cos - x2 * sin, x1 * sin + x2 * cos], dim=-1)50    return turned.flatten(-2).type_as(x)5152class MultiHeadAttention(nn.Module):    def __init__(self, d_model: int, num_heads: int, dropout: float = 0.1):        super().__init__()        assert d_model % num_heads == 0, "d_model must be divisible by num_heads"        self.d_model, self.num_heads, self.d_k = d_model, num_heads, d_model // num_heads        self.W_q = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model)        self.W_k = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model)        self.W_v = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model)        self.W_o = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model)        self.dropout_p = dropout        self.attn_dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout)    def _split(self, x):  # 1class BPETokenizer:2    """3    Byte-Pair-Encoding tokenizer.45    [v2] vs. v1.5:6      * Incremental training: after each merge only the words that contain the merged7        pair are updated (instead of re-scanning all 50k words), and the most frequent8        pair is taken from a heap.  ~40 min -> well under a minute for 16k merges.9      * Rank-based encoding (like GPT-2): merges are applied by priority, not by looping10        over all 16k merges for every word.11      * Vocabulary = base characters + every merge result, so unseen words can always be12        spelled out from smaller pieces instead of becoming <UNK>.13      * save() / load() to JSON, so the tokenizer is trained once, not on every run.14    """15    EOW = "</w>"1617    def __init__(self, num_merges: int = 16000):18        self.num_merges = num_merges19        self.merges = []20        self.merge_ranks = {}21        self.token_to_id, self.id_to_token = {}, {}22        self.PAD, self.SOS, self.EOS, self.UNK = "<PAD>", "<SOS>", "<EOS>", "<UNK>"23        self._cache = {}2425    # ---------- helpers ----------26    def _word_to_symbols(self, word):27        return list(word[:-1]) + [word[-1] + self.EOW]2829    @staticmethod30    def _merge_pair(symbols, pair):31        merged, i = [], 032        while i < len(symbols):33            if i < len(symbols) - 1 and symbols[i] == pair[0] and symbols[i + 1] == pair[1]:34                merged.append(symbols[i] + symbols[i + 1])35                i += 236            else:37                merged.append(symbols[i])38                i += 139        return merged4041    @staticmethod42    def zipf_word_freqs(word_list_text, scale=1_000_000):43        """44        [v2] Your vocabulary is ordered from most to least common ("the", "of", "and", ...).45        A plain word list gives every word a count of 1, so BPE would treat "the" the same46        as "empyema". Zipf's law says frequency ~ 1 / rank, so we turn the rank into an47        estimated count. BPE then spends its merges on pieces of common words first,48        just as it would when trained on real text.49        """50        freqs = Counter()51        for rank, word in enumerate(word_list_text.lower().split(), start=1):52            freqs[word] += max(1, round(scale / rank))53        return freqs5455    # ---------- training ----------56    def train(self, corpus=None, word_freqs=None, verbose=True):57        if word_freqs is None:58            word_freqs = Counter(w for text in corpus for w in text.lower().split())59        word_freqs = {w: f for w, f in word_freqs.items() if w}6061        words = [self._word_to_symbols(w) for w in word_freqs]62        freqs = list(word_freqs.values())63        base_symbols = {s for syms in words for s in syms}6465        pair_counts = Counter()66        where = defaultdict(set)                 # pair -> indices of words containing it67        for wi, syms in enumerate(words):68            for pair in zip(syms, syms[1:]):69                pair_counts[pair] += freqs[wi]70                where[pair].add(wi)7172        heap = [(-c, p) for p, c in pair_counts.items()]73        heapq.heapify(heap)7475        start = time.time()76        self.merges = []77        while len(self.merges) < self.num_merges and heap:78            neg_count, best = heapq.heappop(heap)79            count = pair_counts.get(best, 0)80            if count != -neg_count:              # stale heap entry -> skip81                continue82            if count < 2:83                break84            self.merges.append(best)8586            changed = set()87            for wi in list(where.pop(best, ())):88                syms = words[wi]89                new = self._merge_pair(syms, best)90                if len(new) == len(syms):         # stale index: pair no longer in word91                    continue92                f = freqs[wi]93                for pair in zip(syms, syms[1:]):94                    pair_counts[pair] -= f95                    changed.add(pair)96                for pair in zip(new, new[1:]):97                    pair_counts[pair] += f98                    where[pair].add(wi)99                    changed.add(pair)100                words[wi] = new101102            pair_counts.pop(best, None)103            for pair in changed:104                c = pair_counts.get(pair, 0)105                if c > 0:106                    heapq.heappush(heap, (-c, pair))107                else:108                    pair_counts.pop(pair, None)109110            if verbose and len(self.merges) % 2000 == 0:111                print(f"  {len(self.merges):>6} merges  ({time.time() - start:.1f}s)")112113        vocab = [self.PAD, self.SOS, self.EOS, self.UNK] + sorted(base_symbols)114        seen = set(vocab)115        for a, b in self.merges:116            if a + b not in seen:117                vocab.append(a + b)118                seen.add(a + b)119        self._build(vocab)120        if verbose:121            print(f"Trained {len(self.merges)} merges -> {self.vocab_size} tokens "122                  f"in {time.time() - start:.1f}s")123124    def _build(self, vocab):125        self.token_to_id = {t: i for i, t in enumerate(vocab)}126        self.id_to_token = {i: t for t, i in self.token_to_id.items()}127        self.merge_ranks = {tuple(p): r for r, p in enumerate(self.merges)}128        self._cache = {}129130    # ---------- save / load ----------131    def save(self, path):132        vocab = [self.id_to_token[i] for i in range(len(self.id_to_token))]133        with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:134            json.dump({"merges": [list(p) for p in self.merges], "vocab": vocab}, f)135136    def state_dict(self):137        vocab = [self.id_to_token[i] for i in range(len(self.id_to_token))]138        return {"merges": [list(p) for p in self.merges], "vocab": vocab}139140    @classmethod141    def from_state_dict(cls, state):142        tok = cls(num_merges=len(state["merges"]))143        tok.merges = [tuple(p) for p in state["merges"]]144        tok._build(state["vocab"])145        return tok146147    @classmethod148    def load(cls, path):149        with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:150            return cls.from_state_dict(json.load(f))151152    # 1# Your sentence pairs. 1# [v2] Dataset + DataLoader with dynamic padding (each batch is padded only to its2# own longest sentence) and truncation to MAX_SEQ_LEN.3class Seq2SeqDataset(Dataset):4    def __init__(self, pairs, tokenizer, max_len=MAX_SEQ_LEN):5        self.items = []6        for s, t in pairs:7            src_ids = tokenizer.encode(s, add_special_tokens=False)[:max_len]8            tgt_ids = tokenizer.encode(t, add_special_tokens=True)9            if len(tgt_ids) > max_len:                       # keep <EOS> at the end10                tgt_ids = tgt_ids[:max_len - 1] + [tokenizer.eos_id]11            self.items.append((torch.tensor(src_ids), torch.tensor(tgt_ids)))1213    def __len__(self):14        return len(self.items)1516    def __getitem__(self, i):17        return self.items[i]1819def collate(batch):20    srcs, tgts = zip(*batch)21    return (pad_sequence(srcs, batch_first=True, padding_value=PAD),22            pad_sequence(tgts, batch_first=True, padding_value=PAD))2324train_loader = DataLoader(Seq2SeqDataset(train_pairs, tokenizer),25                          batch_size=min(BATCH_SIZE, len(train_pairs)),26                          shuffle=True, collate_fn=collate)27val_loader = DataLoader(Seq2SeqDataset(val_pairs, tokenizer),28                        batch_size=min(BATCH_SIZE, len(val_pairs)),29                        shuffle=False, collate_fn=collate)

1class BPETokenizer:2    """3    Byte-Pair-Encoding tokenizer.45    [v2] vs. v1.5:6      * Incremental training: after each merge only the words that contain the merged7        pair are updated (instead of re-scanning all 50k words), and the most frequent8        pair is taken from a heap.  ~40 min -> well under a minute for 16k merges.9      * Rank-based encoding (like GPT-2): merges are applied by priority, not by looping10        over all 16k merges for every word.11      * Vocabulary = base characters + every merge result, so unseen words can always be12        spelled out from smaller pieces instead of becoming <UNK>.13      * save() / load() to JSON, so the tokenizer is trained once, not on every run.14    """15    EOW = "</w>"1617    def __init__(self, num_merges: int = 16000):18        self.num_merges = num_merges19        self.merges = []20        self.merge_ranks = {}21        self.token_to_id, self.id_to_token = {}, {}22        self.PAD, self.SOS, self.EOS, self.UNK = "<PAD>", "<SOS>", "<EOS>", "<UNK>"23        self._cache = {}2425    # ---------- helpers ----------26    def _word_to_symbols(self, word):27        return list(word[:-1]) + [word[-1] + self.EOW]2829    @staticmethod30    def _merge_pair(symbols, pair):31        merged, i = [], 032        while i < len(symbols):33            if i < len(symbols) - 1 and symbols[i] == pair[0] and symbols[i + 1] == pair[1]:34                merged.append(symbols[i] + symbols[i + 1])35                i += 236            else:37                merged.append(symbols[i])38                i += 139        return merged4041    @staticmethod42    def zipf_word_freqs(word_list_text, scale=1_000_000):43        """44        [v2] Your vocabulary is ordered from most to least common ("the", "of", "and", ...).45        A plain word list gives every word a count of 1, so BPE would treat "the" the same46        as "empyema". Zipf's law says frequency ~ 1 / rank, so we turn the rank into an47        estimated count. BPE then spends its merges on pieces of common words first,48        just as it would when trained on real text.49        """50        freqs = Counter()51        for rank, word in enumerate(word_list_text.lower().split(), start=1):52            freqs[word] += max(1, round(scale / rank))53        return freqs5455    # stale heap entry -> skip81                continue82            if count < 2:83                break84            self.merges.append(best)8586            changed = set()87            for wi in list(where.pop(best, ())):88                syms = words[wi]89                new = self._merge_pair(syms, best)90                if len(new) == len(syms):         # ---------- save / load ----------131    def save(self, path):132        vocab = [self.id_to_token[i] for i in range(len(self.id_to_token))]133        with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:134            json.dump({"merges": [list(p) for p in self.merges], "vocab": vocab}, f)135136    def state_dict(self):137        vocab = [self.id_to_token[i] for i in range(len(self.id_to_token))]138        return {"merges": [list(p) for p in self.merges], "vocab": vocab}139140    @classmethod141    def from_state_dict(cls, state):142        tok = cls(num_merges=len(state["merges"]))143        tok.merges = [tuple(p) for p in state["merges"]]144        tok._build(state["vocab"])145        return tok146147    @classmethod148    def load(cls, path):149        with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:150            return cls.from_state_dict(json.load(f))151152    # How the numbers were made. The token ids come from running the notebook's own
BPETokenizer to completion (13,076 merges, vocabulary 12,917). Shapes, masks,
positional encodings, softmax rows, ReLU, LayerNorm statistics, dropout scaling and the
cross-entropy at initialisation are computed exactly, in pure Python. The learned parameters are
seeded draws from the distributions init_weights and PyTorch's own
defaults produce, so every diagram is a genuine forward pass of a freshly initialised model of
exactly this shape, and none of them claims to come from a trained checkpoint. Each
.svg carries its own light and dark palette, so the plates follow your
theme here and stand alone anywhere else.




How the numbers were made. The tokenizer is re-run here in pure Python — 15 merges over
11 distinct words, instant where v1's 13,076-merge run took minutes — so the vocabulary, the merge
list and every token id on these pages are the real ones. Shapes, the learning-rate schedule, the
label-smoothing floor and every parameter count are computed exactly, and the parameter total is
checked against the 14,728,218 the notebook itself prints on its first
line of output. Untrained activations are seeded draws from the notebook's own initialisers. The
one set of trained numbers — the loss curve, the token accuracy and the generated text on
page 8 — is the notebook's own printed output, copied verbatim and labelled as such.




How the numbers were made. The tokenizer is the notebook’s own
BPETokenizer, compiled from cell 3 and trained here on cell 0’s word
list with cell 5’s Zipf counts — 16,000 merges, 16,111 tokens, in 2.6 seconds — so every
token id on these pages is the real one. The notebook has never been run and holds no output, so
every weight is a seeded draw from the notebook’s own initialisers: these are the numbers of an
untrained v2 model, computed exactly in pure Python, and the parameter total (22,979,823) is checked
against the architecture. Generation is traced for real on that untrained model — the KV cache,
_block_special, the top-k cut, the beams and their re-ordered caches
— which is why its words repeat: an untrained model has nothing to say yet. The one thing that
cannot be reproduced without PyTorch is torch.multinomial’s random
draw; the sampling frames use a seeded Python draw from exactly the same distribution, and say
so.




How the numbers were made. Two kinds, always labelled on the pages. Trained numbers come
from running the v2.5 notebook here, cell by cell, with PyTorch on the CPU and the notebook’s own
seeds: its printed lines, the loss of every epoch, the checkpoint it kept and the attention it learned.
Untrained numbers are a pure-Python trace of the same code on v2’s own seeded starting weights, so
a v2 page and a v2.5 page differ only by what the code does — and the trace was checked against the
notebook’s own PyTorch model: every logit agrees to 1.3e-06. Every v2.5 change was also tested on the
notebook’s code (check25.py), and the notebook file is only ever read.




How the numbers were made. The v3 notebook is written by nb3.py from the v2.5 notebook — a
list of exact replacements, each tagged [NEW v3] — and run here, cell by
cell, with PyTorch on the CPU and its own seeds (run3.json). Every change is tested on the notebook’s
own code by check3.py; the walkthroughs use the same classes built tiny and trained on five sentences
(toy3.py); the experiment trains v2.5, v3 and v3 without each of its parts on thousands of sentences,
three seeds each (experiment3.py). Your notebooks are only ever read.
